Argentina beef consumption has slipped to 46.3 kilos per person a year, the lowest reading in more than two decades. That figure covers the 12 months to July 2026 and comes from CICCRA, the country’s meat industry chamber.

Argentines are now eating 4.8 kilos less beef each than they did a year ago.

The Number Behind the Argentina Beef Consumption Slide

CICCRA publishes a rolling 12-month average, so the series smooths out seasonal noise. Its July 2026 reading came in at 46.3 kilos per person, against 51.1 kilos a year earlier.

That is a 9.4% drop, and the chamber called it a historic low. Argentina beef consumption has not been this thin since the early 2000s.

The wider supply picture is starker still. Between January and July, the domestic market absorbed 1.202 million tonnes of beef.

About 12% less than in the same stretch of 2025.

Why the Fall Happened So Fast

Price did most of the work. Beef in the Buenos Aires area cost around 52% more in July 2026 than in July 2025.

According to the IPCVA beef promotion institute. Butcher shops pushed hardest, at 56.6% year on year, while supermarkets rose 43.3%.

Prices did steady over four months, yet the damage to household budgets was already done. Wages have been recovering, but not fast enough to close that gap.

Because beef climbed further than almost anything else in the basket, families simply bought less of it.

Chicken Overtakes Beef on the National Plate

For a country built on the asado, this is the headline shift. Chicken consumption now sits near 49 to 50 kilos per person a year, according to figures from CEPA and industry data.

That puts poultry ahead of beef for the first time in the statistical record. Pork has climbed too, from about 6 kilos per person twenty years ago to roughly 19 kilos today.

The reason is arithmetic, not taste. Chicken prices rose about 30% over the year, barely half the pace of beef, so shoppers switched.

Total meat consumption has held up better than beef alone. Argentines still eat plenty of protein overall, so the change is about which animal, not how much.

Fewer Cattle, Less Meat

Supply tightened as well. Argentina slaughtered 7.09 million head of cattle between January and July 2026, down 9.8% from a year earlier.

Beef output over the same seven months reached 1.689 million tonnes, a 6.8% decline. Producers have been holding back females to rebuild herds, which trims short-term supply.

Carcass weights did rise, softening the blow. Even so, less meat reached the counter while demand for it was already sagging.

Exports Take a Bigger Slice

A shrinking herd is now feeding a growing export book. Shipments between January and July hit 487,200 tonnes carcass equivalent, up 8.8% year on year.

That means roughly 30% of production went abroad, against about a quarter a year earlier. In the first half alone, Argentina sold 280,140 tonnes for about US$2.26 billion.

Analysts expect full-year beef exports above US$3 billion. Since foreign buyers pay in dollars, packers naturally chase them first.

Cheaper Beef Starts Arriving From Brazil

Something unusual is happening at the same time. Argentina, a byword for beef, is importing more of it, mostly from Brazil.

Purchases of Brazilian beef reached about 13,700 tonnes in the first half, up 122% by volume. That is still only around 1.3% of domestic consumption, so the shift is a trend rather than a takeover.

Industry voices describe a slow move toward the Uruguayan model. In short, import cheaper cuts for the home market and send premium local beef overseas.

Lamb Exports Jump 34%

Away from the beef counter, one Argentine meat is booming. Sheep meat exports rose 34% by volume in the first half of 2026, the Agriculture Secretariat reported in mid-August.

Shipments totalled 4,669,757 kilos of product weight, against 3,497,311 kilos a year earlier. Export earnings climbed 46%, and average value per tonne rose 10%.

The European Union remains the main buyer, with Middle Eastern markets growing. Argentina now has 44 open destinations for sheep meat, most of it raised in Patagonia.

Sheep farming remains small next to cattle, yet the growth matters for southern provinces. Santa Cruz and Chubut supply much of the flock behind those shipments.

Panama Opens to Argentine Citrus

The other piece of good news came from Central America. Panama agreed phytosanitary terms for four fresh Argentine citrus fruits in August 2026.

The list covers lemons, mandarins, oranges and grapefruit. Argentina’s Agriculture Secretariat handled the deal through SENASA, its food safety agency, with Panama’s agriculture ministry MIDA.

Panama published the rules as resolutions DNSV 427 to 430 of 2026. Tucumán, the world’s largest lemon producer, stands to gain most, although neither government published a volume target.

What This Means for Visitors and Residents

If you are eating out in Buenos Aires, the steak is still excellent. The difference is what it costs relative to everything else on the menu.

Parrillas have leaned harder on chicken, pork and cheaper cuts. Meanwhile many households now save beef for weekends instead of weekdays.

Restaurant menus tell the same story. Cheaper cuts and chicken dishes have spread, while the premium steaks increasingly target visitors paying in dollars.

What to Watch Next

Two things will decide whether the slide continues. The first is whether real wages keep gaining ground on food prices through the rest of 2026.

The second is the cattle cycle. Once herd rebuilding ends, more animals should reach market, and that extra supply could finally cool prices at the counter.

Imports are the wild card. If Brazilian beef keeps arriving at lower prices, it could put a ceiling on what Argentine butchers can charge.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much beef do Argentines eat now?

About 46.3 kilos per person a year, measured over the 12 months to July 2026. That is 4.8 kilos less than a year earlier, and the lowest figure in more than two decades.

Who publishes the Argentina beef consumption figure?

CICCRA, the Argentine chamber of meat industry and commerce, publishes a monthly report with a rolling 12-month per-capita average. Infobae and other outlets carried the July 2026 reading on 19 August 2026.

Is chicken really more popular than beef in Argentina?

Yes, by volume. Chicken now runs at roughly 49 to 50 kilos per person a year.

Which citrus fruits can Argentina now send to Panama?

Lemons, mandarins, oranges and grapefruit. Panama approved the phytosanitary requirements in resolutions DNSV 427 to 430 of 2026, after talks between SENASA and Panama’s MIDA.

Sources: Infobae; CICCRA; La Nación; IPCVA; Agritotal.

World.title: Argentina Digital Health Plan Lands US$700 Million IDB Credit Line
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts — The headline number a conditional credit line of up to US$700 million with the Inter-American Development Bank, approved by Decree 757/2026.

— The date the decree was signed on August 18, 2026 and published in Argentina’s official gazette on August 19, 2026.

— The borrower the Argentine Republic, not a state bank; provinces receive the money through individual loans.

— The first loan US$85 million for Mendoza’s public hospital network, with disbursements planned over four years.

— The second loan up to US$60 million approved on August 10, 2026 for Rio Negro, aimed at about 320,000 public-system patients.

The first US$85 million goes to Mendoza, and the province has already warned the cash has not landed yet.

Illustrative photo: the Hospital Central and FUESMEN complex in Mendoza, the province set to receive the first US$85 million loan under the US$700 million credit line. (Photo: Federico Gomez Aghetta, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Argentina Digital Health spending is about to get a large foreign credit line. A presidential decree published on August 19 approves a framework worth up to US$700 million with the Inter-American Development Bank.

The money is meant to drag provincial hospital systems out of paper files and into shared digital records.

What Argentina Actually Signed Off On

Decree 757/2026 approves the model agreement for a conditional credit line numbered AR-O0033. The lender is the Inter-American Development Bank, known in the region as the BID.

The ceiling is US$700 million. However, the decree does not hand over a single cheque, because a conditional credit line works more like an approved overdraft.

Why the Argentina Digital Health Line Is Not One Big Loan

A conditional credit line is an umbrella. Individual loans are then carved out of it, one at a time, each with its own contract and its own conditions.

The umbrella stays open for ten years from the day the agreement takes effect. As a result, provinces can queue up over a decade rather than compete in a single round.

Mendoza Is First in the Queue

The same decree authorises the first individual loan, worth US$85 million, for Mendoza. It funds a project with a very literal name: the Consolidation of the Digital Transformation of the Provincial Health System.

Local reporting says the money will be drawn down over four years and repaid over 25. Interest is tied to SOFR, the dollar benchmark that replaced Libor.

Approved Money Is Not Arrived Money

In mid-August, Mendoza folded the operation into its 2026 budget. Even so, the province spelled out that the accounting entry did not mean the dollars had landed.

That distinction matters across the whole package. Board approval, a decree, a signed contract and an actual disbursement are four different milestones.

And only the first two have clearly happened.

Rio Negro Is Already Second

On August 10, 2026, the bank’s board approved up to US$60 million for Rio Negro. Coverage of the operation describes it as the second project under the same digital health line.

The stated goal is to reach roughly 320,000 people who rely only on the public network. In addition, the loan is set to cover the entire cost of that provincial programme.

What the Money Buys Inside a Hospital

The Argentina Digital Health shopping list is unglamorous and, for patients, quite useful. It covers electronic medical records, appointment systems, laboratory and imaging software, connectivity and cybersecurity.

Telemedicine sits alongside all of that. Because Argentine provinces are enormous and thinly populated in places, a remote consultation can replace a very long drive.

Why Provinces Do the Spending

Argentina runs health care through 24 jurisdictions: 23 provinces plus the city of Buenos Aires. Each one owns its hospitals, hires its staff and buys its own software.

That is why a national credit line has to be sliced into provincial loans. The federal government signs as guarantor, with provincial revenue-sharing transfers standing behind the promise.

Who Borrows, and a Common Mix-Up

The borrower here is the Argentine Republic. The country’s state development bank, BICE, is not a party to this credit line, despite occasional confusion in early summaries.

BICE has been busy with its own peso lending instead, including leasing and small-business facilities announced during 2026. Those programmes are separate from the multilateral loan described in the decree.

Two Other Rule Changes Landed the Same Fortnight

On August 6, the Central Bank issued Communication A 8464. It lets local insurers covering projects under the large-investment incentive regime buy foreign currency to pay reinsurance premiums abroad.

The access is narrow, not general. Insurers must use funds transferred by the project vehicle from its own foreign borrowing, and must act within 72 business hours.

A New Register for Mining Investors

Also published on August 19, Resolution 68/2026 from the Mining Secretariat creates the Mining Investment Registry, or RIM. It replaces the annex of a 2018 resolution and moves filings onto the state’s remote-paperwork platform.

Every beneficiary is identified by tax number, and every declared project gets a unique code. Since the registry also handles single-project vehicles, it links the older mining law to the newer incentive regime.

The Wider Lending Relationship

The health line is not an isolated cheque. In 2026 the bank has also approved US$500 million for Argentina’s targeted energy subsidy system and US$300 million for public administration modernisation.

Those operations follow the same pattern of long tenors and SOFR-linked pricing. Overall, the lender is financing plumbing rather than headline projects, which is slow work and rarely makes front pages.

What to Watch Next

Three things will show whether this is real. First, the signed loan contracts; second, the first disbursement dates; third, which province is chosen third.

Demand for public care is rising. Since the share of Argentines with no union or private health plan has grown in recent years.

Therefore the queue for these provincial loans is unlikely to stay short.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Argentina borrowing for digital health?

Up to US$700 million, as a framework credit line with the Inter-American Development Bank. Individual loans are then approved one by one, so the full amount is a ceiling rather than a transfer.

Has any money been paid out yet?

No disbursement has been reported. Mendoza’s US$85 million loan was written into the provincial budget in August 2026.

Is BICE, the state development bank, the borrower?

No. The borrower is the Argentine Republic, and provinces are the beneficiaries. BICE runs its own separate credit programmes and is not part of this agreement.

What will patients notice from the Argentina Digital Health programme?

Mainly shared electronic records, easier appointments and more telemedicine. Rio Negro’s programme alone targets about 320,000 people who depend only on public hospitals and clinics.

Sources: Boletin Oficial de la Republica Argentina; El Cronista; Infobae; El Sol (Mendoza); Devdiscourse; Uxolo.

World.title: Brazil Electoral Fund Frees US$440 Million in Public Campaign Money
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — The release Brazil’s top electoral court freed R$2.3 billion (about US$440 million) on August 18, 2026.

— The trigger the Workers’ Party (PT) dropped its own lawsuit, and the court closed the case without ruling on it.

— The slice that R$2.3 billion is the 48% share split by how many federal deputies each party holds.

— The whole pot the 2026 fund is R$4,961,519,777, roughly US$950 million, shared by 30 parties.

— The clock campaigning began August 16, and parties must pass the cash to candidates by August 30.

The unlocked slice is one piece of a nearly US$950 million pot that taxpayers hand political parties before the October 4 vote.

Illustrative photo: a voter uses a Brazilian electronic voting machine. The 2026 Electoral Fund totals R$4,961,519,777, about US$950 million, split among 30 parties. (Photo: TSE – Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.)

Money from the Brazil Electoral Fund is moving again. On August 18, 2026, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) released R$2.3 billion, about US$440 million, to political parties.

The payment had been frozen for days because the Workers’ Party (PT) was suing over how its own share was calculated.

What the Brazil Electoral Fund Actually Is

Brazilian campaigns run mostly on public money. Companies were banned from donating in 2015, and Congress replaced them in 2017 with a taxpayer-funded pot.

That pot is the Fundo Especial de Financiamento de Campanha, or FEFC. In English it is simply the Brazil Electoral Fund, and every real inside it comes from the federal budget.

Why the Payment Got Stuck

The court had already published each party’s number on July 1. Yet the biggest chunk of the money never left the account.

On August 13, minister Estela Aranha asked to review the PT case, which paused the judgment. As a result, R$2.3 billion sat frozen for every party, not just the PT.

Other parties could only wait. Because the 48% band is calculated as one block, a dispute over one party’s seat count froze everyone’s transfer.

The Fight Was Over a Single Deputy

The PT did not attack the formula. Instead, it argued that its bench in the Chamber of Deputies should count 69 members rather than 68.

The extra name was Paulão, a PT deputy from Alagoas. He lost his seat after a 2022 vote recount.

Although a May 2026 order from Supreme Court minister Dias Toffoli suspended that process.

How the Court Closed the Case

TSE president Kassio Nunes Marques, who was also the case rapporteur, voted against the party. He held that Toffoli’s order paused the proceeding but did not force a fresh recount.

The PT then withdrew the petition. On August 18 the full court unanimously accepted the withdrawal and shut the case without judging the merits.

There was a second reason to give up. On August 12, Supreme Court minister Cristiano Zanin rejected Paulão’s separate bid to recover his mandate.

How the Cash Is Divided

The split is written into Brazil’s election law and leaves the court almost no discretion. Two percent goes equally to every registered party, so even tiny ones get something.

After that, 35% follows votes cast for the Chamber, 48% follows the number of federal deputies, and 15% follows Senate seats. The 48% band is the piece that was blocked.

Who Takes Home the Most

The Liberal Party (PL), which backs the Bolsonaro camp, leads with roughly R$881.7 million, near US$169 million. The PT follows with about R$615.4 million, or some US$118 million.

União Brasil takes around R$526.2 million (US$101 million), the PSD about R$421 million (US$81 million). And the PP roughly R$417.1 million (US$80 million).

Together those five hold 57.68% of the fund. Small parties are not left empty-handed.

The 2% equal share guarantees each of the 30 registered parties a floor. Although it is a rounding error next to the PL’s total.

What the Money Can Buy

Spending limits were kept at 2022 levels and only adjusted for inflation. A presidential campaign may spend up to R$88.9 million in the first round, close to US$17 million.

A runoff adds R$44.4 million more, near US$8.5 million. Governor races in São Paulo are capped at R$26.6 million, while a federal deputy may spend roughly R$3.2 million, near US$610,000.

Those ceilings cover the obvious costs. Rallies, sound trucks, printed material, marketing teams and paid social media boosts all come out of the same pot.

Why Brazilians Call It the Fundão

Critics use the nickname fundão, meaning the big fund, and the arithmetic explains why. Divided by 158,745,463 registered voters, the fund costs roughly R$31 a head, about US$6.

Lawmakers set the amount themselves. In October 2025, the budget committee lifted the 2026 figure from R$1 billion to R$4.9 billion.

Moving R$2.9 billion away from parliamentary earmarks.

The Argument on the Other Side

Defenders say the alternative was worse. Before 2015, construction giants bankrolled campaigns, and the Lava Jato scandal showed what those favors bought.

Public money is also easier to police. Because the court controls the flow, it can force parties to send at least 30% of the fund to women candidates.

There is a practical argument too. Public funding is traceable, so auditors can follow each transfer instead of chasing hidden company favours.

The Fund Is Shrinking in Real Terms

The headline number looks frozen in time. The FEFC has stayed near R$4.9 billion since 2022, even though prices have climbed since then.

A separate permanent pot, the fundo partidário, adds R$1.43 billion a year for party running costs. That is another US$274 million, paid monthly whether or not there is an election.

Wealthy donors have not disappeared. Individuals may still give up to 10% of their previous year’s income, which keeps a private lane open beside the public one.

What Happens Next

Parties must now hand the money to candidates. The general deadline is August 30, while transfers tied to the quotas for women, Black and Indigenous candidates run to September 8.

Voting is on October 4, with any runoff four weeks later. Since the campaign opened on August 16, the released cash arrives just as television and online advertising begin in earnest.

Leftover money does not stay with the parties. Campaign accounts are audited by the court, and unused public funds must be reported and returned rather than pocketed.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much was released and when?

The TSE released R$2.3 billion, about US$440 million, on August 18, 2026. It is the 48% slice of the campaign fund tied to the size of each party’s bench in the Chamber of Deputies.

What was the Workers’ Party suing about?

The PT wanted its Chamber bench counted as 69 deputies instead of 68, which would have lifted its share. It dropped the case, and the court closed it without ruling.

How big is the whole fund?

The 2026 Brazil Electoral Fund totals R$4,961,519,777, roughly US$950 million at R$5.22 to the dollar. Thirty parties share it, and the top five take 57.68%.

Where does the money come from?

The federal budget. Congress sets the amount each year, and the fund exists because the Supreme Court banned corporate donations in 2015.

Sources: Tribunal Superior Eleitoral; Folha de S.Paulo; O Globo; Estadão; CartaCapital.

World.title: Brazil Election Polls: Big Leads in Brasília and São Paulo
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — The Brasília governor race Real Time Big Data puts Celina Leão on 34%, José Roberto Arruda on 22% and Leandro Grass on 18%.

— The Brasília Senate race Michelle Bolsonaro leads on 25%, ahead of Leila Barros on 17%, with Bia Kicis and Erika Kokay tied on 15%.

— The runoff caveat Flávio Bolsonaro 44% to Lula 39% is a Federal District result from 1,600 local voters, not a national poll.

— The São Paulo race Paraná Pesquisas has Governor Tarcísio de Freitas on 50% and Fernando Haddad on 33.8%, a gap of just over 16 points.

— The method Brasília fieldwork ran 14-18 August with a 2-point error margin; São Paulo ran 16-18 August with 2.4 points.

The eye-catching Flavio Bolsonaro lead over Lula comes from Brasília alone, a right-leaning enclave, not from Brazil as a whole.

Illustrative photo: Celina Leão at a Brasília government ceremony handing over police vehicles. She leads the Federal District governor race with 34% in the Real Time Big Data survey of 14-18 August 2026. (Photo: Agência Brasília, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Two fresh Brazil election polls landed this week, and both carry a warning label. In Brasília, Celina Leão leads the race for governor and Michelle Bolsonaro leads for the Senate.

In São Paulo, Governor Tarcísio de Freitas sits on 50%, some 16 points clear of Fernando Haddad.

What the Brasília Poll Found

Real Time Big Data surveyed 1,600 voters in Brazil’s Federal District between 14 and 18 August. Celina Leão, the sitting governor, leads the race to keep her job with 34%.

Former governor José Roberto Arruda follows on 22%, while Leandro Grass of the Workers’ Party takes 18%. Paula Belmonte has 6% and Ricardo Cappelli has 5%.

Blank and spoiled ballots account for 6%, and another 8% of voters are undecided. The margin of error is two percentage points, at 95% confidence.

The Senate Race in the Capital

Michelle Bolsonaro, the former first lady, leads the Senate contest with 25%. This is her first run for office, and she stands for the Liberal Party.

Leila Barros follows on 17%. Bia Kicis and Erika Kokay are tied on 15%, so the fight for the second seat still looks wide open.

The Federal District elects two senators in October. Because voters pick two names, more than one of these candidates can win a seat.

Bia Kicis also runs for the Liberal Party, so the two allies share a base. Erika Kokay, a Workers’ Party veteran, holds the left flank.

Why the 44-39 Runoff Number Is Not National

The same survey also asked about a presidential runoff. Flávio Bolsonaro took 44% against 39% for President Lula, a five-point gap.

However, that question went to the same 1,600 Brasília voters. It is a Federal District result, and it is not a national one.

The distinction matters, because the capital leans well to the right of Brazil as a whole. Reading it as a nationwide verdict would be a mistake.

In the first round in Brasília, the two men are almost level. Lula has 36% and Flávio Bolsonaro has 35%.

How These Brazil Election Polls Compare With National Ones

National Brazil election polls this month tell a different story. Quaest, released on 14 August, had Lula on 43% and Flávio Bolsonaro on 40%.

BTG/Nexus, released three days later, put Lula on 47% and Flávio on 44%. Both gaps sit inside the margin of error, so the national race is effectively tied.

By contrast, the Brasília figure flips the order around. That is what a regional stronghold looks like once you break the numbers down.

Brazil holds a runoff only if nobody wins half the valid votes nationally. Local samples therefore say little about who eventually takes the presidency.

São Paulo: Tarcísio Well Clear of Haddad

Paraná Pesquisas polled 1,680 voters across 80 São Paulo municipalities from 16 to 18 August. Governor Tarcísio de Freitas leads with 50%.

Fernando Haddad, the former finance minister, has 33.8%. The gap is a little over 16 points, and it is far wider than the survey’s error margin.

In a simulated runoff, Tarcísio takes 53% to Haddad’s 36.9%. The margin of error is 2.4 points, and the poll is registered as SP-08913/2026.

Is Tarcísio Running for President?

No. Tarcísio registered with the electoral court as a candidate for re-election as governor of São Paulo. Registrations closed on 15 August, so the field is now fixed.

Despite years of speculation, he is not on the presidential ballot. The Liberal Party’s presidential candidate is Flávio Bolsonaro instead.

His father, Jair Bolsonaro, is ineligible and cannot run this year.

Who Is Celina Leão?

Celina Leão was elected vice-governor in 2022 on Ibaneis Rocha’s ticket. She took the top job on 30 March 2026, after he stepped down to chase a Senate seat.

Ibaneis later abandoned that bid. Celina Leão therefore goes into October as an incumbent with only a few months in the chair.

The Arruda Question

José Roberto Arruda governed the Federal District from 2007 to 2010. He left office during the Caixa de Pandora corruption scandal and was later convicted of administrative misconduct.

His party launched him anyway. Still, the courts have not settled whether the Clean Record law bars him, so his place on the ballot remains uncertain.

How the Two Surveys Were Run

Brazilian pollsters must register each survey with the electoral court before publication. The Brasília study carries registration DF-07849/2026 for the state races.

Its presidential question was filed separately as BR-05423/2026, even though it used the same 1,600 local respondents. Real Time Big Data paid for the work itself.

Paraná Pesquisas also funded its own São Paulo survey. Face-to-face interviews covered 80 municipalities, and the confidence level is 95%.

What Happens Next

Brazilians vote on 4 October, with runoffs on 25 October where no one clears half the valid votes. About 158.7 million voters are registered nationally.

More Brazil election polls will land through September, so these numbers will move. For now, treat the Brasília runoff figure as a local snapshot rather than a national verdict.

The capital holds only a small slice of Brazil’s electorate. Even a landslide there barely moves a national total of 158.7 million registered voters.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the 44% to 39% runoff result a national poll?

No. It comes from Real Time Big Data’s survey of 1,600 voters in Brazil’s Federal District only. National polls in August put Lula narrowly ahead of Flávio Bolsonaro.

Is Tarcísio de Freitas running for president in 2026?

No. He registered as a candidate for re-election as governor of São Paulo before the 15 August deadline. Paraná Pesquisas tested him for the governorship, not the presidency.

Who leads the Federal District Senate race?

Michelle Bolsonaro, on 25%. Leila Barros has 17%, while Bia Kicis and Erika Kokay are tied on 15%.

When does Brazil vote?

The first round is on 4 October 2026. Runoffs for president and state governors take place on 25 October 2026.

Sources: Poder360; Metrópoles; R7; UOL; Gazeta do Povo.

World.title: Brazil Justices Push to Revisit the Journalism Degree Requirement
World.content:
Brazil · Media

Key Facts — The date On August 18, 2026, Justices Alexandre de Moraes and Flavio Dino said in open session that Brazil’s Supreme Court should debate the diploma rule again.

— The setting Their remarks came in a First Panel case about a right of reply won by a Rio clinic against TV Globo and its news site G1.

— The precedent In June 2009 the full court struck the rule down 8-1 in RE 511961, with Gilmar Mendes as rapporteur and only Marco Aurelio dissenting.

— The status There is no new case, no vote and no majority; Justice Carmen Lucia asked for extra time in the Globo case, pausing it.

— The other route PEC 206/2012, passed by the Senate in 2012, has sat ready for a floor vote in the Chamber and needs 308 votes in two rounds.

No case has been filed and no vote has been cast, so the 2009 ruling that freed the profession still stands.

Illustrative photo: the Justice statue outside Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court in Brasilia, where the court voted 8-1 in June 2009 to strike down the journalism diploma rule. (Photo: Dasfour2022, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Brazil’s Supreme Court has not restored the journalism degree requirement, and nothing about the law changed this week. Two justices simply said out loud, in open session on August 18, 2026, that the country should argue about it again.

Those were spoken opinions in an unrelated case, not votes.

What Actually Happened in Court

The First Panel of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court met on August 18, 2026. It was hearing an appeal by TV Globo and G1 against a right-of-reply order won by a Rio de Janeiro clinic.

During the debate the conversation drifted to who counts as a journalist. Justices Alexandre de Moraes and Flavio Dino then said the court should look again at the diploma rule it scrapped in 2009.

Neither man cast a vote on diplomas, because no diploma case was before them. Their votes that day went to upholding the clinic’s right of reply.

The panel did not finish. Justice Carmen Lucia asked for more time to study the file, which suspends the judgment until she returns it.

Why the Journalism Degree Requirement Fell in 2009

The journalism degree requirement came from Decree-Law 972 of 1969, written under military rule. It obliged anyone practising journalism to hold a university degree in the field and register with the labour ministry.

On June 17, 2009, the full court ruled 8-1 in Recurso Extraordinario 511961 that the 1988 Constitution had not absorbed that rule. Gilmar Mendes was the rapporteur, and Marco Aurelio was the lone dissenter.

The reasoning was blunt. Journalism is an exercise of free expression.

So demanding a state-approved diploma to speak was treated as a restriction the Constitution does not allow. Judges also leaned on Article 13 of the American Convention on Human Rights.

Since then, anyone in Brazil may work as a journalist without a degree, and appeals against the ruling were rejected in 2019.

What Moraes Said From the Bench

Moraes reached for a historical parallel. Early last century Brazil let unqualified advocates known as rabulas practise law.

And that was phased out with a transition rule for those already working. He argued that social media has created the same problem in reverse.

Anyone can wake up, declare themselves a journalist, and start attacking reputations from a blog, in his description. So, he said, perhaps it is time to reflect again, with protection for people who already do the job seriously.

He framed it as regulating a profession like any other in Brazil. He did not spell out whether that means a compulsory degree, a licence, or something looser.

No draft text exists, and no proposal has been filed at the court.

What Dino Said From the Bench

Dino was working through a narrower worry about legal protections. Because press guarantees are strong, he said, extending them automatically to any blogger creates an obvious loophole.

He put it vividly. Warning that criminal groups such as the PCC and Comando Vermelho could hold a contest to pick their own bloggers.

Shielding those people as journalists would then be absurd, in his view. He also said that the 2009 decision, which he respects, might one day be debated again.

That single sentence is what set off two days of headlines in Brazil. Dino has separately argued that a reporter’s duty to protect a source is not absolute.

That claim matters, because it runs alongside a live dispute over one of his own cases.

The Rapporteur of the 2009 Ruling Now Says Rediscuss

The most striking response came from inside the court. Gilmar Mendes wrote the 2009 opinion, and on August 19, 2026, he told reporters in Brasilia that the ruling could be reopened.

He said the decision waived the diploma but never waived training, since people could bring qualifications from many fields. Still, he added, the court can rediscuss it if information quality is genuinely suffering.

He also cautioned against drawing a firm conclusion from one episode. He was referring to a serious dispute in Maranhao state that has dominated the debate.

Even so, a rapporteur inviting a rethink of his own precedent is unusual. It is the clearest signal yet that the question is no longer settled inside the court.

The Backdrop: A Search Order and a Reporter’s Source

None of this arrived out of nowhere. On August 11, 2026, federal police searched the home of Raimundo Cutrim.

A former Maranhao state secretary, on an order signed by Moraes. Investigators treat Cutrim as the source behind reporting by journalist Luis Pablo about official cars used by Dino’s family.

Press bodies read the operation as an attack on source confidentiality. Moraes defended the order, drawing a line between protecting a source and taking part in a crime.

Meanwhile, court president Edson Fachin publicly backed press freedom and source secrecy. Fachin signalled that Moraes’s decision should go to the full court.

Therefore the diploma comments landed in a week already loaded with press-freedom tension.

How Brazil’s Press Bodies Reacted

The journalists’ federation FENAJ welcomed the opening. Its president, Samira de Castro, said no decision has aged as badly as the one that abolished the diploma requirement.

FENAJ has campaigned for the rule’s return for seventeen years. It says either Congress or the court could fix what it sees as a mistake.

And it offered to help with the debate. Newspaper publishers were colder.

Marcelo Rech of the national newspaper association ANJ called it strange to reopen the topic while justices defend piercing a journalist’s confidentiality. As if the end justified the means.

Abraji, the investigative journalism association, kept its focus on source protection as a constitutional guarantee. In short, the industry is split, and the split does not follow the usual left-right lines.

The Route Through Congress

There is a legislative path that has existed for years. The Senate approved a constitutional amendment restoring the diploma in two rounds, by 65-7 in November 2011 and 60-4 in August 2012.

It moved to the Chamber of Deputies as PEC 206/2012 and cleared the constitutional affairs committee in 2013. Since then it has sat ready for a floor vote that never gets scheduled.

A constitutional amendment needs 308 votes in the Chamber, twice. That is a high bar, and no party has spent political capital on it.

Congress could act tomorrow without any help from the court. Yet the practical reality is that the proposal has been parked for more than a decade.

What Would Change if the Rule Returned

Today the answer is simple: nothing has changed. Anyone may report, edit, film or publish in Brazil without a degree or a state register.

If the rule returned, employers would have to check credentials before hiring newsroom staff. Moraes has floated a transition rule so people already working would keep their jobs.

The harder question is what happens to everyone outside a newsroom. Bloggers, podcasters, YouTubers and independent newsletter writers would face a line between protected journalism and ordinary speech.

Brazil has about 295 active undergraduate journalism programmes, according to an April 2026 count by the teaching association ABEJ. A restored rule would make those courses the gateway to the trade.

What to Watch Next

First, watch for a case. Nothing can change until someone files a suit that squarely asks the court to overturn the 2009 ruling.

Second, watch Carmen Lucia. Her return of the Globo file will show whether the panel wants to write anything broad about who deserves press protection.

Third, watch the Chamber. If leaders suddenly schedule PEC 206/2012, the court becomes a sideshow rather than the main stage.

Until one of those happens, the position is unchanged. The journalism degree requirement remains unconstitutional in Brazil, and only a new majority or a new amendment can alter that.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Brazil reinstated the journalism degree requirement?

No. As of August 19, 2026, the 2009 ruling stands, and no degree is needed to work as a journalist in Brazil. Two justices only said the question deserves a fresh debate.

Did Moraes and Dino vote to bring the diploma back?

No. They spoke during a First Panel hearing on a right-of-reply appeal by TV Globo. Their votes in that case were about the right of reply, not about diplomas.

What did the 2009 decision actually say?

In RE 511961, decided 8-1 on June 17, 2009. The court held that the 1988 Constitution did not absorb the 1969 decree requiring a journalism degree and labour ministry registration.

Could Congress restore the requirement instead?

Yes. PEC 206/2012 already passed the Senate and awaits a floor vote in the Chamber of Deputies.

Sources: Folha de S.Paulo; Poder360; Agencia Brasil; O Povo; Supremo Tribunal Federal.

World.title: Ten Days of Free Short Films in São Paulo, and How to Get a Seat
World.content:
Brazil · Cinema

Key Facts Free everywhere Every session of the 37th Curta Kinoforum is free, in seven cinemas across the city, from 20 to 30 August.

Every session of the 37th Curta Kinoforum is free, in seven cinemas across the city, from 20 to 30 August. Get there early At MIS, tickets are handed out at the box office one hour before each session. There is no online booking, and the room seats about 170.

At MIS, tickets are handed out at the box office one hour before each session. There is no online booking, and the room seats about 170. The dates The festival runs 20 to 30 August, after an opening night at CineSesc on 19 August.

The festival runs 20 to 30 August, after an opening night at CineSesc on 19 August. Where to start MIS, at Avenida Europa 158 in Jardim Europa, carries the Brazilian selection — twelve blocks of it — plus the closing best-of.

MIS, at Avenida Europa 158 in Jardim Europa, carries the Brazilian selection — twelve blocks of it — plus the closing best-of. Thirty-seventh year This is the 37th Curta Kinoforum, one of the oldest short-film festivals in Latin America.

This is the 37th Curta Kinoforum, one of the oldest short-film festivals in Latin America. The numbers 260 films from 58 countries — 127 Brazilian, 133 foreign — including an international selection of 109 films from 55 countries.

260 films from 58 countries — 127 Brazilian, 133 foreign — including an international selection of 109 films from 55 countries. Something for children MIS runs Kids sessions on 23 August at 2pm, and two on 30 August, at 10.30am and noon.

Ten days of short films, none of them longer than your lunch break, and not one of them costs anything.

Short films are the easiest cinema to watch in a language you are still learning. Nothing lasts long, the story is usually told with pictures rather than dialogue, and if one does not work there is another along in four minutes. From Thursday there are free short films in São Paulo by the hundred — 260 of them, to be exact.

The 37th Curta Kinoforum screens 260 shorts across seven São Paulo cinemas, all free. (Photo internet reproduction)

Where to see free short films in São Paulo

The Museu da Imagem e do Som is one of seven cinemas in this year’s Curta Kinoforum, and it is the one worth building an evening around. Its share of the programme is the Brazilian selection — the Mostra Brasil blocks, numbered one to twelve — plus the children’s sessions and the closing best-of. It screens on 20, 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29 and 30 August, and is dark on the 24th and 28th.

Most evenings run two sessions, at 6pm and 8pm. On 25 August there are two Diálogos Urbanos sessions, one on São Paulo and one on Recife, which is as good an introduction to how Brazilians film their own cities as you will get in one night.

The closing weekend is the strongest. On 29 and 30 August MIS shows the 10+ blocks — ten Brazilian and ten foreign — plus a Destaques session of the festival’s highlights.

How to actually get in

This is the part people get wrong. Entry is free, but there is no online reservation and no advance booking. Tickets are released at the MIS box office one hour before each session, and popular blocks do fill.

So for a 6pm session, be at Avenida Europa 158 by 5pm. The room seats about 170, so the queue is real. On most evenings there is a second block two hours later, though on 22 and 23 August the 6pm session is the last one.

If you are bringing children, the Kids sessions are on 23 August at 2pm and 30 August at 10.30am and noon. The 30 August morning slot is billed as a marathon, which in practice means a long, cheerful, sit-down-and-stay session.

The rest of the festival

The full 37th Kinoforum is much larger: 260 films from 58 countries across the Cinemateca Brasileira, CineSesc, the Spcine circuit at the Centro Cultural São Paulo, Espaço Petrobras de Cinema, MIS and the two CINUSP rooms. Of those, 109 films from 55 countries make up the international selection — which is where to go if you want the view from outside Brazil. The opening was at CineSesc on 19 August at 8pm.

If you cannot get to a cinema, part of the programme streams free on Spcine Play, Porta Curtas, Itaú Cultural Play and Sesc Digital — useful if you are outside São Paulo, or outside Brazil.

Why this is worth your Thursday

If you have moved to Brazil recently, the cost of going out is the thing that surprises people most. A cinema ticket in São Paulo typically runs from about R$30 to R$60 (about US$6 to US$12), and a festival night elsewhere in the world would cost several times that. This costs nothing at all.

It is also a low-effort way to understand where you now live. Twelve blocks of Brazilian shorts is twelve blocks of Brazilians describing their own country to each other, without the filter of an export market. You will learn more in two hours there than in a month of news.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the short film festival in São Paulo free? Yes. Every session of the 37th Curta Kinoforum is free, in every venue, and part of the programme also streams free online. There is no advance booking at MIS: tickets are handed out at the box office one hour before each session, on a first-come basis. How many films are showing and where? The 37th Curta Kinoforum shows 260 films from 58 countries — 127 Brazilian and 133 foreign — of which 109 films from 55 countries form the international selection. They screen across seven cinemas: MIS, the Cinemateca Brasileira, CineSesc, the Spcine room at the Centro Cultural São Paulo, Espaço Petrobras de Cinema and the two CINUSP rooms. MIS carries the Brazilian selection. Where is MIS and how do I get there? The Museu da Imagem e do Som is at Avenida Europa 158, Jardim Europa, in the west of São Paulo. It is a short taxi or ride-hailing trip from Avenida Paulista; the nearest metro stations are a walk away, so most people arrive by car or app. Allow an hour before your session to collect a ticket. Are the films subtitled? Foreign films are subtitled in Portuguese, and every in-person session carries Portuguese subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing, so Brazilian films are subtitled too — which many language learners find useful. Short films lean heavily on images, so the barrier is lower than at a feature-film festival.

World.title: Brandon Nakashima Saves Three Match Points to Stun Daniil Medvedev at Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Brandon Nakashima saved three consecutive match points before completing a dramatic comeback against Daniil Medvedev on Tuesday at the Cincinnati Open. The 27th-seeded American defeated the fourth seed 6-7(3), 7-6(4), 6-1, advancing to the round of 16 after two hours and 51 minutes.

Nakashima appeared headed for elimination when he served at 4-5, 0-40 in the second set. Medvedev had already taken the opening set in a tiebreak and stood one point away from closing the match on three occasions. Instead, Nakashima attacked. He saved the first match point with a forehand approach and volley, survived an 18-shot rally on the second and used serve-and-volley to erase the third. He eventually held serve before forcing another tiebreak.

“Down match points, I was just trying to tell myself to keep fighting for every point,” Nakashima said during his on-court interview. The American carried that momentum into the tiebreak, winning it 7-4 to force a deciding set. Medvedev never recovered. Nakashima broke early in the third and pulled away as the former Cincinnati champion became increasingly frustrated.

Nakashima closed the final set 6-1 to earn his first victory over Medvedev in four career meetings. Medvedev had won their previous encounter in the Brisbane final in January. The result continued an impressive North American hard-court run for Nakashima. The 25-year-old reached the semifinals in Washington before advancing to his first Masters 1000 final in Montreal, where he lost to fellow American Ben Shelton.

Now ranked a career-high No. 22, Nakashima has won 20 hard-court matches this season. Only Jakub Mensik, with 21, has recorded more on the ATP Tour. Tuesday’s victory was also Nakashima’s fifth against a top-10 opponent. It came against a player who has traditionally produced some of his best tennis on hard courts and won the Cincinnati title in 2019.

Nakashima will next face Portugal’s Nuno Borges, who produced another upset by defeating 13th-seeded Andrey Rublev 6-3, 6-4. Borges entered that match having lost all five of his previous meetings with Rublev. The winner will advance to the Cincinnati Open quarterfinals as the tournament moves closer to its August 23 championship match.

World.title: Costa Rica Audit Finds 157 Unfinished Works and Safety Risks on Route 32
World.content:
A new technical audit of the Route 32 expansion has identified 157 unfinished works, unstable slopes and road-safety problems along the highway connecting central Costa Rica with Limón and the Caribbean coast. The National Laboratory of Materials and Structural Models at the University of Costa Rica (LanammeUCR), examined the expansion between the Route 4 intersection near Sarapiquí and Limón. The audit covered work carried out between April 2025 and May 2026.

Inspectors reviewed 402 items recorded as pending in partial acceptance documents for 23 sections of the project. Of those, 145 had been completed, 48 were being addressed and 157 remained open without corrective action. Inspectors could not locate or verify another 52 items.

Drainage represented the largest area of concern. The audit identified 154 drainage-related items, including 62 that remained unresolved. LanammeUCR described the situation as particularly important because the highway passes through one of Costa Rica’s rainiest regions, where poorly functioning drains can contribute to flooding, erosion and damage to the road.

Other pending work involved vehicle barriers, the road surface, pedestrian infrastructure and signs. Among the pedestrian projects reviewed, 27 of 39 remained unresolved. Inspectors also found 20 outstanding road-surface items, 16 involving vehicle containment systems such as barriers, and 16 related to signs.

The audit raised separate concerns about slope stability, particularly between kilometers 100 and 112. Inspectors documented erosion, falling material and problems controlling surface water. Two slopes, located near kilometers 101.6 and 111.5, were singled out because inspectors found no evidence that permanent solutions were being implemented. Other unstable locations were also observed along the expanded section.

The findings carry particular cause for concern during periods of heavy rainfall. Route 32 often experiences closures because of landslides and falling material, disrupting travel between San José and the Caribbean and affecting access to Limón’s ports and popular destinations such as Cahuita and Puerto Viejo.

LanammeUCR also questioned the use of roundabouts built at several intersections along the expanded highway. The roundabouts have provided temporary improvements to traffic movement, but the audit concluded that they do not replace the grade-separated intersections originally planned for a highway carrying fast-moving traffic and large numbers of heavy trucks.

Inspectors recommended monitoring the roundabouts while moving ahead with permanent solutions. Quality control was another area of concern. During some site visits, work was taking place without the presence of supervisory personnel or laboratories responsible for testing and verifying construction quality.

Tests also found trends of noncompliance in some asphalt-mixture measurements, including the size distribution of the material and the amount of space within the mixture. However, much of the cement-stabilized base material tested within the limits established in the project contract.

The audit was based on 29 technical inspection visits, 27 rounds of material sampling and a review of project records. Findings were communicated to the project administration through 16 separate notices while the audit was underway. LanammeUCR recommended completing the outstanding work, adopting permanent solutions for unstable slopes and intersections, strengthening technical supervision and improving quality controls.

The laboratory warned that unresolved drainage, barriers and pedestrian infrastructure could affect the safety, operation and long-term condition of a highway used daily by thousands of drivers.

World.title: Costa Rica Closes Turrialba Volcano and Guayabo Monument Due to Heavy Rains
World.content:
Two popular to visit in the Turrialba area have closed temporarily as continued rainfall and saturated ground raise the risk of landslides and other emergencies. The public areas of Turrialba Volcano National Park and Guayabo National Monument closed today and will remain off-limits until further notice. The measure goes for tourists, guides and government personnel working at both sites.

The National System of Conservation Areas said the closure responds to unstable weather conditions and the orange alert in effect for the canton of Turrialba. Officials will reassess both sites once the emergency period ends before deciding whether visitors can safely return. The decision is tied to the weather rather than a change in volcanic activity at Turrialba Volcano.

Authorities said the purpose is to prevent people from entering areas where heavy rain may have weakened the ground, affected trails or increased the possibility of falling material. Visitors should not attempt to enter either protected area while the closure remains in place. Tour operators and travelers with planned visits are being advised to check official updates before traveling to the area.

Guayabo National Monument protects Costa Rica’s most important pre-Columbian archaeological site. Its stone roads, aqueducts, foundations and ceremonial structures offer a look at a settlement that flourished centuries before the arrival of Europeans. Turrialba Volcano National Park, meanwhile, gives visitors access to one of the best-known active volcanoes here in Costa Rica.

The park’s location and elevation also make it particularly exposed to rapidly changing weather, strong winds and difficult trail conditions. The closures come as Costa Rica continues dealing with the effects of consecutive tropical waves. More than 1,300 people remained in emergency shelters Tuesday, while authorities delivered assistance to isolated communities in the Caribbean and mountainous Indigenous territories.

Heavy rainfall has also caused flooding, landslides and repeated road closures. Although conditions improved in some locations Tuesday, emergency officials warned that saturated soil could continue producing incidents even when rainfall temporarily decreases. SINAC will determine when Turrialba Volcano National Park and Guayabo National Monument can reopen after reviewing conditions and receiving updated guidance from emergency officials. No reopening date had been announced as of yet.

World.title: El Niño Deepens Costa Rica’s Divide Between Drought and Heavy Rain
World.content:
Costa Rica is experiencing two sharply different rainy seasons at once, with a growing drought across the Pacific side and Central Valley while unusually heavy rainfall affects the Caribbean. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) has confirmed that meteorological drought now covers the entire Pacific slope, the Central Valley and the western Northern Zone, including areas around Upala, Los Chiles and Guatuso.

The latest climate outlook, which runs through February 2027, offers little sign of a substantial recovery in the driest regions. El Niño is expected to remain strong through August and could reach “very strong” intensity between September and November. “This El Niño will remain strong through August, but from September through November, it is expected to intensify into a ‘very strong’ El Niño,” said Karina Hernández, a specialist with the IMN’s Climatology Unit.

That classification describes the warming of the equatorial Pacific Ocean, not necessarily how severe the effects will be in Costa Rica. A strong El Niño involves ocean temperatures more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above average, while the threshold for a very strong event exceeds 2 degrees Celsius.

Hernández said current measurements are already above those recorded during the 2015 El Niño event, although the warming trend has remained relatively stable during the past two months. If the event intensifies further, the final quarter of 2026 is the most likely period because El Niño typically reaches its peak toward the end of the year.

The effects are already visible in Costa Rica’s rainfall totals. The Pacific North could finish August with up to 80% less rain than normal. Deficits of roughly 60% are projected for the Central Pacific, South Pacific and Central Valley, while the western Northern Zone could receive about 40% less rain.

The shortfall has expanded considerably since July, when drought had been confirmed in the Central Valley, the western Northern Zone and much of the North Pacific. At that time, the IMN was still monitoring the Nicoya Peninsula, Osa Peninsula and parts of the Central Pacific. Those areas have since fallen within the broader drought zone.

Meteorological drought does not mean that rain has stopped completely. Some communities may still experience downpours and thunderstorms, but isolated heavy rainfall may not be enough to compensate for months of accumulated shortages.

The IMN also does not declare drought after only a few dry weeks. Its assessment requires sustained rainfall deficits across several weather stations using complete 30-year records. The conditions must persist through three consecutive moving three-month periods, representing roughly five months of deficient rainfall.

As of now, the designation refers specifically to meteorological drought. If the dry pattern continues, it could eventually develop into agricultural drought, affecting soil moisture and crops. A longer and more severe shortage could later affect rivers, reservoirs, drinking-water supplies and hydroelectric generation.

On the other hand, the Caribbean is facing the opposite problem. For August, rainfall is forecast to reach approximately 60% above normal in the Northern Caribbean and 40% above normal in the Southern Caribbean. The eastern Northern Zone could receive around 30% more rain than usual. From September through November, the Caribbean is expected to record about 15% more rainfall than normal. Totals in the eastern Northern Zone should remain closer to their usual range.

This difference is characteristic of El Niño’s effects in Costa Rica. The phenomenon generally reduces rainfall and raises temperatures along the Pacific and in the Central Valley while directing more moisture toward the Caribbean. Temperatures are also expected to remain well above normal. The IMN projects increases of between 1.5°C and 2°C (2.7°F and 3.6°F) across the Pacific, Central Valley and western Northern Zone. The Caribbean and eastern Northern Zone could run between 0.5°C and 1°C (0.9°F and 1.8°F) above average.

Costa Rica has already registered a series of heat records. Thirteen weather stations recorded historic maximum temperatures during July, followed by 14 records on August 11. Temperatures reached 37.5°C (99.5°F) in Santa Cruz and 37.2°C (99°F) at Finca La Ceiba in Nicoya. The contrasting outlook means Costa Rica must prepare for both sides of the same climate pattern: prolonged water shortages and pressure on agriculture in the Pacific, alongside a heightened risk of flooding, saturated soil and landslides in the Caribbean.

World.title: Williams Sisters Lose Cincinnati Open Doubles Thriller
World.content:
Serena and Venus Williams came within two points of completing a dramatic comeback Monday night, but their long-awaited doubles reunion ended with a 2-6, 6-1, 10-8 loss to Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns in the opening round of the Cincinnati Open. Playing together for the first time since the 2022 US Open, the Williams sisters recovered from a difficult opening set and dominated the second. They then nearly erased a 6-0 deficit in the deciding match tiebreak before Venus double-faulted on match point.

The defeat ended their first doubles appearance together outside a Grand Slam tournament since the 2016 Italian Open. Still, the match offered flashes of the chemistry that helped them win 14 Grand Slam doubles titles and three Olympic gold medals. Kostyuk and Stearns controlled the opening set as the Williams sisters worked to rediscover their rhythm. Serena and Venus responded forcefully in the second, dropping only one game and sending the match to a first-to-10 tiebreak.

The momentum shifted again when Kostyuk and Stearns raced through the first six points of the decider. The Williams sisters refused to let the match slip away quietly. Consecutive double faults from Kostyuk helped open the door, and the crowd grew louder as Serena and Venus closed the gap to 8-7. Kostyuk and Stearns reached match point at 9-7, but Serena kept the match alive with an overhead winner.

Venus then double-faulted, bringing a sudden end to a comeback that had appeared almost impossible minutes earlier. “I thought it was fun. I thought it was special,” Serena said afterward. “It was really cool to be able to do this again.” The Cincinnati crowd strongly backed the Williams sisters, even though Stearns grew up in Mason, the Ohio suburb where the tournament is held. Stearns and Ukraine’s Kostyuk, both 24, were competing together for the first time.

Serena, 44, returned to professional tennis this summer after stepping away following the 2022 US Open. She and Venus had planned to play doubles at Wimbledon, but they withdrew after Serena sustained a knee injury during her opening-round singles match. The sisters accepted a wild card into Cincinnati, where Serena won consecutive singles titles in 2014 and 2015. She entered only the doubles competition this year.

Venus, 46, also received a singles wild card but lost 6-2, 6-2 to Colombian qualifier Emiliana Arango in the first round. Monday’s result leaves unanswered whether the sisters will play together again before the end of the season. Their return lasted only one match, but the close finish and the crowd’s response showed that a Williams sisters doubles appearance remains one of the biggest attractions in tennis.

World.title: Route 32 shut again with a reopening decision due this morning
World.content:
If you are going to the Caribbean coast today, check the road before you load the car. Route 32, the main highway between the Central Valley and Limón, closed again on Monday and was still shut as of early this morning. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport closed the road on Monday after material came down in the mountain area during heavy rain.

The ministry said the closure would stay in place as long as conditions could compromise driver safety, and that crews would assess the highway first thing Tuesday to decide whether traffic can move again. That decision has not been announced yet. Until it is, assume the road is closed.

The pattern this week has been open, close, repeat. The road reopened at 6 a.m. Monday after a weekend of closures, then shut again the same afternoon. Anyone planning around a single reopening announcement is likely to get caught out. The reason the mountain stretch keeps failing is the ground above it, not the road surface.

The slopes through Braulio Carrillo and around Cerro Zurquí have absorbed as much water as they can hold. Once soil reaches that point it stops soaking up rain and starts sliding. Clearing the debris does not fix that. It only clears what has already fallen, and more comes down with the next downpour.

The rain behind it was exceptional as the National Meteorological Institute recorded all-time daily records at nine weather stations for the 24 hours ending 7 a.m. Monday, eight of them on the Caribbean slope. Roxana de Pococí measured 263.4 millimeters (10.4 inches) in that period, the highest total in the set.

Your alternatives are limited and none of them is quick. The ministry has pointed drivers toward the Turrialba route, Vara Blanca for light vehicles only, and the Bajos de Chilamate-Vuelta de Kopper corridor. The catch is that these have been taking damage too. Route 10 through Turrialba has had its own landslide closures at Chitaría and at Santa Marta in Siquirres, and Route 4 has been blocked at Recta del Tigre in Sarapiquí with the río Sucio bridge shut over problems at its foundations.

Check each one on the day rather than assuming a detour is clear. Officials counted 24 damaged national routes over the weekend, with ten of those between Cartago and Turrialba, seven in the Zona Norte, six in the Atlantic region and one in the south.

More rain is expected. The National Meteorological Institute forecasts stronger Caribbean trade winds on Tuesday, with unstable and humid conditions continuing because the Intertropical Convergence Zone is sitting just south of Central America. Scattered rain is likely on the Caribbean slope from early morning, with downpours and possible thunderstorms over the mountains through the day. Twelve cantons remain under orange alert.

If you are visiting us and have booking in Tortuguero, Cahuita or Puerto Viejo in the next few days, call ahead. Boat transfers from Caño Blanco and La Pavona depend on road access that is not guaranteed right now.

The ministry publishes real-time road status to its Facebook page rather than its website, so that is where a reopening will appear first. Give yourself the option to turn back, and do not drive around barriers on a closed section. The closures on this road exist because the hillside above it is still moving.

World.title: $38,000 cash and company truck gone, employee now charged
World.content:
$38,000 cash and company truck gone, employee now charged

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 35 year old labourer of Yo Creek Village has been charged after a company vehicle and thousands of dollars in sales money went missing in Orange Walk.

Luis Javier Cordova was formally arrested and charged with theft of $38,000 in different denominations and taking of conveyance on August 11.

Police say Cordova reported for duty at a company located at Fort Carnes Market on the morning of August 4. He was assigned to conduct sales within Orange Walk Town and took the keys to a grey 2006 Nissan Frontier four door pickup valued at $20,000.

By 6:30 that evening, the company’s supervisor was told that neither the vehicle nor the cash collected had been returned.

Border records later showed that Cordova had left Belize through the northern border that same day and crossed into Mexico.

The supervisor reported that company vehicles are for business use only, must be returned by 5pm unless otherwise authorised, and are not to be used for personal purposes.

Cordova was detained on August 9 and the pickup was impounded. He was cautioned and remained silent.

World.title: Department of Environment’s authorized officers to ticket violators for littering offences in Placencia
World.content:
Department of Environment’s authorized officers to ticket violators for littering offences in Placencia

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Department of the Environment (DOE), under the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, announced the appointment of 9 Authorized Officers in Placencia to issue violation tickets for littering offences under Belize’s existing legislation.

The DOE thanked Warren Garbutt, Brice Dial, Sheldon Lopez, Conrad Villanueva, Christine Small, Henry Hamilton, Charles Westby Jr., Edwin Westby, and Naomi Anderson for stepping forward to serve their community and protect Belize’s environment.

The DOE says that this marks an important step in the implementation of the National Anti-Littering Campaign, which aims to reduce visible litter in key areas of Belize by 30% within two years.

The Authorized Officers will support the enforcement of littering laws while promoting greater public awareness, accountability, and proper waste disposal.

The Department says that this is part of a broader national initiative through which additional littering officers will be trained and authorized across the country.

World.title: 64-year-old man gets 1-year sentence for crack and unpaid fines
World.content:
64-year-old man gets 1-year sentence for crack and unpaid fines

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 64-year-old Belize City man has been sentenced to prison after pleading guilty to possession of 0.11 grams of crack cocaine and acknowledging in court that he struggles with drug addiction.

Charles Llewelyn Bennett, a handyman of Freetown Road, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug stemming from a police encounter on Monday, August 17.

For the latest conviction, Bennett was sentenced to three months’ imprisonment. However, because of outstanding unpaid fines from previous drug convictions, he will have to serve a total of one year behind bars.

Court records reportedly show that Bennett has previous drug convictions dating back to 2007, 2008 and 2021. The Magistrate noted that Bennett had failed to make payments toward previous fines and determined that imposing another fine would be ineffective.

During mitigation, Bennett admitted that he is a drug addict but expressed skepticism about rehabilitation, telling the court that he had seen people participate in drug programs without changing their behavior. He also said that when he is working, he uses drugs less frequently.

Despite his reservations, Bennett agreed to participate in a drug rehabilitation program while incarcerated.

His outstanding default prison terms were ordered to run concurrently with his new three-month sentence. Because the longest outstanding default term is one year, Bennett will serve one year in prison.

The Magistrate told Bennett that once he completes his sentence and addresses the outstanding fines, he will leave prison with a clean slate and encouraged him to use the rehabilitation program as an opportunity for a fresh start.

According to police, officers on motorcycle patrol on Craig Street saw Bennett riding a bicycle after allegedly exiting a known drug yard. Officers stopped and searched him and reportedly found a matchbox containing suspected crack cocaine and matchsticks in his pocket.

The substance was taken to the Queen Street Police Station, where police say it weighed 0.11 grams.

World.title: International News: Could this be a Cancer vaccine breakthrough? Moderna stock soars
World.content:
International News: Could this be a Cancer vaccine breakthrough? Moderna stock soars

By Zoila Palma: Moderna’s stock surged more than 140% on Wednesday after the company announced promising results from a clinical trial of an experimental personalized mRNA vaccine designed to treat melanoma, one of the deadliest forms of skin cancer.

Moderna and its development partner, Merck, said the treatment helped prevent melanoma from returning or spreading in high-risk patients.

Moderna shares jumped $91.52, or 145%, to $154.48 in morning trading after reaching an intraday high of $163, CBS reports.

The study involved patients with high-risk melanoma who had undergone surgery to remove their tumors. Researchers tested Moderna’s personalized cancer vaccine, intismeran, in combination with Merck’s Keytruda, an immunotherapy drug.

The companies said the combination extended the time before the cancer returned and reduced the risk of the disease spreading to other organs.

The drugmakers plan to present the unpublished findings to regulators at an upcoming international medical meeting.

Professor Georgina Long, the study’s principal investigator, described the results as a “landmark moment for adjuvant melanoma treatment,” saying the study is the first of its kind to demonstrate a reduction in the risk of recurrence or death among melanoma patients.

The Skin Cancer Foundation estimates that more than 234,000 melanoma cases will be diagnosed in the United States in 2026. Merck Research Laboratories President Dr. Dean Y. Li said the findings highlight the importance of treating cancer earlier, when it may be more responsive to treatment, while Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel called the results a “pivotal moment for the field of cancer research.”

The companies said the personalized mRNA approach could potentially transform treatment after surgery by tailoring therapy to an individual patient’s cancer.

World.title: Mopan Technical High School thanks Mayor Rosales for school maintenance assistance
World.content:
Mopan Technical High School thanks Mayor Rosales for school maintenance assistance

By Zoila Palma: Mopan Technical High School has expressed appreciation to Benque Viejo del Carmen Mayor Jorge Rosales for providing assistance with the use of a tractor to carry out much-needed maintenance work on the school compound ahead of the new academic year.

Mopan Tech said the assistance went beyond the use of equipment and represented an investment in the school community. “This support represents more than the use of equipment. It is an investment of time, resources, and financial assistance that has made a meaningful difference to our school,” the administration stated.

The school explained that maintaining its large campus requires significant effort and said the assistance helped prepare the grounds for the return of students and staff.

Mopan Technical High School also thanked Mayor Rosales for his continued support and for recognizing the importance of providing students with a conducive learning environment.

“Thank you, Mayor Jorge Rosales, for helping us prepare our campus and for being a partner in building futures together,” the school stated.

World.title: Mega-Bingo winner takes home $292,000!
World.content:
Mega-Bingo winner takes home $292,000!

By Zoila Palma: A Dangriga woman is $292,000 richer after winning the Mega Bingo jackpot following the purchase of her winning ticket from Xian Dali Store.

The longtime player said she was at work when she decided to purchase a ticket, despite initially deciding not to.

The winner said she has been purchasing Mega Bingo tickets for years and never expected to land the jackpot.

Recalling the moment she realized she had won, she said, “I was at work playing but I said I wasn’t gonna buy but I did and when I won, I didn’t even want to finish the hours.”

The winner said she plans to use the money to complete construction of her house.

Describing the experience of winning the life-changing prize, she joked about suddenly gaining new acquaintances, saying she felt “nervous like right now because you have friends that you didn’t have and boyfriends that you didn’t have.”

World.title: Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo 2026 celebrated as major success!
World.content:
Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo 2026 celebrated as major success!

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Livestock Producers’ Association (BLPA) says that the Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo 2026 was a tremendous success, while expressing appreciation to the businesses, sponsors, vendors, exhibitors, participants and supporters who contributed to the event.

The BLPA said that the event brought together members of Belize’s livestock industry, local businesses, farmers, families and communities for a day of entertainment and celebration.

“Your participation and support helped bring together our livestock industry, local businesses, farmers, families, and the wider community,” the BLPA expressed.

The event featured a livestock exhibition, rodeo activities, a grilling competition, food, entertainment and family activities, showcasing the work and talent of those involved in Belize’s livestock and agricultural sectors.

The BLPA also thanked the grillers, rodeo participants, farmers, volunteers, staff, judges, vendors and others who worked behind the scenes to make the event possible.

The Belize Livestock Producers’ Association hosted the event in collaboration with the Wild West Rodeo Club and thanked everyone who attended and supported Beef Fest 2026.

World.title: Belize Livestock Producers’ Association congratulates winners of Belize Beef fest grilling competition
World.content:
Belize Livestock Producers’ Association congratulates winners of Belize Beef fest grilling competition

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Livestock Producers’ Association (BLPA) has congratulated the winners of the Grilling Competition held as part of the Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo on August 15, 2026.

The association also thanked all participants whose skill, passion and participation contributed to the success of the competition.

In the beef category, Marc Antonio Uck captured first place, followed by Sandra’s Meat Shop in second and Brian Plett in third. In the pork category, David Flores took first place, with Brian Plett placing second and John Wall finishing third.

The lamb category saw Carl Johnston claim the top spot, while Brian Plett secured second place and David Flores placed third.

The winners were recognized for their grilling skills and culinary expertise showcased during the competition.

The BLPA also extended appreciation to all participants, judges, sponsors and supporters who helped make the grilling competition a memorable part of the Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo.

World.title: CXC success
World.content:
Sixteen months after announcing a pilot for its Caribbean Targeted Education Certificate (CTEC) in mathematics to tackle “the perennial under-performance of students” in the subject, the Caribbean Examinations Council (CXC) on Tuesday reported an 88 per cent pass rate among the 2,535 candidates who sat the exam in the May-June 2026 sitting. A total of 2,230 candidates passed.

Dr Wayne Wesley, CXC registrar and chief executive officer, made the disclosure during the live results ceremony from Anguilla, saying the results were proof that the region has “overwhelmingly accepted CTEC”.

“I am pleased indeed, and I am proud to announce that of these 2,535 candidates who wrote CTEC module one in the mathematics pilot examinations, 88 per cent achieved acceptable grades, and across the entire Caribbean only one candidate received the lowest grade. It simply means that most candidates are benefiting from the approach. Measured against a generation in which barely one in three candidates succeed in a typical sitting, this achievement represents a remarkable turnaround,” Wesley said.

Acknowledging, however, that “a module is not a whole subject”, the CXC registrar pointed out that “the full qualification still requires completion of every module at the full standard”.

“But that is precisely what these results demonstrate. When learning is assessed in focused, achievable stages, our students do more than cope; they excel, they engage, persist, and succeed. The May-June mathematics pilot proves that the modular approach works for students, for classrooms, and for the region. This landmark result belongs to the young people who earned it,” Wesley stated.

CTEC, the new qualification which was unveiled by CXC in April 2025, is at the same standard of Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) and Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) and utilises the same syllabus.

“For years in mathematics — the subject that is foundational to every vocation in life — only about a third of our candidates have achieved acceptable grades in a typical sitting. Behind that statistic are hundreds of thousands of young people who sat in our classrooms for five years and walked away with nothing in hand to show for what they did learn. Not because they learn nothing, but because our instrument of assessment was an all-or-nothing event. One subject, one sitting, one verdict. If the verdict went against you, the system did not recognise you and stayed silent about your progress,” Wesley noted in explaining the motivation behind CTEC.

“I described CTEC as a game-changer, and I promised then that we are witnessing the beginning of the end of the Caribbean Examinations Council as we know it. Today we keep that promise and we make history in Anguilla by announcing that the achievement of the highly successful CTEC pilot in mathematics in the May/June 2026 examinations and, with the approval of our board of governors, CXC is pleased to officially launch the Caribbean Targeted Education Certificate,” the CEO said.

“At CXC we hold to the position that competence is competence, no matter how long it takes to achieve and no matter how the route and… no matter the route by which it comes. This is how things and times have changed. This is how we have to meet this generation of learners where they are,” he added.

Wesley contended that “an assessment model built in the [20th] century cannot be expected to adequately serve a 21st century generation”, but said “CTEC is assessment redesigned for learners without lowering by a single degree the standard to which we hold”.

“When we were designing CTEC we asked ourselves, would the region embrace it? Today we have proof of concept from a region that has overwhelmingly accepted CTEC.
