The TAFE Queensland IT manager said working a level above the training salon meant he could save time getting a haircut, but the $10 price tag was the main selling point.

"It's good because it matches the level [of experience] where the apprentices are," he said.

Benefits blow both ways

The increasing number of customers has benefited the apprentices honing their skills in the training salons too.

Hairdressing educator Naomie Diamond said "more bums on seats" meant her students got a better feel for life in a busy boutique.

Naomie Diamond says talking is a huge part of being a hairdresser, but listening is important too. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby )

"When the turnover is higher, that allows them to work on their timing and their accuracy," Ms Diamond said.

"What we replicate in a simulated environment is what they then take out into their home environment … so being able to produce those skill sets with them is really important."

Second-year apprentice Ahrielle Jeffery said working at the training salon, as opposed to the professional hairdresser that she was based in, gave her a different learning experience.

Client Denise Kelly (front) and apprentice hairdresser Ahrielle Jefferey share a laugh. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"Being surrounded by other apprentices and other people your age … means we're helping each other rather than sticking to yourself," Ms Jeffery said.

"We're all going through the same thing, we're all training, trying to do better and trying to learn, so that's really important."

The language of style

First-year apprentice Chevy Lawford was yet to debut with the scissors but agreed working alongside other junior hairdressers in the busy Gold Coast training salon was helping him develop other important skills.

"I love talking, so it's good to just talk all day, every day," Mr Lawford said.

Chevy Lawford is in the first year of his apprenticeship but says he is learning from others in the training salon. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

While a scholarship in style is the primary goal for hairdressing apprentices, Ms Diamond said learning the art of language was often just as important.

"Communication is key in our job, [but] we have to be extremely good listeners," Ms Diamond said.

" We all talk a lot, but we have to have moments in our time where we stop and listen because our clients like to be heard. "

And for the inevitable cantankerous customer — Ms Jeffery said she had learned the best approach was one well-known in the industry.

"I always find you can just fight it with kindness," she said.

World.title: AFL Players Association labels Swans allegations 'very serious'
World.content:
The AFL Players Association (AFLPA) has added its voice to the chorus of organisations expressing concern over a sexual assault allegation at the centre of a scandal engulfing the Sydney Swans.

Victorian sex crime detectives were due to travel to Sydney as part of their investigation into the incident, multiple law-enforcement agencies yesterday told the ABC, after some of the players involved spoke informally to police while still in Melbourne.

The ABC understands the investigation centres on an allegation of touching without consent following a complaint regarding players' behaviour during celebrations at the Pullman East Melbourne Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

AFLPA CEO James Gallagher issued a statement on Wednesday evening calling the allegation "very serious".

"Our thoughts are with the woman who brought this matter to the relevant authorities, and they should be afforded our respect, privacy and support," he said.

"The AFLPA acknowledges the impact this has had on our AFLW members, as well as recognise the effect on their families, industry staff, the football community and members of the public."

Sydney Swans players (clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney. (ABC News/Getty Images)

Five players involved in the scandal — Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — issued a statement on Wednesday evening, saying they were "deeply sorry to everyone involved" and accepted the Swans' decision to suspend them for the rest of the season for failing to meet club standards.

It is not suggested that they are being accused of sexual assault, and no-one has been arrested or charged in relation to the alleged incident.

Noting the players' statement, Mr Gallagher said the AFLPA, the representative body for AFL and AFLW players, "acknowledges the accountability they've rightly taken and will continue to support them".

"We understand the police investigation is ongoing and any public discussion should be conducted with care," he added.

Investigation expanding over alleged hotel incident Sydney Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich explain the decision to suspend five players for the rest of the AFL season amid an investigation into an alleged incident at a Melbourne hotel.

The AFLPA was just one of several organisations that spoke out yesterday expressing concern over the scandal, with club sponsors QBE and realestate.com.au issuing statements calling the allegations "serious" and saying they would wait for the outcome of the police investigation before commenting further.

Telstra, which the ABC understands has brand ambassador arrangements with two of the players involved, said those players would not be participating in any ambassador activity while the police investigation is ongoing, adding that the arrangements would be reviewed after the investigation is complete.

Governor-General Sam Mostyn, a former Swans board member and the first female AFL commissioner, also spoke out, saying she was "shocked and troubled" by the allegations and "devastated" for all women affected by the alleged incident, including those not directly involved.

The decision by the Swans to suspend five of their players for the rest of the season was welcomed by some advocates, with Respect Victoria CEO Helen Bolton calling the club's statement "clear and accountable".

Greens leader Larissa Waters similarly said it was good to see the club act, "but it's a disgrace that it took a national outcry before they did so".

"This is a serious issue that is bigger than one AFL club, and a serious response with consequences for the players involved is warranted," she wrote on social media.

"We need to challenge gender inequality and disrespect wherever it occurs, whether that's at a school, within an AFL club or at home."

The alleged incident has rocked the Sydney Swans and prompted the club to sanction five of its star players. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich yesterday stressed the decision to suspend the players was not directly related to the allegation being investigated by police, although they said they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare of the women involved.

The bans instead related to the players' decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women to their hotel, they said, with Mr Pavlich adding the behaviour fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players".

In addition to spelling the end of the players' seasons, the club's sanctions mean the players will not be eligible for All Australian selection.

World.title: 'Entire streets' in regional towns miss out on census information in the post
World.content:
Some residents of South Australia's largest federal electorate say they are yet to receive census information by post, prompting confusion and concern about the possibility of fines.

Federal Liberal MP for Grey Tom Venning told ABC News his office had fielded at least 80 calls from constituents in the lead-up to census night, expressing concern they had not received anything ahead of the poll or that they needed assistance to fill out the census online.

Households should have received an envelope containing a census number and a temporary password in the lead-up to last Tuesday.

But the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) confirmed that some areas on the Yorke Peninsula were yet to receive census letters, but made assurances that those impacted would not be fined.

Mr Venning said the delay had caused "unjust anxiety".

He said "entire streets" missed out, including a 3-kilometre stretch near Port Pirie, between the townships of Nelshaby and Napperby.

"Many tried to get a hard copy but gave up on the process, it was too difficult and included extensive wait times," he said.

Tom Venning says his office has fielded more than 80 calls from constituents reporting issues with the census. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

Among the towns in reported black spots were Maitland and Arthurton, on the Yorke Peninsula, less than two hours away from Adelaide.

Creina Cullen, who lives in Arthurton, did not receive a census letter.

"I know that a number of people went into our local post office assuming that maybe they [the forms] had gone there so I'm not the only person in my area that didn't receive one," she said.

Arthurton resident Creina Cullen says she has yet to receive her census letter or form. (ABC News)

Arthurton resident Arty Glazbrook said he had to enlist the help of his granddaughter to fill out his census.

"In other years, we've always had someone leave them at your doorstep or in the letterbox," he said.

"I was aware that you could do it online, but not being tech-savvy, I probably wouldn't have done it, because I wouldn't know where to go in the first place.

"You get some of those little places in the middle of nowhere … they don't get any paperwork, they'll probably just pass it by."

Mr Glazbrook said he was aware of six other locals who did not receive census information by post.

Robert Fidock of Weeroona Island, 15 kilometres from Port Pirie, also said he had not receive any census information.

On August 11, he rang the census helpline before the ABS dispatched a field officer with a hard copy that afternoon.

Robert Fidock says he was surprised to not get a paper census form. (ABC News)

Mr Fidock said he only became aware later on that there was a digital option.

"I'm a 74-year-old retired pensioner and we don't do anything online at all," he said.

"So, it was a surprise to us that we didn't receive anything [in the post]."

No fines for no-shows: ABS

The ABS previously said it expected about 85 per cent of Australians to complete the census online this year, although paper forms could still be requested.

In a statement, the agency said it was "aware that some households have not yet received their census forms and letters".

"We are still dropping forms off in some areas of Yorke Peninsula, if people haven't received their forms yet, they will soon," a spokesperson said.

An ABS spokesperson did not clarify how many census forms or letters were not delivered.

"People who need help to complete their census or are still awaiting their form will not be fined," the spokesperson said.

"Our message is that there is still time to complete your census and we are here to help."

People could request paper forms to complete the census. (Supplied: Australian Bureau of Statistics)

It also said a form number or hard copy could be requested through census.abs.gov.au or via the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227.

The ABS will contact those who have not completed it, but if there is no response to the reminder, the agency may serve a written legal direction.

Failing to comply with the legal instruction to complete the census could result in a court prosecution and a fine of up to $364 per day.

Paper still rules in regions

Mr Venning said many residents still relied on paper-based communication.

"Some people still have old-school telephones, they don't even use smartphones," he said.

"... they're still hearing about it on the radio, they're hearing risks about getting fined. It's unjust anxiety that they're experiencing."

World.title: UK-based firm eyes Tasmanian smelter in liquidation
World.content:
A UK-based green technologies company that wants to acquire Australia's only manganese alloy smelter says the state and federal governments should still be working to secure the site's future, despite it being in liquidation.

Northern Tasmania's 66-year-old Liberty Bell Bay went into liquidation earlier this month, after being placed into administration in March due to financial issues with former owner Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance.

While a consortium that included US-based private equity firm White Oak was selected as the preferred buyer, the deal collapsed and the smelter closed, with around 200 workers losing their jobs.

Creditors then voted to wind up Liberty Bell Bay, with EY Parthenon appointed liquidators.

Their primary role is now to recover as much as possible for creditors.

White Oak is among the smelter's secured creditors and, according to the Australian Workers' Union, is reported to have fresh interest in acquiring the site.

It is understood it would first want the state government to waive its environmental liabilities.

But British-based Natrium Redox Technologies executive chairman Dr Bill Higgs said his company has been in talks with state and federal governments since March on its own proposal, which it says offers better outcomes for creditors and Australia.

Natrium Redox Technologies executive chairman Dr Bill Higgs wants to acquire the Liberty Bell Bay site. (Supplied: Natrium Redox Technologies)

"I think the challenge becomes how to manage a strategic question for the state and the federal government in a world where you've got a clearly defined administration and liquidation process that is running the show," he said.

Tasmanian Industry Minister Felix Ellis said he had formally requested EY ensure all credible proposals are properly considered through an appropriate market testing process before the site's future is settled.

"EY controls the site as liquidator and any decision about its future is ultimately a matter for EY," Mr Ellis said, adding that last week he wrote to ASIC, along with the federal treasurer, seeking its support for the liquidators to investigate the conduct of GFG Alliance and "pursue any appropriate asset recovery or enforcement action".

Tasmanian Industry Minister Felix Ellis confirmed it had been speaking with Natrium Redox, White Oak and other parties interested in the Liberty Bell Bay site. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Multiple ideas for site

Dr Higgs said Natrium Redox had developed technology that produces high-purity manganese without emitting carbon.

Manganese is a critical component in steel making.

He said the Liberty Bell Bay site was an ideal location to test that technology at a commercial scale.

"It's a chemical-based process where we, rather than using coke to strip the oxygen from manganese ore, we actually use sodium to do that same process," he said.

"And it essentially enables us to produce high-purity manganese powder without emitting any CO2."

He said Natrium Redox has two proposals for the site.

The smelter was bought by Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance in 2020 following a period of uncertainty under its previous owner, South32. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The first would see it restart the traditional furnaces while also putting in a manganese processing plant, to scale their technology.

Dr Higgs said it would process 35,000-70,000 tonnes a year, which would add 20-40 per cent to the existing plant's manganese production.

But he said it was approaching the point where restarting the furnaces would not be viable.

"The longer those submerged arc furnaces go without being restarted, the more cost and risk there is in the restart," he said.

"So there comes a point of diminishing returns where they will naturally become abandoned.

" I think we're probably not far from when that occurs. "

The second proposal would see them put in a plant to process around 20,000 tonnes a year of the site's existing waste, which would help remediate the area.

"The nature of smelting is that it's a fairly rough way of cutting metal," Dr Higgs said.

"There's quite a lot of alloy carryover into the slag and into the fines (leftover ore particles).

"Because of that … we can apply our technology to recover those carryover metals."

The Liberty Bell Bay manganese smelter had employed around 200 people before it closed. (Supplied)

Dr Higgs said the restart proposal could eventually employ more than 220 workers, while the remediation proposal would initially employ around 14.

Mr Higgs said the model would fit with many of the federal government's green energy ambitions: from its critical minerals and Future Made in Australia strategies to decarbonisation.

"Being able to deliver ultra-high purity manganese powder for the EV and battery world maximises the value of the asset to Australia," he said.

But he said it would require some support from governments.

He claimed the Bell Bay site "has never been insured on a standalone basis" and believed around $30m needed to be invested immediately to "get to that start line".

He said a combined $15m should come from the state and federal governments, while Natrium Redox would contribute the rest.

A spokesperson for Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres confirmed the liquidators were in talks with interested buyers.

It is understood any discussion between potential buyers and the federal government would be commercial-in-confidence.

Dr Bill Higgs believes the Liberty Bell Bay site is a strategic national asset. (Supplied: Natrium Redox Technologies)

Writing down liability

Dr Higgs pointed out the Tasmanian government is also among Liberty Bell Bay's secured creditors and should be making its views on the site's future known.

"So, it's in their interest to try to get a strategic outcome for the state," he said.

'Substantial clean-up' needed for smelter Australia's only manganese alloy smelter has closed, leaving the future of the site uncertain and the country more reliant on imported alloys for steel production.

He said if the site was disclaimed or if another company took on the site but with the environmental liability waived, the site would be left with an estimated $200m clean-up bill.

He said while Natrium Redox would also want environmental liabilities waived, he said the remediation proposal would see that liability written down over time.

"Our proposal enables the remediation of the site, plus also putting that site back to immediate use where there is no waste that needs to be remediated, and then a progressive return of the site to other uses as we work through the remediation of the stockpile."

Both Natrium Redox and reportedly White Oak want access to the power deal previously negotiated between Hydro Tasmania and Liberty Bell Bay.

Tasmanian Industry Minister Felix Ellis said any proposal involving energy arrangements, environmental liabilities or taxpayer support must be in the best interests of Tasmanian taxpayers and the community.

Tasmanian Labor's Janie Finlay said the state government should be doing "everything it reasonably can" to support a proposal that restarts operations and delivers the strongest long-term outcome.

The Tasmanian Government purchased a $14.5m shipment of ore for the site, which has not been used. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Natrium Redox is a young company with technology yet to be tested at scale.

Asked if that could give the government pause, Dr Higgs said: "you've got to start somewhere".

"We've been working on the technology for about six, seven years now," he said.

Dr Higgs said Natrium Redox planned to finance the proposal through private equity, debt financing and potentially some UK government streams.

It has already registered an office on Launceston's Paterson Street.

But he said it would also look for opportunities elsewhere.

"We're going to widen our search and start talking to others about processing other raw materials using the technology."

An 'intriguing' proposal

Tasmanian Minerals, Manufacturing and Energy Council chief executive Ray Mostogl said he was not surprised the Liberty Bell Bay site was attracting interest, despite being in liquidation.

He said while the smelter was now without a workforce, it also meant a new company would be spared employee entitlements and other liabilities.

Liberty Bell Bay's 200 or so workers were let go before the site went into liquidation. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

He said the Natrium Redox proposal, from the little he had read about it, was "intriguing".

He said building pilot plants to test new technology was expensive, so there would be benefits in doing it at an existing site.

He also said Natrium Redox's decarbonisation ambitions could be "a big step forward" for the site.

"I think we'd accepted the news that [Liberty Bell Bay] was over, which was quite sad — to think that there might be a 13th-hour bid is interesting," he said.

World.title: Coalition's power line pledge could win back farmer votes
World.content:
In a bid to win back support from farming communities ahead of the November state election, the Coalition has promised to cancel the controversial VNI West Transmission Line Project.

The proposed corridor for the controversial energy interconnector between Victoria and New South Wales slices through the centre of Ripon — a state seat held by Labor incumbent Martha Haylett by a margin of 5.98 per cent.

Ripon has also become a focus of One Nation's election campaign in Victoria where the party has gained significant support due to its disapproval of project, valued at between $7.6 billion and $11.4 billion.

Yesterday, 100 days from the election, the Liberal and National parties hardened their former promise to pause the build, declaring they would instead cancel the project entirely if they were elected in November.

Emma Kealy says if the Coalition is elected, a final decision on transmission infrastructure would be made. (ABC Horsham: Alexander Darling)

Deputy leader of the Nationals Emma Kealy said the Coalition viewed VNI West as "dead, buried and cremated".

"We've gone back and had a look at all of the data that surrounds VNI West and it's really clear that the project isn't going to ever stack up," Ms Kealy said.

Nationals reconsidered in Ripon

Gre Gre North farmer Jason Barratt, whose property is in the planned corridor, said the Coalition's announcement was "fantastic".

"It's basically what we've been pushing for a long time and it's not a moment too soon," Mr Barratt said.

"They [the Victorian Labor government] want to basically cut our farm in half with this massive transmission line."

Jason Barratt says Gre Gre is normally "Nationals country". (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

A week ago, Mr Barratt said he was planning on voting for One Nation, saying he was dissatisfied with the Coalition's commitment to pause the project.

But he said the Coalition's new policy announcement had reopened the question for voters who had previously seen One Nation as the only party offering to end VNI West.

"We are Nationals people, normally," Mr Barrat said.

"But obviously when we've got another option that is supporting the way we think, I think we've still got to weigh up everything that's put on the table.

"One Nation having that push, I think, has certainly given the Coalition the nudge that they needed."

Competition welcome

The transmission project has caused sustained tension, protest and upset within west-Victorian communities in its path.

Mr Barratt said the attention from competing parties was welcome after years of campaigning.

"It's good to see that they're actually starting to pay attention and listen to us," Mr Barratt said.

"They just assumed that if you're in the country, your vote doesn't really matter.

" Now people are actually starting to sit up and listen. "

Many Ripon farmers, including Mr Barratt, had thrown their support behind One Nation before the party had formally announced its VNI West policy.

Mr Barratt and FFB chair Ben Duxson previously told the ABC they assumed One Nation would stop the project if elected, because of the party's opposition to Australia's net zero targets.

One Nation has not announced its candidate for the seat of Ripon.

Coalition triggers One Nation

Until the Coalition's announcement, One Nation had refused to publicise its formal stance on whether it would either pause or stop the project.

Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell is One Nation's sole Victorian sitting member. (Supplied: Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell)

Ms Tyrrell said One Nation had been planning to announce its key policies on energy, farming and cost-of-living at an event in Marnoo on August 29, co-hosted by anti-VNI campaign group Farmers Fightback.

Federal party leader Pauline Hanson will be at that event.

Pauline Hanson speaking at a press conference. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Only after the Coalition made its announcement did One Nation answer whether it would pause or stop the project.

"One Nation was always going to get rid of it, and it didn't take us a decade to come to that conclusion," One Nation Victoria leader Warren Pickering told the ABC.

'Retribution and a voice'

The announcement from the Coalition came after Kos Samaras told the ABC that One Nation support in Ripon had climbed above 40 per cent.

Kos Samaras says One Nation could win the seat of Ripon. (ABC News)

Mr Samaras, director at strategy and analytics group Redbridge, said the electorate had traits associated with a strong One Nation vote: an older-than-average population feeling overlooked by the major parties and facing economic decline.

"It's [One Nation support in Ripon is] about retribution and a voice," Mr Samaras said.

" They know by voting for One Nation, it's upsetting the two party system. "

Predicted Labor topple

Mr Samaras said it was likely One Nation would topple Labor incumbent Martha Haylett at the election, describing Ripon as "ground zero" for Labor in regional Victoria.

In response, Ms Haylett did not address the threat to her position directly, instead defending her record by citing a list of local achievements.

"I have fought for upgrades to our local hospitals, schools, sporting clubs, and community facilities," she said.

" There is more to do, but all my opponents want to do is make $40 billion of cuts under a Liberal-One Nation Coalition. "

Earlier this month, Labor's Premier Ben Carroll appointed Ms Haylett as the Parliamentary Secretary for Rural and Regional Development.

'Some sensible policy'

Mr Duxson has been a prominent local figure opposing VNI West for years, and has recently been loudly supporting One Nation.

Ben Duxson is a sixth-generation farmer near Marnoo in western Victoria. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

When asked if the Coalition's announcement would impact the state election, Mr Duxson told ABC: "One hundred per cent."

World.title: Injured farm worker left homeless as labour hire firm collapses
World.content:
On Christmas Day, Davis Lausii slept in a park in country New South Wales.

The Tongan mechanic had arrived in Australia under the federal government's Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme and was recovering from a serious workplace injury, leaving him unable to work for months.

Hidden human cost of cheap food Behind the fruit and vegetables on Australia's supermarket shelves are workers whose stories are rarely heard.

On Christmas Eve, he says he was told the accommodation provided through his employer would no longer be paid for. With little notice and nowhere else to go, he spent four days sleeping in a borrowed car.

" That's what hurt me the most … no friends, no family. That's how I spent my Christmas Day. "

For Mr Lausii, a workplace injury was only the beginning.

His labour hire employer, Plant Grow Pick (PGP), was already under regulatory scrutiny after entering administration in late 2023.

What is the PALM scheme? The PALM scheme, with its origins in the Pacific seasonal worker program established in 2008, helps fill labour shortages in regional Australia by recruiting workers from Pacific nations and Timor-Leste.



The federal government says it is beneficial for both employers and workers, but critics argue the scheme can leave participants vulnerable because their employment, accommodation and visa status are closely linked.

The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) later confirmed it had identified breaches of PGP's PALM obligations and imposed recruitment caps and freezes after the company entered administration.

Despite this, PGP remained an approved PALM employer until April 2025, when the department terminated its PALM deed due to non-compliance.

While other affected PALM workers were redeployed to new approved employers, Mr Lausii was not.

The Victorian Labour Hire Authority separately cancelled PGP's labour hire licence after finding relevant persons "were no longer fit and proper" to operate a labour hire business, but it continued to operate in New South Wales.

Mr Lausii's experience is raising fresh questions about what happens when PALM workers are seriously injured, particularly when the labour hire companies responsible for them enter financial distress or collapse.

Davis Lausii says he suffered a broken wrist in a workplace accident while employed by a labour hire company. (ABC News: Bronwyn Herbert)

It also comes as new joint analysis from the McKell Institute and Unions NSW raises questions about New South Wales' lack of labour hire licensing laws.

The review found 171 businesses with cancelled or refused labour hire licences elsewhere in Australia appeared to have operations in NSW.

Critics have argued the findings highlight a growing regulatory gap, with NSW remaining Australia's largest jurisdiction without a labour hire licensing scheme.

Meanwhile, experts in labour migration, workplace law and labour hire regulation said Mr Lausii's case illustrated broader vulnerabilities within the PALM scheme.

The PALM scheme was introduced to fill jobs in agriculture and meat processing. (ABC Rural: Daniel Fitzgerald)

"When an employer is responsible not only for a worker's job, but also their accommodation, welfare and visa status, problems can quickly cascade when something goes wrong," Dr Matt Withers, a labour migration researcher at the Australian National University, said.

Chris Wright, a professor of work and labour market policy from the University of Sydney, said Mr Lausii's story highlighted failures that extended beyond a single employer.

"He's effectively cut loose, not just by the employer, but by the system," Professor Wright said.

" Australia increasingly relies on temporary migrant workers but provides little support when things go wrong. "

'It's hard to have any job with one hand'

Mr Lausii said he was injured on March 15, 2024, while repairing a broken nut-harvesting shaker machine at Kerarbury Orchard near Darlington Point in the NSW Riverina.

He said it was late on a Friday night. His shift had finished, but another worker asked him to fix the machine so they could continue working through the night.

"I felt sorry for him, because if I said no … he will go back home, he will not work on that day," he said.

Davis Lausii was injured while working as a mechanic at Kerarbury Orchard, in the NSW Riverina region. (ABC News: Bronwyn Herbert)

Mr Lausii said he was reinstalling a hydraulic ram and holding part of the machine in place with one hand, while operating a jack with the other, when another worker pushed the machine.

The heavy machinery arm shifted and crushed his left wrist, leaving it badly broken.

"It's hard to have any job with one hand," he said.

SafeWork NSW confirmed its inspectors later attended the site and issued an improvement notice, requiring the business to review the maintenance activity being undertaken, assess the adequacy of existing risk controls and implement improvements to manage identified risks.

Following an initial operation, Mr Lausii developed complications, including ongoing pain in the back of his legs.

He alleged his employer failed to provide adequate welfare support during his recovery or assist him to navigate workers compensation and visa issues.

Davis Lausii didn't feel supported by his employer after his workplace accident. (ABC News: Bronwyn Herbert)

"Nobody came to see me in hospital or check on me after surgery," he said.

As regulators investigated and ultimately shut down PGP, Mr Lausii said he was left to manage his injury, housing and worker compensation alone.

More than two years after arriving under the PALM scheme, he remains stranded in immigration limbo.

A 'regulatory mess'

Professor Wright has described the current PALM system as a "regulatory mess", arguing that workplace safety, labour hire regulation, immigration and PALM administration are spread across multiple agencies, increasing the risk that injured workers can fall through gaps between systems.

Employment lawyer Giles Fryer, who has worked extensively with PALM workers and other temporary migrant workers in regional NSW, said Mr Lausii's circumstances exposed a particularly difficult issue for injured workers.

"If that worker is injured, that is going to make it significantly harder for that worker to be picked up by another approved employer," Mr Fryer said.

He said PALM workers whose employment ends can in some circumstances be redeployed to new approved employers, but there appeared to be no obvious pathway prioritising workers who were injured and unable to immediately return to full duties.

The ABC understands many former PGP PALM workers were subsequently transferred to other approved employers, including Top of the Crop.

Mr Fryer said New South Wales' lack of a labour hire licensing scheme created an "intelligence and enforcement gap" compared with Victoria and Queensland, where dedicated regulators collect compliance information and monitor labour hire operators.

He said labour hire licensing was not a panacea but acted as an important barrier to entry for poor operators.

"New South Wales is one of the few states left without a labour hire licensing scheme," he said.

The collapse of the proposed national labour hire licensing scheme has renewed pressure on NSW to establish its own regulator, with critics arguing Mr Lausii's case highlighted the challenges of overseeing labour hire companies operating across multiple jurisdictions under a patchwork of state and federal regulation.

"It would be just much cleaner and much more effective if we had a national labour hire licensing scheme," Professor Wright said.

The NSW government said in a statement, it was examining all options for a scheme and has already established a migrant workers centre to assist exploited workers.

It's also strengthened SafeWork NSW to ensure it has the powers and funding needed to crack down on unsafe workplaces and has developed a labour hire code of practice that will be legally binding.

The mobility problem

Dr Withers said there was also a broader structural issue, with Australia's PALM workers tied to approved employers in a way that limited their ability to move elsewhere when relationships broke down.

Report finds persistent problems in PALM scheme Changing jobs is a basic right for most people, but it is not so simple for Pacific Australia Labour Mobility workers.

He argued Australia now lagged behind some Gulf states, including Qatar, in allowing temporary migrant workers to change employers.

"Workers in Qatar and across the Persian Gulf now have rights to change employers of their own volition," he said.

"In this sense, Australia lags behind quite dramatically in offering basic protections for Pacific and Timorese guest workers."

He argued Mr Lausii's case demonstrated what could happen when an injured worker's employment, accommodation, welfare support and visa status were all linked to an employer that subsequently unravels.

"What struck me is how acutely his case demonstrates a sequence of problems,” he said.

" There are many good faith employers in the PALM scheme who are genuinely concerned with the wellbeing of the workers they employ, but luck of the draw is not a sound basis for worker protection. "

DEWR said in a statement PALM workers had the same workplace rights and protections as Australian workers and that employers were required to support workers' welfare, accommodation and wellbeing during illness or injury.

Calls for dedicated pathway for injured workers

The department said it supported workers affected by the collapse of PGP, including facilitating redeployment to other approved employers where possible.

Thousands leave PALM scheme Pacific Islanders have been leaving Australia's guest worker scheme, a decision that breaches their visa conditions and leaves them "extremely vulnerable".

However, Mr Lausii was never redeployed, and the department said it could not comment on individual cases.

The Approved Employers Association (AED) acknowledges support arrangements can come under pressure when an employer becomes insolvent, and a worker cannot be redeployed.

The industry body has called for clearer transition protocols, defined responsibilities for medical, welfare and visa support; and a dedicated pathway for injured workers unable to return to work.

"A defined pathway would clarify how workers compensation entitlements continue, how visa status is managed during recovery, and what options exist for rehabilitation, future employment or return home arrangements," it said in a statement.

Today, Mr Lausii has largely recovered from his wrist injury.

Davis Lausii has been unable to secure another job because of visa issues. (ABC News: Bronwyn Herbert)

He has obtained a forklift licence and was offered a job. But because of his unresolved visa issues following his injury, he said he still could not legally work in Australia.

"They come and recruit the workers from Tonga," he said.

"It's very sweet how they talk and they encourage us to come here … and they just leave us like this.

" At the end of the day, we're still human beings. We need to be treated properly. "

The ABC sent multiple detailed questions to a former Plant Grow Pick director but did not receive a response.

Mr Lausii has an active civil proceeding in the NSW District Court against the company that leased and operated the orchard where he was injured.

World.title: ASX set to inch up, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to inch up, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results Stan Choe Updated August 20, 2026 — 6:34am ,first published 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rose after the US Treasury Department announced a move that could ease pressure coming from the bond market. Strong profit reports for the spring from Estee Lauder, Target and other US companies also helped support Wall Street. The S&P 500 climbed 0.2 per cent for its first gain in four days after setting its all-time high last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 119 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite ticked 0.2 per cent higher. Wall Street notched another winning week. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to edge higher, with futures at 5am AEST pointing to a rise of 13 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX fell for a sixth-straight session on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.24¢. A busy day on the reporting season calendar is ahead, with Fortescue and Northern Star among companies due up. Financial markets have come under growing strain as Treasury yields charged higher through the summer on worries about inflation, big government debts and other factors. That makes borrowing money more expensive for everyone, which slows the economy and undercuts prices for stocks and other investments.



Related Article Opinion

Retail Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets Elizabeth Knight Business columnist But Treasury yields fell in the morning after the US Treasury Department said it will at least double the size of its planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from September 9 through November 4. The department said it’s doing so “to provide greater liquidity support in longer-dated nominal sectors where there is consistent strong sponsorship from market participants.” These longer-term 10- and 30-year Treasurys are less beholden to the Federal Reserve, which can raise or lower very short-term interest rates for overnight loans. President Donald Trump has lobbied for the Fed to lower interest rates to help the economy. Longer-term yields are set instead by investors in the bond market, who decide how much interest they need to get paid by the US government in exchange for lending it money. And recently, they have been demanding more in interest to make up for the growing risks of high inflation, continued government deficits and other factors. After the Treasury department’s announcement, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.71 per cent late Tuesday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher.



The 30-year Treasury yield, which recently touched its highest level since 2007, fell more sharply to 5.18 per cent from 5.28 per cent late Tuesday. The relief could be short lived, some analysts warn. The amount of bonds the US Treasury is proposing to repurchase is a fraction of the overall total. “The boost to buybacks is also happening in a world of challenged Fed credibility,” according to strategists at BNP Paribas. Investors are questioning whether the Federal Reserve will raise the federal funds rate soon to match the tough talk its chairman, Kevin Warsh, has been offering on getting inflation down toward its 2 per cent target. “We do not believe buybacks will be enough to offset a continued loss in Fed credibility,” the BNP Paribas strategists wrote in a report, calling them “necessary, but not sufficient.” On Wall Street, Moderna and Merck helped lead the market after they announced encouraging initial results from a study of a cancer vaccine they co-developed. The new drug showed better recurrence-free survival in melanoma patients who had a combination of it and Keytruda, a prescription immunotherapy drug made by Merck, than with Keytruda alone.



Moderna soared 177 per cent, while Merck jumped 12.6 per cent. The continuing parade of US companies reporting bigger profits for the spring than analysts expected, meanwhile, continues to support stocks. Estee Lauder rallied 16.3 per cent after CEO Stéphane de La Faverie said a key measure of its revenue growth accelerated for a fourth straight quarter. It reported growth in revenue around the world, with the strongest in mainland China. The skin care company reported earnings per share of 39 cents, after excluding some restructuring and other one-time expenses. That’s up from just 9 cents a year earlier and was better than the 32 cents that analysts expected, according to FactSet. Such growth is imperative because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. And strong growth helps allay criticism that stock prices shot too high in their runs to records.



Target rose 4.3 per cent, Lowe’s added 2 per cent and homebuilder Toll Brothers climbed 4 per cent after they all reported better profits for the latest quarter than expected. Related Article Analysis

Home loans Five charts that explain what’s really happening with housing They helped offset drops for some Big Tech stocks, which restrained the overall market. Broadcom fell 4.6 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom have been swinging sharply through the summer on worries that their stocks may have shot too high and that the AI frenzy may not be sustainable if it doesn’t produce big-enough profits. All told, the S&P 500 rose 16.22 points to 7,707.98. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 119.65 to 53,463.05, and the Nasdaq composite added 41.38 to 26,331.09.



In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Asia and mixed in Europe. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 sank 3.2 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi, which has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings because of its heavy reliance on AI stocks, slumped 5.8 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
