World.title: Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more Craig Mathieson August 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Airport Chaplain ★★★★ I devoured the first four episodes of this new Australian drama. The individual instalments are not quite a half hour in length and that works all too well – any longer and the show’s inherent interest about how people and structures genuinely operate would become overwhelming. The Airport Chaplain has a thrilling sense of curiosity, for characters and organisations. It shows you enough to leave you wanting more, helping make it the timeliest Australian series in recent memory. Hugo Weaving and Claudia Karvan in The Airport Chaplain. As the fictional chaplain of Melbourne Airport, Tobias Wallace (Hugo Weaving) is the first responder of choice for the emotional, erratic and misplaced. Armed with empathy, vouchers, and intricate knowledge of the facility’s infrastructure, the old hand rushes from one pressing issue to the next, be it an unregistered support animal, a flight arriving with a passenger who has died onboard, or someone barricading themselves in the prayer room. “No, I’m not authorised,” Tobias will note, then carry on as if he is. Weaving suggests, without ever stressing the point, a myriad of qualities in Tobias, including the contradictory. Is he so determined to solve a problem that he creates more? Is he a humble aide or the possessor of a hero complex? Estranged from his own family, for reasons hinted at, Tobias is so dedicated to his unpredictable job that he appears to be living in a remote corner of the airport. He’s a people-first humanist lodged in a billion-dollar business. That’s tricky.



Editor's pick ★★

Review Hot priest? I wish! This holy love story will instead have you praying for a better script “Your role here is undefined,” his new boss, Terminal Manager Mira Ansari-Cole (Shabana Azeez), tells Tobias, bringing an end to his unsupervised pastoral care. A beacon of efficiency from a different generation and background than Tobias, Mira is at the pointy end of corporate growth – she’s being squeezed from above and defied from beneath, while her own domestic situation is plainly fraught. Tobias and Mira are wary of each other, sometimes adversarial, but there’s also a sense that perhaps they could help each other. The Airport Chaplain was created by Elise McCredie (Stateless) and Jude Troy (The Clearing). The storytelling has a sense of people and place that feels authentic – the bustle and friction is perpetual. The airport is a living organism, complete with a black economy, undocumented favour bank and anthropological edges. The first time Mira tries to make demands of the lead baggage handler, Lex Pascoe (Erroll Shand), he explodes with pent-up complaints about the substandard work conditions his subterranean crew endures. Shabana Azeez as airport manager Mira Ansari-Cole in The Airport Chaplain. There has been a slew of reality series about airport terminal chaos, but in this setting every day brings new issues: don’t get rostered on Valentine’s Day, do help the fearful wife trying to get on a flight before her abusive husband finds her. But in a broader, unspoken way, The Airport Chaplain is about how things work at scale in Australia, and the individuals who influence them. The theoretical and the practical are constantly at odds, as are people and profits.

World.title: The 30 best movies to stream on Disney+ right now
World.content:
10 Things I Hate About You, starring Heath Ledger and Julia Stiles.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The chills of winter demand a night in with a great movie. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Disney+ right now. Related Article Streaming The best 30 movies to stream on Amazon Prime Video right now Don’t have Disney+? Check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix and Amazon Prime Video. 10 Things I Hate About You (1999) Heath Ledger arrived in Hollywood with this quick-witted American high school take on Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, playing the rebel who falls for Julia Stiles’s antisocial classmate after being paid to date her. Aliens (1986) The rare sequel – written and directed by James Cameron – that is just as good as its predecessor. Sigourney Weaver returns as the lone survivor, with the science-fiction setting switching from horror to furious Xenomorph action.



Andrew Scott and Paul Mescal in All of Us Strangers. Parisa Taghizadeh/Searchlight Pictures All of Us Strangers (2023) A beautifully bittersweet invocation from Andrew Haigh, this London-set romantic fantasy stars Andrew Scott and Paul Mescal as marooned high-rise neighbours whose connection transcends time and loss. The Avengers (2012) Marvel’s original superhero team-up remains the genre’s benchmark, with Joss Whedon helming a drily bemused campaign to save the world that gave purposeful roles to the likes of Robert Downey Jr, Chris Evans and Scarlett Johansson. Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson in The Banshees of Inisherin. Searchlight Pictures The Banshees of Inisherin (2022)



On a remote Irish island in 1923, the friendship shared by Brendan Gleeson and Colin Farrell’s characters is unilaterally severed by the former, bewildering the latter. Absurdist humour and bloody ramifications ensue. Black Panther (2018) A true masterpiece of the Marvel age. Ryan Coogler’s African epic is rich in anthropological detail, thrilling action and the tragic rivalry between Chadwick Boseman’s titular superhero and Michal B. Jordan’s ruthless usurper. Chadwick Boseman was the star of Black Panther. AP Broadcast News (1987) The apex of the sophisticated Hollywood romantic-comedy, with writer and director James L. Brooks charting a memorable love triangle between William Hurt’s charming correspondent, Holly Hunter’s driven news producer and Albert Brooks’ yearning pal. Con Air (1997)



A bonkers action-thriller pitting the likes of Nicolas Cage, Nicolas Cage’s mullet, John Malkovich, and – yes – John Cusack against each other. This airborne jailbreak is so over the top it acquires a screw-loose charm. Nicolas Cage in Con Air. Dawn of the Planet of the Apes (2014) Prior to The Batman, filmmaker Matt Reeves announced himself with a compelling entry in this science-fiction saga that charts revolutionary compromise as apes and humans try to share a post-apocalyptic world. The Descendants (2011) With George Clooney and a young Shailene Woodley expertly matched as a father and defiant daughter dealing with a tragic mutual loss, this Alexander Payne tragicomedy explores familial forgiveness through messy circumstances and eloquent acceptance. Action flick or Christmas classic? Bruce Willis as John McClane in Die Hard. 20th Century Fox



Die Hard (1988) With a barefoot and bloodied Bruce Willis defying Alan Rickman’s suave terrorist and his dedicated crew, this landmark action-thriller is a treat. The action goes vertical as a skyscraper is filled with gunfire and sardonic dialogue. Ed Wood (1994) Tim Burton is at his most compassionate in this tragicomic homage to the titular 1950s director judged by history as Hollywood’s worst. A zesty Johnny Depp embodies Wood’s enthusiasm, with Martin Landau as a screen legend fallen on hard times. Darth Vader (David Prowse), Lando Calrissian (Billy Dee Williams) and Boba Fett (Jeremy Bulloch) in The Empire Strikes Back. Lucasfilm The Empire Strikes Back (1980) It’s still the best Star Wars movie. The adolescent heroics of George Lucas’ blockbuster space opera become a darkly powerful and resonant fable of family, faith, and looming doom.

World.title: Enough with the boring alpha men, this is the TV trend I can’t get enough of
World.content:
CultureMoviesThe Verdict Opinion Enough with the boring alpha men, this is the TV trend I can’t get enough of Paul Kalina Contributor August 20, 2026 — 5:30am

August 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ride or Die, Prime Video’s new eight-part series starring Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer, is loud, silly, funny, escapist and as moreish as the popcorn that it deserves to be paired with. Since when does a show about people who kill for a living have the right to be so enjoyable? Maybe since posturing, humourless and amoral sharpshooter men, ostensibly saving the world from bad guys, passed the baton – and their weapons – to their female counterparts. May all our TV assassins be wise-cracking, arse-kicking women of a certain age. Sydney Morning Herald The premise here is that Judith Burton (Waddingham) has led a secret life for 20-plus years as a professional assassin, codenamed Whiptail, for an MI6-type spy outfit. It’s a secret that not even her bestie, Debbie (Octavia Spencer), has any inkling of. This is despite their ability to finish each other’s sentences, correctly guess if a contestant on Antiques Roadshow owns trash or treasure, and rescue each other from sanctimonious snobs at their weekly book club. While Whiptail has kept her shadow life secret (“I kill people for a living,” she finally blurts out), Debbie, who is American, has spent the past 20 years of hers raising children and steering the political career of her dimwit husband (Jamie Parker). That is, until her wet-eared husband, who is on the cusp of becoming the next prime minister, casually reveals he’s divorcing her and has taken money from the kinds of people that Whiptail hunts down.



After a hit gone wrong, Whiptail is handed an assignment to redeem herself and, before you know it, Debbie and Whiptail are dodging bullets and Albanian mobsters, having deep and meaningful conversations about their friendship and trying to find the bad guys who want to take them out, which involves numerous shootouts across a range of glamorous, postcard-perfect European backdrops and guilt-free trysts with younger men. Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer (with Ed Skrein) in Ride or Die. Along with her immaculate wardrobe and coiffure, Waddingham infuses her character with sass, brassiness and sly humour. “Where’s the showmanship?” she asks when instructed to poison her next target. Debbie, who really is the smartest person in the room, never misses the chance for a throwaway quip and to serve comeuppance to anyone who doubts her. And behind the humour and cartoony spectacle there’s the burning indignation of two women who have been underestimated, disregarded and mistreated, and won’t be bound by social and marital expectations. “You’re a WOACA – you turned 50 and started acting out,” Whiptail’s insipid young handler tells her in a tone that suggests that’s a problem.



Understandably, Ride or Die is frequently compared to Killing Eve, the groundbreaking thriller co-created by Phoebe Waller-Bridge and Emerald Fennell (among others) that aired between 2018 and 2022. There, Jodie Comer played a ruthless and wonderfully demented psychopath named Villanelle who works for a secret organisation named The Twelve and becomes the singular obsession of intelligence officer Eve Polastri, played by Sandra Oh. Like Judith/Whiptail, Villanelle was raised in an orphanage (a key selection criterion for TV serial killers and assassins), has a dazzling wardrobe, insatiable taste for luxury (despite her humble beginnings) and complete indifference for authority figures, males in particular. Both shows pivot on the relationships between women bound by a mutual cause and a magnetic bond. Keira Knightley popping off in Black Doves. Netflix via AP The most memorable bits of the otherwise disposable Netflix thriller Black Doves also involves female assassins who are in possession of darkly comic streaks. The plot is largely incoherent and overblown – something about a murdered Chinese ambassador and his missing daughter, nuclear armaments and deep state operatives – but it’s mostly saved by Keira Knightley’s comic-book turn as a sharpshooting spy who is married to Britain’s defence secretary. One minute she’s hosting a posh Christmas party in her Belgravia pile and tucking the kids into bed, the next she’s wiping blood spatter off her face. And that’s before a pair of hilarious, trigger-happy lesbian mercenaries, played by Gabrielle Creevy and Ella Lily Hyland, become involved. If a spin-off isn’t in the works, it should be.



The humorous tone of both Ride or Die and Black Doves is more consistent and omnipresent than it is in The Assassin (Stan). Here Keeley Hawes plays the title role as the middle-aged woman whose sinister past has caught up with her. Related Article The Verdict The most underrated film of the 21st century? It’s nice, guys She’s retired from her role as a gun-for-hire, and living on a Greek island. Then a visit from her estranged son Edward (Freddie Highmore), hoping for a rapprochement, kicks off what ultimately turns out to be a formulaic shoot-em-up thriller. There are glimpses of black comedy as Hawes’ no-nonsense and reckless Julie reveals her deficit of maternal instincts and tries to bond with her meek and introspective son, but it’s not long before this is overshadowed by testosterone-fuelled bloodbaths and acrobatic violence sequences.

World.title: ‘It’s a really intense experience’: The reality show that’s more like a ‘therapy session’
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Robert Wellington, associate professor of art history at the Australian National University, was first contacted about being a judge on the ABC’s Portrait Artist of the Year, he thought it was a scam. “Strangely, they found me on LinkedIn of all places,” he says. “I thought the whole thing was a hoax. I thought it was a big ad and I was about to get charged for LinkedIn Premium or something, but no, it turned out to be legit.” His fellow judge, award-winning multidisciplinary artist Abdul Abdullah, couldn’t believe it either. “I was always a massive fan of the British program,” he says of Sky Arts’ Artist of the Year, which began in 2013. “When I was contacted to be a part of the show I was really, really, really excited and just wanted to be involved in whatever capacity. To be a judge, it is such a joy. It’s the dream job I didn’t know was possible.” Portrait Artist of the Year hosts Luke McGregor and Miranda Tapsell, with judges Robert Wellington, Bree Pickering and Abdul Abdullah. With their judging colleague, director of the National Portrait Gallery Bree Pickering, the three return for Portrait Artist of the Year’s second year, hosted again by actor Miranda Tapsell and comedian Luke McGregor. The judges must find a winner from 54 entrants, a mix of emerging, amateur and professional artists of all ages and backgrounds who, each have four hours to create a portrait of a well-known person who arrives minutes before the clock starts.



Some of the artists use oils, charcoal or soft pastels; other sear into their canvas with a blowtorch or brush gouache across a camping swag or sprinkle salt crystals into their paint to trigger star-like explosions in the background. All are fairly gobsmacked to be selected from the hundreds who apply to compete for a portrait commission that will hang in the National Portrait Gallery. Related Article Australian TV There’s no more Mother and Son, but Denise Scott has found a new path to travel “What is beautiful about the show is it shows you an artist at work,” Pickering says. “We have to remember that behind every art work is a person pouring their skill and their inner worlds out into the public, and for the public to judge and hopefully enjoy.” In 2026, the portrait-sitters range from country music star Troy Cassar-Daley to singer and TV personality Dannii Minogue, broadcaster Carrie Bickmore, food writer and presenter Matt Preston, filmmaker, author and radio presenter John Safran, radio, TV and podcast presenter Kate Langbroek and 2026 Australian of the Year and space engineer and astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, among others. Judge Bree Pickering watches artist Cherie Ceberano at work in season two of Portrait Artist of the Year. Besides the pressure on each artist, it is common for the show’s sitters to express great emotions once they view their finished portrait. “It’s a really intense experience,” Wellington says. “The sitter’s on the little stage for four hours, the judges are scrutinising the works, the artists are scrutinising the sitters. There’s cameras everywhere and they’re being asked personal questions.



“They’ve brought a special object with them and often the object carries a really powerful story about their lives, maybe about a relative that’s passed, or it evokes something very powerful to their own origin story. “It’s like a therapy session. An attachment grows between the sitter and artist. So, when the portrait is turned and shown it’s like a crescendo and all of those emotions of the day come out. It’s a perfect storm for creating that kind of emotional response.” Judge Abdul Abdullah chats to artist Jarrod Prince in Portrait Artist of the Year. Like any TV awards show, winning comes with a caveat: victory does not ensure future success. But that’s not the point. “Not many people can make such a commercial success of their practice that they can live off it,” Wellington says. “That’s a really exceptional thing, particularly in Australia, but probably anywhere in the world. “But choosing to have a life of arts practice or to have art practice in your life is something we can all do. The show reveals how broad our artistic community in Australia is, how many people are spending a lot of time practising and honing their skills who may not have other avenues to show people what they’re doing. This show does give them another avenue, which is really, really precious.” Wellington, Pickering and Abdullah are also extremely conscious of the responsibilities that come with being a judge.



“In all areas of our work we are constantly tussling with each other over what we like,” Pickering says. “A new art movement comes forward, and we’re like, ‘Oh, that’s a bit challenging’, ‘That’s a bit new. We don’t like that’. Related Article Opinion

Australian TV If you are still complaining about Australian TV, it’s time to shut up Louise Rugendyke National TV editor “That’s been the history of art. We all love talking about how modernism changed everything and people hated it when it first came out. It’s part of the beauty of the creative process over time and the show celebrates that.” Abdullah agrees. “The judging part is really difficult,” Abdullah says. “But one of the most valuable things is how the show brings art and the joy of art-making to a new audience. “I have had so many conversations with people who aren’t otherwise gallery-goers or art connoisseurs and they’re rapt with the program and going on this journey with this artist. The more people that like art or are exposed to art, the better.” Wellington, known for his work specialising in the art of France in the 17th and 18th centuries and for wearing fabulous Vivienne Westwood outfits, recalls his first introduction to art.



“I don’t come from a particularly arty or privileged background and my access point to art and culture was through TV shows like [by] my beloved Sister Wendy Beckett,” he says of the late British nun and presenter of popular BBC art documentaries in the 1990s. Portait sitter Kate Langbroek with host Luke McGregor on Portrait Artist of the Year. “Seeing her on television, a great eccentric and wonderful access to art was amazing. “If we can’t be out there being passionate and talking about works of art, there’s going to be a whole generation of kids who don’t get to see it, who don’t get that little light turned on and think, ‘Oh, hang on a minute, there’s something else out there for me’. Related Article ★★★★

Review Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more “This is showing people we’re passionate and that this is a world for them. It’s not exclusive. Art is for anyone who wants to join.” Portrait Artist of the Year airs at 7.30pm on Sundays on the ABC and is streaming on ABC iview.

World.title: Dolphins pitch Redcliffe precinct upgrade as way to ease Games crunch
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Dolphins pitch Redcliffe precinct upgrade as way to ease Games crunch Cameron Atfield August 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NRL’s high-flying Dolphins have pitched their Redcliffe home as a major asset for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games, backed by plans for a hotel, convention centre, high-performance facility, and expanded stadium. Dolphins chief executive Terry Reader said while the club’s immediate priority was a $50 million high-performance centre behind Kayo Stadium, its master plan for the Kippa-Ring precinct extended far beyond rugby league infrastructure. “We’ve got the ability here to actually help with some of the things that are going to become more relevant and important as we edge closer to ’32,” Reader said. The Dolphins have pitched plans for their Redcliffe precinct, including an expanded stadium, as a help to Olympic planning. Dolphins “We’re in constant communication with all levels of government on the opportunities within the Dolphins precinct and the benefits that it can also provide the community.”



The plans include a hotel of up to eight storeys above a new leagues club on the site’s south-east corner, and a new southern grandstand and convention centre to replace the existing leagues club. “Our master planning is aspirational, and it’s something that might be able to kill three birds with one stone,” Reader said. Dolphins chief executive Terry Reader is thinking big about the club’s Redcliffe base. Cameron Atfield “It’s the ability to add the [high-performance] facility, the ability to have the community element in the allied health and education part, but also have a hotel, which is also important given the continued growth of the Moreton Bay region.” It was music to the ears of Moreton Bay Mayor Peter Flannery, who said the region was sadly lacking when it came to hotel capacity.



“We’re short about 1500 rooms across our whole city,” he said. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics NRL to make way for softball, as World Cup locks Dolphins out “We’ve got a huge amount of day visitors, but they go away because there is nowhere to stay. We’re trying to turn those day visitors into three- or four-day visitors, so we do need more hotels.” The master plan would also add a covered southern stand, which would boost Kayo Stadium’s capacity to about 16,000 and include corporate facilities that are currently lacking at the venue. Flannery said that would make the venue more attractive for additional Dolphins matches and other major sporting events, beyond next year’s Women’s Softball World Cup.



“I’d love to see the Dolphins play more home games there,” he said. “We always consider ourselves the home of the Dolphins, and the [Kayo Stadium] games get sold out before they even make them public because the members get first rights.” Brisbane Roar has also been forced to play seven of its 13 home games at Kayo Stadium for their upcoming A-League campaign, due to fixture congestion at Suncorp Stadium during the summer concert season. The Roar and Football Queensland are pushing for a redeveloped Perry Park to serve as a home ground. Last year, Sports Minister Tim Mander said the upgrade of the inner-city venue would be announced “in the near future” but, 15 months later, there has been no publicly acknowledged progress.



Regardless, Reader said Kayo Stadium would be well-used. It would continue to serve as the Dolphins’ occasional home ground and, eventually, the permanent base for a Dolphins NRLW team. But he said that women’s team could not be realised without the new high-performance centre. “It will have allied health, where we envisage having X-ray, doctor, physio, and we’re also talking to the University of Sunshine Coast about having a satellite campus for sports science to enhance and complement the university’s existing programs with the Dolphins,” he said. The Dolphins say they cannot have an NRLW team without their planned $50 million high performance centre. Dolphins “Then we’ll have like-for-like change rooms and facilities for both male and female players, which will allow us to have NRLW, which we’re not in a position to do right now.”



Reader said the Dolphins hoped to have the precinct ready for 2032, at which time it could host on-site accommodation and training for Olympic teams before the Games. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Ekka upgrade’s quarter-billion-plus price tag revealed Around the Games, Reader said Kayo Stadium could help absorb displaced teams and competitions – including their arch rivals, the Brisbane Broncos. “An upgraded stadium might be needed to help with a number of teams and codes, not just the NRL sides that might be displaced during 2032 and the lead-up,” he said. But, despite the Dolphins’ status as one of the NRL’s most profitable clubs, Reader said the master plan could not be delivered without government support.



“We’ve had a couple of false starts with funding support, but now our focus is on making sure we can deliver a facility that our club and players deserve, and also to put us on par with the other teams,” he said. “There are only two teams in the NRL that don’t have new performance centres [the Dolphins and the Gold Coast Titans], but it’s not just about the football side of things, it’s also about the community, not to mention the education and health elements that come with our planned facility.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Ten new ways to experience one of our most compelling destinations
World.content:
InspirationGreat Ocean Road Ten new ways to experience one of our most compelling destinations Mex Cooper August 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s impossible to take the Great Ocean Road for granted: those sweeping ocean views at every twist and turn simply won’t let you. International travellers have made it Victoria’s most popular region for overnight stays, and Visit Victoria chief executive Brendan McClements describes it as “one of Australia’s most compelling destinations”. But whether you’re crossing oceans to get here or you live close enough for a weekend getaway, it’s easy to stick to the same tourist stops. From off-grid retreats to sustainable dining, here are 10 ways to bypass the obvious and make travelling this spectacular stretch of bitumen a once-in-a-lifetime experience. Get blown away Loch Ard Gorge lookout has stunning sights with fewer onlookers. The 12 Apostles rightly remain a must-see for tourists, even if there are only seven of the limestone pillars left. However, mere moments away, Loch Ard Gorge has similar stunning sights with fewer onlookers. Here you can delve into maritime history, including the famous shipwreck for which the gorge is named, before finding the blowhole lookout Poombeeyt Koontapool. Meaning “breath of the whale” in the Keerray Woorroong language, the elevated viewing platform allows you to hear the deep rumbles that precede crashing waves and the ocean whispers that carry calmer waters. Give the view time: watching it shift from serene to explosive can be mesmerising.



Sleep among the vines 



Staying at Sky Pods makes you feel as if you have the edge of the ocean to yourself with 180-degree views across the Cape Otway coast. At dusk, a mob of grazing kangaroos hop into view before the sun sets over the Southern Ocean. Star gazing is unrivalled on clear nights but if too cloudy, a projector screen turns the luxury pod into a boutique cinema. This off-grid retreat, fed by solar power and filtered rain water, sits on 81 hectares of land being restored to its pre-farming state; 60,000 native trees have been planted over the past decade. A 20-minute walk down a bush track leads to Station Beach and access to the Great Ocean Walk, Aire River and Rainbow Falls. It’s a stay and view you will never forget. Meet the locals At Wildlife Wonders guides take groups through bushland for close encounters with koalas, emus and kangaroos. At Wildlife Wonders (five kilometres from Apollo Bay), expert guides take groups through protected bushland for close encounters with koalas, emus, kangaroos and many more. Visitors may be lucky enough to meet the rufous-bellied pademelon, a small wallaby-like marsupial that is extinct on the Australian mainland, or the even smaller long-nosed potoroo, while listening to the sounds of kookaburras, cockatoos and tree frogs. The 14-hectare sanctuary was established to raise funds for the Conservation Ecology Centre’s research projects. Dusk and dawn tours are available and in winter months there’s even a chance of spotting a migrating whale from the property’s commanding position. Feast from the sea



The Apollo Bay Fishing Co-op team with a fresh catch. No fancy five-star restaurant could compete with tucking into a freshly caught southern rock lobster at Apollo Bay’s Fishing Co-Operative. Since its establishment in 1948, the co-op has become a must for tourists and locals alike with its “ocean to plate” dining. The menu changes depending on the daily catch, but the true star is always there: grilled half rock lobster with garlic butter, chips and salad. The Apollo Bay harbour redevelopment shifted the co-op to a pop-up shop and separate fish market store, but both will reunite and return to their original and refurbished digs, including a new public viewing deck, by Christmas 2026. Go retro Angelsea’s The Monty sports a 1950s Palm Springs aesthetic. It’s only fitting that along one of the world’s best road trips, the classic roadside motel is being resurrected with a playful new vibe. Much like Australia’s original motor inns, Angelsea’s The Monty is inspired by American design, sporting a 1950s Palm Springs aesthetic. Mint-green walls, wavy mirrors, chequered bathrooms and bold orange accents bring the fun, while king-sized beds, curated mini-bars and coffee pod machines provide modern comforts. You can charge your EV or rent an electric bike. The lobby, which overlooks the Anglesea River, will morph into a new Mexican Cantina, Nina, to open in late 2026. It will feature a gluten-free menu with the right mix of sticky, tangy and fresh dishes with margaritas to match. The perfect spot to unwind after kayaking on the river or swimming at nearby beaches.



Ride a wave ... You may be surprised how far you go during a Go Ride a Wave surf lesson. Taking a surf lesson can feel daunting. There are the unpredictable waves, the ocean chill, the threat of rips, and the locals carving up the water, but halfway into a Go Ride A Wave two-hour class, and doubts begin to turn into a feeling you can do this. Some in your group may make it to standing, some to their knees, others stay flat, but most will likely leave surging with adrenaline and an urge to return. Supplied with a wetsuit, learner-friendly surfboard and plenty of expert guidance, the tutorial at famed Torquay beach is above all else exhilarating fun. … Then watch a pro Not a pro yet, but 13-year-old Leihani Zoric carves up a wave at Bells Beach’s Indigenous Surfing Titles in May. Justin McManus



Once you’ve realised just how tricky a pop-up can be, check out the masters at play as they weave through the waves at the Rip Curl Pro at Bells Beach. The World Surf League Champion event, the longest running in competitive surfing, is held each Easter at the iconic beach. On days when the swell isn’t suitable, the action is halted but can provide the perfect opportunity to dive into Australia’s surfing culture and history at Torquay’s Australian National Surfing Museum. Enjoy a tasting tour Mediterranean-inspired deli Mortadeli serves sandwiches that demand your attention. Joe Armao The shared ingredient of the Great Ocean Road’s most delicious and diverse food is a commitment to quality seasonal produce. At the gateway to the road, the Booln Booln Cafe takes seemingly simple dishes such as sourdough jaffles and pastries and elevates them with native ingredients such as slow-cooked roo ragu and lemon myrtle meringue. At Aireys Inlet, cosy wine bar Le Comptoir invites you to while away hours grazing on a traditional French menu that incorporates local ingredients. Back in Torquay, Mortadeli, a Mediterranean-inspired deli and “caffeteria” serves seasonal soups, salads and pastas alongside its smash-hit sandwiches that demand both hands. Feed your soul



Samesyn 2.0 has a unique not-for-profit model with proceeds going to charity. Bec Hudson And then there is one Surf Coast restaurant that is taking a really radical approach to sustainable dining. Torquay’s Samesyn 2.0 has a unique not-for-profit model with proceeds going to local charity Feed Me, to help supply nutritious food to those in need. Using the food bank’s surplus vegetables, Samesyn transforms unwanted produce into critically acclaimed dishes, such as chewy carrots that are dehydrated then rehydrated in a carrot juice reduction and served with a maple sauce made from discarded Halloween pumpkins. There are no waiting staff, only chefs, who rotate through service shifts to share Samesyn’s mission – including achieving near zero waste – with customers. The nine-course tasting menu is a meal that will feed your soul. Related Article Great Ocean Road Australia’s wild and unforgiving coast makes this ‘great walk’ sublime THE DETAILS Visit

Wildlife Wonders offers a range of guided tours from $24-$75 for children and $59-$95 for adults. Family tickets and concessions available. See wildlifewonders.org.au. Go Ride A Wave in Torquay has two-hour surfing lessons for $84, wetsuit and surfboard hire included. See gorideawave.com.au/location/torquay. Admission to The Australian National Surfing Museum is between $8 and $25. See australiannationalsurfingmuseum.com.au; The Rip Curl Pro at Bells Beach is on between March 25 and April 4, 2027.



Stay

An adults-only private villa at Basalt Retreat, including a breakfast hamper, is $495 a night with a two-night minimum stay Friday and Saturday. See basaltwines.com.au/stay. The adults-only Sky Pods are $485 a night for a minimum two-night stay. If you want one night’s accommodation, smaller Sky Ships can be booked for $420 a night. See skypods.com.au; rooms (king or twin) at The Monty from $120-$180 a night. See themontymotel.com.au The writer travelled as a guest of Visit Victoria.

World.title: This city has a bad reputation. It’s part of why I love it so much
World.content:
In this series, My Happy Place, our writers reflect on the holiday destinations in Australia and around the world that they cherish the most.

I’m in Tangier, trying to eat my breakfast, but this involves a delicate dance with the bees. They arrive as soon as the waiter brings my semolina pancakes, known as thousand-hole bread here in Morocco, which come with a bowl of honey. The bees perch on the edge of the bowl, dipping their devil-red tongues until finally they topple in. When I fish them out they stagger drunkenly across the table, leaving a sticky trail. I’m sympathetic because Tangier has the same narcotic effect on me. I could become addicted, tumble in and forget to leave.

From a distance, Tangier is a huddle of white cubes stacked on hills. iStock

I first set eyes on Tangier aboard the ferry coming from Spain: a huddle of white cubes stacked on hills overlooking the Strait of Gibraltar. A web of alleyways took me upwards through bazaars and tiny squares where men in hooded cloaks gossiped over coffee, finally to my hotel in the kasbah at the top of the city.

I have a weakness for bad reputations, and if you were looking for a devil to sell your soul to, Tangier was once the place. From 1925 to 1956 the city was an international zone, governed jointly by the European powers. Anything went, and Tangier quickly became a refuge for misfits, drifters, grifters, dispossessed aristocrats and anyone with a shady past. The heiress Barbara Hutton, one of the world’s wealthiest women, arrived in the 1940s, bought a house and threw legendary parties for a guest list that featured Jean Cocteau, Ava Gardner, Truman Capote and Errol Flynn.

Writers loved it. Tangier gave them warmth, cheap hotels, the raw material any writer needs and permission to do what they liked. William Burroughs stayed for four years in the 1950s, consumed vast quantities of illicit drugs and wrote The Naked Lunch. Jack Kerouac, Allen Ginsberg, Orson Welles and Samuel Beckett all stayed and played. Its most enduring literary presence was Paul Bowles, who lived in Tangier for more than 50 years, caught by its spell. “The city existed in a dreamlike suspension,” he wrote, and the separation from reality, logic and identity endures.

World.title: ASX set to inch up, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to inch up, Wall Street higher as US launches bond buyback; Moderna rockets 177% on cancer trial results Stan Choe Updated August 20, 2026 — 6:34am ,first published 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rose after the US Treasury Department announced a move that could ease pressure coming from the bond market. Strong profit reports for the spring from Estee Lauder, Target and other US companies also helped support Wall Street. The S&P 500 climbed 0.2 per cent for its first gain in four days after setting its all-time high last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 119 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite ticked 0.2 per cent higher. Wall Street notched another winning week. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to edge higher, with futures at 5am AEST pointing to a rise of 13 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX fell for a sixth-straight session on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.24¢. A busy day on the reporting season calendar is ahead, with Fortescue and Northern Star among companies due up. Financial markets have come under growing strain as Treasury yields charged higher through the summer on worries about inflation, big government debts and other factors. That makes borrowing money more expensive for everyone, which slows the economy and undercuts prices for stocks and other investments.



Related Article Opinion

Retail Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets Elizabeth Knight Business columnist But Treasury yields fell in the morning after the US Treasury Department said it will at least double the size of its planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from September 9 through November 4. The department said it’s doing so “to provide greater liquidity support in longer-dated nominal sectors where there is consistent strong sponsorship from market participants.” These longer-term 10- and 30-year Treasurys are less beholden to the Federal Reserve, which can raise or lower very short-term interest rates for overnight loans. President Donald Trump has lobbied for the Fed to lower interest rates to help the economy. Longer-term yields are set instead by investors in the bond market, who decide how much interest they need to get paid by the US government in exchange for lending it money. And recently, they have been demanding more in interest to make up for the growing risks of high inflation, continued government deficits and other factors. After the Treasury department’s announcement, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.71 per cent late Tuesday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher.



The 30-year Treasury yield, which recently touched its highest level since 2007, fell more sharply to 5.18 per cent from 5.28 per cent late Tuesday. The relief could be short lived, some analysts warn. The amount of bonds the US Treasury is proposing to repurchase is a fraction of the overall total. “The boost to buybacks is also happening in a world of challenged Fed credibility,” according to strategists at BNP Paribas. Investors are questioning whether the Federal Reserve will raise the federal funds rate soon to match the tough talk its chairman, Kevin Warsh, has been offering on getting inflation down toward its 2 per cent target. “We do not believe buybacks will be enough to offset a continued loss in Fed credibility,” the BNP Paribas strategists wrote in a report, calling them “necessary, but not sufficient.” On Wall Street, Moderna and Merck helped lead the market after they announced encouraging initial results from a study of a cancer vaccine they co-developed. The new drug showed better recurrence-free survival in melanoma patients who had a combination of it and Keytruda, a prescription immunotherapy drug made by Merck, than with Keytruda alone.



Moderna soared 177 per cent, while Merck jumped 12.6 per cent. The continuing parade of US companies reporting bigger profits for the spring than analysts expected, meanwhile, continues to support stocks. Estee Lauder rallied 16.3 per cent after CEO Stéphane de La Faverie said a key measure of its revenue growth accelerated for a fourth straight quarter. It reported growth in revenue around the world, with the strongest in mainland China. The skin care company reported earnings per share of 39 cents, after excluding some restructuring and other one-time expenses. That’s up from just 9 cents a year earlier and was better than the 32 cents that analysts expected, according to FactSet. Such growth is imperative because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. And strong growth helps allay criticism that stock prices shot too high in their runs to records.



Target rose 4.3 per cent, Lowe’s added 2 per cent and homebuilder Toll Brothers climbed 4 per cent after they all reported better profits for the latest quarter than expected. Related Article Analysis

Home loans Five charts that explain what’s really happening with housing They helped offset drops for some Big Tech stocks, which restrained the overall market. Broadcom fell 4.6 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom have been swinging sharply through the summer on worries that their stocks may have shot too high and that the AI frenzy may not be sustainable if it doesn’t produce big-enough profits. All told, the S&P 500 rose 16.22 points to 7,707.98. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 119.65 to 53,463.05, and the Nasdaq composite added 41.38 to 26,331.09.



In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Asia and mixed in Europe. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 sank 3.2 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi, which has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings because of its heavy reliance on AI stocks, slumped 5.8 per cent. World.title: Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more Craig Mathieson August 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Airport Chaplain ★★★★ I devoured the first four episodes of this new Australian drama. The individual instalments are not quite a half hour in length and that works all too well – any longer and the show’s inherent interest about how people and structures genuinely operate would become overwhelming. The Airport Chaplain has a thrilling sense of curiosity, for characters and organisations. It shows you enough to leave you wanting more, helping make it the timeliest Australian series in recent memory. Hugo Weaving and Claudia Karvan in The Airport Chaplain. As the fictional chaplain of Melbourne Airport, Tobias Wallace (Hugo Weaving) is the first responder of choice for the emotional, erratic and misplaced. Armed with empathy, vouchers, and intricate knowledge of the facility’s infrastructure, the old hand rushes from one pressing issue to the next, be it an unregistered support animal, a flight arriving with a passenger who has died onboard, or someone barricading themselves in the prayer room. “No, I’m not authorised,” Tobias will note, then carry on as if he is. Weaving suggests, without ever stressing the point, a myriad of qualities in Tobias, including the contradictory. Is he so determined to solve a problem that he creates more? Is he a humble aide or the possessor of a hero complex? Estranged from his own family, for reasons hinted at, Tobias is so dedicated to his unpredictable job that he appears to be living in a remote corner of the airport. He’s a people-first humanist lodged in a billion-dollar business. That’s tricky.



Editor's pick ★★

Review Hot priest? I wish! This holy love story will instead have you praying for a better script “Your role here is undefined,” his new boss, Terminal Manager Mira Ansari-Cole (Shabana Azeez), tells Tobias, bringing an end to his unsupervised pastoral care. A beacon of efficiency from a different generation and background than Tobias, Mira is at the pointy end of corporate growth – she’s being squeezed from above and defied from beneath, while her own domestic situation is plainly fraught. Tobias and Mira are wary of each other, sometimes adversarial, but there’s also a sense that perhaps they could help each other. The Airport Chaplain was created by Elise McCredie (Stateless) and Jude Troy (The Clearing). The storytelling has a sense of people and place that feels authentic – the bustle and friction is perpetual. The airport is a living organism, complete with a black economy, undocumented favour bank and anthropological edges. The first time Mira tries to make demands of the lead baggage handler, Lex Pascoe (Erroll Shand), he explodes with pent-up complaints about the substandard work conditions his subterranean crew endures. Shabana Azeez as airport manager Mira Ansari-Cole in The Airport Chaplain. There has been a slew of reality series about airport terminal chaos, but in this setting every day brings new issues: don’t get rostered on Valentine’s Day, do help the fearful wife trying to get on a flight before her abusive husband finds her. But in a broader, unspoken way, The Airport Chaplain is about how things work at scale in Australia, and the individuals who influence them. The theoretical and the practical are constantly at odds, as are people and profits.

World.title: The 30 best movies to stream on Disney+ right now
World.content:
10 Things I Hate About You, starring Heath Ledger and Julia Stiles.

The chills of winter demand a night in with a great movie. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Disney+ right now. Related Article Streaming The best 30 movies to stream on Amazon Prime Video right now Don’t have Disney+? Check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix and Amazon Prime Video. 10 Things I Hate About You (1999) Heath Ledger arrived in Hollywood with this quick-witted American high school take on Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, playing the rebel who falls for Julia Stiles’s antisocial classmate after being paid to date her. Aliens (1986) The rare sequel – written and directed by James Cameron – that is just as good as its predecessor. Sigourney Weaver returns as the lone survivor, with the science-fiction setting switching from horror to furious Xenomorph action.



Andrew Scott and Paul Mescal in All of Us Strangers. Parisa Taghizadeh/Searchlight Pictures All of Us Strangers (2023) A beautifully bittersweet invocation from Andrew Haigh, this London-set romantic fantasy stars Andrew Scott and Paul Mescal as marooned high-rise neighbours whose connection transcends time and loss. The Avengers (2012) Marvel’s original superhero team-up remains the genre’s benchmark, with Joss Whedon helming a drily bemused campaign to save the world that gave purposeful roles to the likes of Robert Downey Jr, Chris Evans and Scarlett Johansson. Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson in The Banshees of Inisherin. Searchlight Pictures The Banshees of Inisherin (2022)



On a remote Irish island in 1923, the friendship shared by Brendan Gleeson and Colin Farrell’s characters is unilaterally severed by the former, bewildering the latter. Absurdist humour and bloody ramifications ensue. Black Panther (2018) A true masterpiece of the Marvel age. Ryan Coogler’s African epic is rich in anthropological detail, thrilling action and the tragic rivalry between Chadwick Boseman’s titular superhero and Michal B. Jordan’s ruthless usurper. Chadwick Boseman was the star of Black Panther. AP Broadcast News (1987) The apex of the sophisticated Hollywood romantic-comedy, with writer and director James L. Brooks charting a memorable love triangle between William Hurt’s charming correspondent, Holly Hunter’s driven news producer and Albert Brooks’ yearning pal. Con Air (1997)



A bonkers action-thriller pitting the likes of Nicolas Cage, Nicolas Cage’s mullet, John Malkovich, and – yes – John Cusack against each other. This airborne jailbreak is so over the top it acquires a screw-loose charm. Nicolas Cage in Con Air. Dawn of the Planet of the Apes (2014) Prior to The Batman, filmmaker Matt Reeves announced himself with a compelling entry in this science-fiction saga that charts revolutionary compromise as apes and humans try to share a post-apocalyptic world. The Descendants (2011) With George Clooney and a young Shailene Woodley expertly matched as a father and defiant daughter dealing with a tragic mutual loss, this Alexander Payne tragicomedy explores familial forgiveness through messy circumstances and eloquent acceptance. Action flick or Christmas classic? Bruce Willis as John McClane in Die Hard. 20th Century Fox



Die Hard (1988) With a barefoot and bloodied Bruce Willis defying Alan Rickman’s suave terrorist and his dedicated crew, this landmark action-thriller is a treat. The action goes vertical as a skyscraper is filled with gunfire and sardonic dialogue. Ed Wood (1994) Tim Burton is at his most compassionate in this tragicomic homage to the titular 1950s director judged by history as Hollywood’s worst. A zesty Johnny Depp embodies Wood’s enthusiasm, with Martin Landau as a screen legend fallen on hard times. Darth Vader (David Prowse), Lando Calrissian (Billy Dee Williams) and Boba Fett (Jeremy Bulloch) in The Empire Strikes Back. Lucasfilm The Empire Strikes Back (1980) It’s still the best Star Wars movie. The adolescent heroics of George Lucas’ blockbuster space opera become a darkly powerful and resonant fable of family, faith, and looming doom.

World.title: Enough with the boring alpha men, this is the TV trend I can’t get enough of
World.content:
CultureMoviesThe Verdict Opinion Enough with the boring alpha men, this is the TV trend I can’t get enough of Paul Kalina Contributor August 20, 2026 — 5:30am

August 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ride or Die, Prime Video’s new eight-part series starring Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer, is loud, silly, funny, escapist and as moreish as the popcorn that it deserves to be paired with. Since when does a show about people who kill for a living have the right to be so enjoyable? Maybe since posturing, humourless and amoral sharpshooter men, ostensibly saving the world from bad guys, passed the baton – and their weapons – to their female counterparts. May all our TV assassins be wise-cracking, arse-kicking women of a certain age. Sydney Morning Herald The premise here is that Judith Burton (Waddingham) has led a secret life for 20-plus years as a professional assassin, codenamed Whiptail, for an MI6-type spy outfit. It’s a secret that not even her bestie, Debbie (Octavia Spencer), has any inkling of. This is despite their ability to finish each other’s sentences, correctly guess if a contestant on Antiques Roadshow owns trash or treasure, and rescue each other from sanctimonious snobs at their weekly book club. While Whiptail has kept her shadow life secret (“I kill people for a living,” she finally blurts out), Debbie, who is American, has spent the past 20 years of hers raising children and steering the political career of her dimwit husband (Jamie Parker). That is, until her wet-eared husband, who is on the cusp of becoming the next prime minister, casually reveals he’s divorcing her and has taken money from the kinds of people that Whiptail hunts down.



After a hit gone wrong, Whiptail is handed an assignment to redeem herself and, before you know it, Debbie and Whiptail are dodging bullets and Albanian mobsters, having deep and meaningful conversations about their friendship and trying to find the bad guys who want to take them out, which involves numerous shootouts across a range of glamorous, postcard-perfect European backdrops and guilt-free trysts with younger men. Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer (with Ed Skrein) in Ride or Die. Along with her immaculate wardrobe and coiffure, Waddingham infuses her character with sass, brassiness and sly humour. “Where’s the showmanship?” she asks when instructed to poison her next target. Debbie, who really is the smartest person in the room, never misses the chance for a throwaway quip and to serve comeuppance to anyone who doubts her. And behind the humour and cartoony spectacle there’s the burning indignation of two women who have been underestimated, disregarded and mistreated, and won’t be bound by social and marital expectations. “You’re a WOACA – you turned 50 and started acting out,” Whiptail’s insipid young handler tells her in a tone that suggests that’s a problem.



Understandably, Ride or Die is frequently compared to Killing Eve, the groundbreaking thriller co-created by Phoebe Waller-Bridge and Emerald Fennell (among others) that aired between 2018 and 2022. There, Jodie Comer played a ruthless and wonderfully demented psychopath named Villanelle who works for a secret organisation named The Twelve and becomes the singular obsession of intelligence officer Eve Polastri, played by Sandra Oh. Like Judith/Whiptail, Villanelle was raised in an orphanage (a key selection criterion for TV serial killers and assassins), has a dazzling wardrobe, insatiable taste for luxury (despite her humble beginnings) and complete indifference for authority figures, males in particular. Both shows pivot on the relationships between women bound by a mutual cause and a magnetic bond. Keira Knightley popping off in Black Doves. Netflix via AP The most memorable bits of the otherwise disposable Netflix thriller Black Doves also involves female assassins who are in possession of darkly comic streaks. The plot is largely incoherent and overblown – something about a murdered Chinese ambassador and his missing daughter, nuclear armaments and deep state operatives – but it’s mostly saved by Keira Knightley’s comic-book turn as a sharpshooting spy who is married to Britain’s defence secretary. One minute she’s hosting a posh Christmas party in her Belgravia pile and tucking the kids into bed, the next she’s wiping blood spatter off her face. And that’s before a pair of hilarious, trigger-happy lesbian mercenaries, played by Gabrielle Creevy and Ella Lily Hyland, become involved. If a spin-off isn’t in the works, it should be.



The humorous tone of both Ride or Die and Black Doves is more consistent and omnipresent than it is in The Assassin (Stan). Here Keeley Hawes plays the title role as the middle-aged woman whose sinister past has caught up with her. Related Article The Verdict The most underrated film of the 21st century? It’s nice, guys She’s retired from her role as a gun-for-hire, and living on a Greek island. Then a visit from her estranged son Edward (Freddie Highmore), hoping for a rapprochement, kicks off what ultimately turns out to be a formulaic shoot-em-up thriller. There are glimpses of black comedy as Hawes’ no-nonsense and reckless Julie reveals her deficit of maternal instincts and tries to bond with her meek and introspective son, but it’s not long before this is overshadowed by testosterone-fuelled bloodbaths and acrobatic violence sequences.

World.title: ‘It’s a really intense experience’: The reality show that’s more like a ‘therapy session’
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Robert Wellington, associate professor of art history at the Australian National University, was first contacted about being a judge on the ABC’s Portrait Artist of the Year, he thought it was a scam. “Strangely, they found me on LinkedIn of all places,” he says. “I thought the whole thing was a hoax. I thought it was a big ad and I was about to get charged for LinkedIn Premium or something, but no, it turned out to be legit.” His fellow judge, award-winning multidisciplinary artist Abdul Abdullah, couldn’t believe it either. “I was always a massive fan of the British program,” he says of Sky Arts’ Artist of the Year, which began in 2013. “When I was contacted to be a part of the show I was really, really, really excited and just wanted to be involved in whatever capacity. To be a judge, it is such a joy. It’s the dream job I didn’t know was possible.” Portrait Artist of the Year hosts Luke McGregor and Miranda Tapsell, with judges Robert Wellington, Bree Pickering and Abdul Abdullah. With their judging colleague, director of the National Portrait Gallery Bree Pickering, the three return for Portrait Artist of the Year’s second year, hosted again by actor Miranda Tapsell and comedian Luke McGregor. The judges must find a winner from 54 entrants, a mix of emerging, amateur and professional artists of all ages and backgrounds who, each have four hours to create a portrait of a well-known person who arrives minutes before the clock starts.



Some of the artists use oils, charcoal or soft pastels; other sear into their canvas with a blowtorch or brush gouache across a camping swag or sprinkle salt crystals into their paint to trigger star-like explosions in the background. All are fairly gobsmacked to be selected from the hundreds who apply to compete for a portrait commission that will hang in the National Portrait Gallery. Related Article Australian TV There’s no more Mother and Son, but Denise Scott has found a new path to travel “What is beautiful about the show is it shows you an artist at work,” Pickering says. “We have to remember that behind every art work is a person pouring their skill and their inner worlds out into the public, and for the public to judge and hopefully enjoy.” In 2026, the portrait-sitters range from country music star Troy Cassar-Daley to singer and TV personality Dannii Minogue, broadcaster Carrie Bickmore, food writer and presenter Matt Preston, filmmaker, author and radio presenter John Safran, radio, TV and podcast presenter Kate Langbroek and 2026 Australian of the Year and space engineer and astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, among others. Judge Bree Pickering watches artist Cherie Ceberano at work in season two of Portrait Artist of the Year. Besides the pressure on each artist, it is common for the show’s sitters to express great emotions once they view their finished portrait. “It’s a really intense experience,” Wellington says. “The sitter’s on the little stage for four hours, the judges are scrutinising the works, the artists are scrutinising the sitters. There’s cameras everywhere and they’re being asked personal questions.



“They’ve brought a special object with them and often the object carries a really powerful story about their lives, maybe about a relative that’s passed, or it evokes something very powerful to their own origin story. “It’s like a therapy session. An attachment grows between the sitter and artist. So, when the portrait is turned and shown it’s like a crescendo and all of those emotions of the day come out. It’s a perfect storm for creating that kind of emotional response.” Judge Abdul Abdullah chats to artist Jarrod Prince in Portrait Artist of the Year. Like any TV awards show, winning comes with a caveat: victory does not ensure future success. But that’s not the point. “Not many people can make such a commercial success of their practice that they can live off it,” Wellington says. “That’s a really exceptional thing, particularly in Australia, but probably anywhere in the world. “But choosing to have a life of arts practice or to have art practice in your life is something we can all do. The show reveals how broad our artistic community in Australia is, how many people are spending a lot of time practising and honing their skills who may not have other avenues to show people what they’re doing. This show does give them another avenue, which is really, really precious.” Wellington, Pickering and Abdullah are also extremely conscious of the responsibilities that come with being a judge.



“In all areas of our work we are constantly tussling with each other over what we like,” Pickering says. “A new art movement comes forward, and we’re like, ‘Oh, that’s a bit challenging’, ‘That’s a bit new. We don’t like that’. Related Article Opinion

Australian TV If you are still complaining about Australian TV, it’s time to shut up Louise Rugendyke National TV editor “That’s been the history of art. We all love talking about how modernism changed everything and people hated it when it first came out. It’s part of the beauty of the creative process over time and the show celebrates that.” Abdullah agrees. “The judging part is really difficult,” Abdullah says. “But one of the most valuable things is how the show brings art and the joy of art-making to a new audience. “I have had so many conversations with people who aren’t otherwise gallery-goers or art connoisseurs and they’re rapt with the program and going on this journey with this artist. The more people that like art or are exposed to art, the better.” Wellington, known for his work specialising in the art of France in the 17th and 18th centuries and for wearing fabulous Vivienne Westwood outfits, recalls his first introduction to art.



“I don’t come from a particularly arty or privileged background and my access point to art and culture was through TV shows like [by] my beloved Sister Wendy Beckett,” he says of the late British nun and presenter of popular BBC art documentaries in the 1990s. Portait sitter Kate Langbroek with host Luke McGregor on Portrait Artist of the Year. “Seeing her on television, a great eccentric and wonderful access to art was amazing. “If we can’t be out there being passionate and talking about works of art, there’s going to be a whole generation of kids who don’t get to see it, who don’t get that little light turned on and think, ‘Oh, hang on a minute, there’s something else out there for me’. Related Article ★★★★

Review Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more “This is showing people we’re passionate and that this is a world for them. It’s not exclusive. Art is for anyone who wants to join.” Portrait Artist of the Year airs at 7.30pm on Sundays on the ABC and is streaming on ABC iview.

World.title: Dolphins pitch Redcliffe precinct upgrade as way to ease Games crunch
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Dolphins pitch Redcliffe precinct upgrade as way to ease Games crunch Cameron Atfield August 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NRL’s high-flying Dolphins have pitched their Redcliffe home as a major asset for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games, backed by plans for a hotel, convention centre, high-performance facility, and expanded stadium. Dolphins chief executive Terry Reader said while the club’s immediate priority was a $50 million high-performance centre behind Kayo Stadium, its master plan for the Kippa-Ring precinct extended far beyond rugby league infrastructure. “We’ve got the ability here to actually help with some of the things that are going to become more relevant and important as we edge closer to ’32,” Reader said. The Dolphins have pitched plans for their Redcliffe precinct, including an expanded stadium, as a help to Olympic planning. Dolphins “We’re in constant communication with all levels of government on the opportunities within the Dolphins precinct and the benefits that it can also provide the community.”



The plans include a hotel of up to eight storeys above a new leagues club on the site’s south-east corner, and a new southern grandstand and convention centre to replace the existing leagues club. “Our master planning is aspirational, and it’s something that might be able to kill three birds with one stone,” Reader said. Dolphins chief executive Terry Reader is thinking big about the club’s Redcliffe base. Cameron Atfield “It’s the ability to add the [high-performance] facility, the ability to have the community element in the allied health and education part, but also have a hotel, which is also important given the continued growth of the Moreton Bay region.” It was music to the ears of Moreton Bay Mayor Peter Flannery, who said the region was sadly lacking when it came to hotel capacity.



“We’re short about 1500 rooms across our whole city,” he said. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics NRL to make way for softball, as World Cup locks Dolphins out “We’ve got a huge amount of day visitors, but they go away because there is nowhere to stay. We’re trying to turn those day visitors into three- or four-day visitors, so we do need more hotels.” The master plan would also add a covered southern stand, which would boost Kayo Stadium’s capacity to about 16,000 and include corporate facilities that are currently lacking at the venue. Flannery said that would make the venue more attractive for additional Dolphins matches and other major sporting events, beyond next year’s Women’s Softball World Cup.



“I’d love to see the Dolphins play more home games there,” he said. “We always consider ourselves the home of the Dolphins, and the [Kayo Stadium] games get sold out before they even make them public because the members get first rights.” Brisbane Roar has also been forced to play seven of its 13 home games at Kayo Stadium for their upcoming A-League campaign, due to fixture congestion at Suncorp Stadium during the summer concert season. The Roar and Football Queensland are pushing for a redeveloped Perry Park to serve as a home ground. Last year, Sports Minister Tim Mander said the upgrade of the inner-city venue would be announced “in the near future” but, 15 months later, there has been no publicly acknowledged progress.



Regardless, Reader said Kayo Stadium would be well-used. It would continue to serve as the Dolphins’ occasional home ground and, eventually, the permanent base for a Dolphins NRLW team. But he said that women’s team could not be realised without the new high-performance centre. “It will have allied health, where we envisage having X-ray, doctor, physio, and we’re also talking to the University of Sunshine Coast about having a satellite campus for sports science to enhance and complement the university’s existing programs with the Dolphins,” he said. The Dolphins say they cannot have an NRLW team without their planned $50 million high performance centre. Dolphins “Then we’ll have like-for-like change rooms and facilities for both male and female players, which will allow us to have NRLW, which we’re not in a position to do right now.”



Reader said the Dolphins hoped to have the precinct ready for 2032, at which time it could host on-site accommodation and training for Olympic teams before the Games. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Ekka upgrade’s quarter-billion-plus price tag revealed Around the Games, Reader said Kayo Stadium could help absorb displaced teams and competitions – including their arch rivals, the Brisbane Broncos. “An upgraded stadium might be needed to help with a number of teams and codes, not just the NRL sides that might be displaced during 2032 and the lead-up,” he said. But, despite the Dolphins’ status as one of the NRL’s most profitable clubs, Reader said the master plan could not be delivered without government support.



“We’ve had a couple of false starts with funding support, but now our focus is on making sure we can deliver a facility that our club and players deserve, and also to put us on par with the other teams,” he said. “There are only two teams in the NRL that don’t have new performance centres [the Dolphins and the Gold Coast Titans], but it’s not just about the football side of things, it’s also about the community, not to mention the education and health elements that come with our planned facility.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Ten new ways to experience one of our most compelling destinations
World.content:
InspirationGreat Ocean Road Ten new ways to experience one of our most compelling destinations Mex Cooper August 20, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s impossible to take the Great Ocean Road for granted: those sweeping ocean views at every twist and turn simply won’t let you. International travellers have made it Victoria’s most popular region for overnight stays, and Visit Victoria chief executive Brendan McClements describes it as “one of Australia’s most compelling destinations”. But whether you’re crossing oceans to get here or you live close enough for a weekend getaway, it’s easy to stick to the same tourist stops. From off-grid retreats to sustainable dining, here are 10 ways to bypass the obvious and make travelling this spectacular stretch of bitumen a once-in-a-lifetime experience. Get blown away Loch Ard Gorge lookout has stunning sights with fewer onlookers. The 12 Apostles rightly remain a must-see for tourists, even if there are only seven of the limestone pillars left. However, mere moments away, Loch Ard Gorge has similar stunning sights with fewer onlookers. Here you can delve into maritime history, including the famous shipwreck for which the gorge is named, before finding the blowhole lookout Poombeeyt Koontapool. Meaning “breath of the whale” in the Keerray Woorroong language, the elevated viewing platform allows you to hear the deep rumbles that precede crashing waves and the ocean whispers that carry calmer waters. Give the view time: watching it shift from serene to explosive can be mesmerising.



Sleep among the vines 



Staying at Sky Pods makes you feel as if you have the edge of the ocean to yourself with 180-degree views across the Cape Otway coast. At dusk, a mob of grazing kangaroos hop into view before the sun sets over the Southern Ocean. Star gazing is unrivalled on clear nights but if too cloudy, a projector screen turns the luxury pod into a boutique cinema. This off-grid retreat, fed by solar power and filtered rain water, sits on 81 hectares of land being restored to its pre-farming state; 60,000 native trees have been planted over the past decade. A 20-minute walk down a bush track leads to Station Beach and access to the Great Ocean Walk, Aire River and Rainbow Falls. It’s a stay and view you will never forget. Meet the locals At Wildlife Wonders guides take groups through bushland for close encounters with koalas, emus and kangaroos. At Wildlife Wonders (five kilometres from Apollo Bay), expert guides take groups through protected bushland for close encounters with koalas, emus, kangaroos and many more. Visitors may be lucky enough to meet the rufous-bellied pademelon, a small wallaby-like marsupial that is extinct on the Australian mainland, or the even smaller long-nosed potoroo, while listening to the sounds of kookaburras, cockatoos and tree frogs. The 14-hectare sanctuary was established to raise funds for the Conservation Ecology Centre’s research projects. Dusk and dawn tours are available and in winter months there’s even a chance of spotting a migrating whale from the property’s commanding position. Feast from the sea



The Apollo Bay Fishing Co-op team with a fresh catch. No fancy five-star restaurant could compete with tucking into a freshly caught southern rock lobster at Apollo Bay’s Fishing Co-Operative. Since its establishment in 1948, the co-op has become a must for tourists and locals alike with its “ocean to plate” dining. The menu changes depending on the daily catch, but the true star is always there: grilled half rock lobster with garlic butter, chips and salad. The Apollo Bay harbour redevelopment shifted the co-op to a pop-up shop and separate fish market store, but both will reunite and return to their original and refurbished digs, including a new public viewing deck, by Christmas 2026. Go retro Angelsea’s The Monty sports a 1950s Palm Springs aesthetic. It’s only fitting that along one of the world’s best road trips, the classic roadside motel is being resurrected with a playful new vibe. Much like Australia’s original motor inns, Angelsea’s The Monty is inspired by American design, sporting a 1950s Palm Springs aesthetic. Mint-green walls, wavy mirrors, chequered bathrooms and bold orange accents bring the fun, while king-sized beds, curated mini-bars and coffee pod machines provide modern comforts. You can charge your EV or rent an electric bike. The lobby, which overlooks the Anglesea River, will morph into a new Mexican Cantina, Nina, to open in late 2026. It will feature a gluten-free menu with the right mix of sticky, tangy and fresh dishes with margaritas to match. The perfect spot to unwind after kayaking on the river or swimming at nearby beaches.



Ride a wave ... You may be surprised how far you go during a Go Ride a Wave surf lesson. Taking a surf lesson can feel daunting. There are the unpredictable waves, the ocean chill, the threat of rips, and the locals carving up the water, but halfway into a Go Ride A Wave two-hour class, and doubts begin to turn into a feeling you can do this. Some in your group may make it to standing, some to their knees, others stay flat, but most will likely leave surging with adrenaline and an urge to return. Supplied with a wetsuit, learner-friendly surfboard and plenty of expert guidance, the tutorial at famed Torquay beach is above all else exhilarating fun. … Then watch a pro Not a pro yet, but 13-year-old Leihani Zoric carves up a wave at Bells Beach’s Indigenous Surfing Titles in May. Justin McManus



Once you’ve realised just how tricky a pop-up can be, check out the masters at play as they weave through the waves at the Rip Curl Pro at Bells Beach. The World Surf League Champion event, the longest running in competitive surfing, is held each Easter at the iconic beach. On days when the swell isn’t suitable, the action is halted but can provide the perfect opportunity to dive into Australia’s surfing culture and history at Torquay’s Australian National Surfing Museum. Enjoy a tasting tour Mediterranean-inspired deli Mortadeli serves sandwiches that demand your attention. Joe Armao The shared ingredient of the Great Ocean Road’s most delicious and diverse food is a commitment to quality seasonal produce. At the gateway to the road, the Booln Booln Cafe takes seemingly simple dishes such as sourdough jaffles and pastries and elevates them with native ingredients such as slow-cooked roo ragu and lemon myrtle meringue. At Aireys Inlet, cosy wine bar Le Comptoir invites you to while away hours grazing on a traditional French menu that incorporates local ingredients. Back in Torquay, Mortadeli, a Mediterranean-inspired deli and “caffeteria” serves seasonal soups, salads and pastas alongside its smash-hit sandwiches that demand both hands. Feed your soul



Samesyn 2.0 has a unique not-for-profit model with proceeds going to charity. Bec Hudson And then there is one Surf Coast restaurant that is taking a really radical approach to sustainable dining. Torquay’s Samesyn 2.0 has a unique not-for-profit model with proceeds going to local charity Feed Me, to help supply nutritious food to those in need. Using the food bank’s surplus vegetables, Samesyn transforms unwanted produce into critically acclaimed dishes, such as chewy carrots that are dehydrated then rehydrated in a carrot juice reduction and served with a maple sauce made from discarded Halloween pumpkins. There are no waiting staff, only chefs, who rotate through service shifts to share Samesyn’s mission – including achieving near zero waste – with customers. The nine-course tasting menu is a meal that will feed your soul. Related Article Great Ocean Road Australia’s wild and unforgiving coast makes this ‘great walk’ sublime THE DETAILS Visit
