Tech.title: I Saw the Future of AI in a Robot That Can Learn on the Spot
Tech.content:
Last week, I ventured a whopping 15 minutes from my house to see robots do some mind-boggling, jaw-dropping stuff.

I visited the Cambridge, Massachusetts, offices of a startup called Generalist AI, where I watched robot arms perform simple chores like stacking cups, putting blocks into bowls, and the like. I was astonished by how quickly they figured things out—it was reminiscent of a flesh-and-blood person.

The arms mastered a range of tasks after ingesting a short, instructional video and, most impressively, no specific training for a given task. One of the most striking examples involved a robot that was instructed to sweep a block into a bowl using a dustpan and brush. When the brush was removed from the scene, the robot improvised by using the dustpan like a brush and flicking the block into the bowl.

Courtesy of Generalist AI

In another case, a two-armed robot watched a videoclip of someone unzipping a purse before removing some banknotes. I watched—somewhat slack-jawed—as the robot unzipped a different kind of purse and carefully removed the notes. Most amazingly, when it couldn’t grab the money, it switched from using its right gripper to its left to get a better angle of attack. “Ha,” said one engineer standing nearby. “It never did that before.”

“This is exactly the kind of thing people were really excited about with GPT-3,” Generalist cofounder and CEO Pete Florence told me, in reference to OpenAI’s breakthrough large language model, released in 2020. “You could take that model and just prompt it to do a new task and it would have a real shot at doing it.”

Generalist appears to be focused on teaching its robots about the physics of the world, which seems inspired by the intuitive sense of physics humans exhibit from an early age. That may well contribute to the model’s ability to transfer what it has learned in one scenario to another. In fact, some of the company’s demos made me think of how children improvise and experiment when shown a task. The researchers have often been surprised by what the robot decides to do—one chose to sweep up items with a banana when it was placed in front of it, for example. This might seem trivial, but physical intelligence is something still largely lacking in machines, and the way babies learn so efficiently about their world may offer important insights for AI researchers.

Tech.title: Coders Say They Already Found Workarounds to Claude’s Invisible Watermarks
Tech.content:
Within four hours of Anthropic confirming that Claude models would globally embed invisible, machine-readable watermarks into any AI-generated content, developer Guillaume Meyer had published his override.

His code to remove watermarks from Claude-generated text has since gone viral on GitHub, has been bookmarked more than 20,000 times on X, and has drawn more than 100 contributors, with many more incorporating the technology into their own projects. “Anthropic is embedding watermarks in its Claude texts … the issue is practically history just one day later,” wrote one AI specialist, accompanied by an image of Meyer breaking out of chains and standing on crumpled EU and Anthropic flags.

Meyer and others started investigating how watermarking works after Anthropic announced last week that Claude would adopt it in order to comply with the European Union’s AI Act.

Some are trying to evade the watermarking because they disagree with the idea that all AI-generated content should be labeled as such, Meyer told WIRED, while others, including himself, say they simply relish the technical challenge. Freelance content writers and social media creators have also contacted Meyer asking for assistance using the code, he says.

The new rules, which came in earlier this month, stipulate that model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI must label synthetic audio, image, video, or text so that this material can be detected by a machine as AI-generated—or face fines of up to 3 percent of annual turnover. While the rules say providers cannot market circumvention tools, there is no legal restriction on independent tools.

Tech.title: Google Pixel Watch 5 Review: More Health, More AI
Tech.content:
Whether you’ll actually use all of this depends on your active lifestyle, but I can see it being particularly useful for someone new to the gym who wants a little structure that feels personal. I do appreciate that it syncs to the watch, so I can see rep counts and rest intervals without unlocking my phone.

Gemini is still one of Pixel Watch’s best features, and it can now tackle offline tasks, such as starting a workout, which is handy if you tend to leave your phone at home on runs. The dual-band GPS is the same, but Google says route tracking is now twice as accurate in urban environments. It now accounts for atmospheric interference and multipath errors, which should help it maintain more accurate positioning around tall buildings. So far, I’ve had zero issues with route mapping in Chicago, and I can say the same for the previous model. I’m curious whether people in New York City might notice a bigger difference.

The Watch 5 retains several health features from its predecessors, including Loss of Pulse detection, ECG, and skin temperature tracking. It also introduces four Health Guardian tools that have undergone clinical validation and will be available in September: Insulin Resistance Trends, Blood Pressure Trends, Breathing Emergency Detection, and Sleep Breathing Quality Trends.

Insulin Resistance Trends analyzes weeks of physiological data to identify shifts in metabolic health without requiring a blood draw. The watch can also passively track pulse and motion patterns throughout the month to estimate blood pressure trends without manual calibration. Breathing Emergency Detection monitors blood oxygen levels for potentially dangerous drops and, if you become unresponsive, can automatically contact emergency services.

Watch 5 sleep tracking. Screenshot: Boutayna Chokrane

Lastly, Sleep Breathing Quality uses minute-by-minute variations in blood oxygen levels to understand your breathing patterns better while you sleep. Every morning, you’ll see how much of the night you spent with optimal breathing, along with a monthly assessment to recognize longer-term trends. Most of these Health Guardian features, except for Breathing Emergency Detection, are more useful for identifying patterns and should not be used for diagnosis. I wasn’t able to evaluate Health Guardian during testing, considering many of these features aren't available yet and they require a month of data before establishing meaningful trends.

On the topic of slumber, sleep tracking gets a refresh, too. Google says the Pixel Watch 5 is 15 percent more accurate at tracking sleep than its predecessor. There’s now a dedicated Bedtime Mode that silences notifications, disables the always-on display, simplifies the watch face, and adds a red tint designed to be easier on your eyes in the dark. If you enable the setting, the watch can also automatically pause media when it detects that you’ve fallen asleep.

Smart Wake Alarms aim to wake you during a 30-minute window when you’re in your lightest stage of sleep. This is one of those features that will depend on your personal preference. I value every last minute of sleep, and I find that Smart Wake inevitably wakes me earlier than I want. It’s also worth remembering that sleep-stage tracking is better as a way to identify long-term patterns than as a precise measurement, which makes me a little skeptical of Smart Wake’s accuracy.

Tech.title: Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL Review: Smart Software, Small Upgrade
Tech.content:
There is one new feature on Google's Pixel 11 series that, I kid you not, caused my jaw to drop. It's an upgrade over one of my most-used Pixel features: voice-to-text.

I am a swipe typer, whizzing my finger across letters to form words instead of tapping each key individually. But I'm also heavily reliant on voice typing. Google's Pixel phones are far and away the best at it; more accurate at understanding my words than iPhones and Samsungs, not to mention sprinkling in punctuation at the right moments.

With the Pixel 11 devices, there's a new feature called Rambler—an upgraded, AI-powered voice-to-text feature—that is smarter than anything you've probably used before. Tap the microphone button on Gboard, and start talking. The Pixel will strip away the “ums” and “uhs,” and if you make a mistake and restate something, it won't bother to include that bit in your message, only keeping the parts it believes you want to convey. You can even ask it to add bullet points or an emoji to format your message, all in the same breath.

Tech.title: Why Is It Absolute Hell to Buy a Movie Ticket Now?
Tech.content:
The conclusion to Denis Villeneuve’s epic Dune trilogy is still four months away, but the anticipation was palpable on Tuesday, the first day of ticket presales.

Theater chain apps suffered apparent outages as moviegoers waited in long virtual lines, hoping to finally glimpse a seat map with some empty spots left on it. In Manhattan, those who have grown mistrustful of this unreliable tech found time on a weekday morning to line up around the block at AMC Lincoln Square—hours before the box office opened. It was the third frenzied rush for blockbuster tickets in a few short weeks, following sky-high demand for Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Destin Daniel Cretton’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

Customers have been particularly keen to see these films on IMAX screens, with Dune: Part Three and The Odyssey also available in the even more exclusive IMAX 70mm format. Only 25 theaters in the US are capable of showing a film this way.

While directors and studios have embraced such premium screenings for tentpole releases (not least because those tickets are more expensive), the rarity of theaters equipped for them has contributed to a scarcity mindset. People are so bent on experiencing these movies in the “best” possible way, and, if not on opening night, as soon after as possible, that ticket resellers have attempted to auction them off for hundreds of dollars, while some cinephiles have embarked on Homeric journeys to IMAX theaters multiple states away.

As such, this week’s competition for Dune: Part Three tickets renewed a feeling of stress and weariness among fans of Hollywood spectacle. Why, some asked, does catching a movie now feel as difficult as scoring tickets to a red-hot concert tour?

Adam Aron, CEO of AMC Theatres, took to his X account to apologize for the latest cinematic frustrations. (Reached for comment, the company directed WIRED to his comments on the platform.) “We thought we were ready, but we weren’t,” he wrote of the Dune launch, noting that the traffic surge to AMC’s website and mobile app was about triple the volume they’d seen for the latest Spider-Man installment.

“It’s a high-class problem to have such staggering demand, but even so it is intolerable and inexcusable,” Aron wrote. He further announced that $2 million in IT costs had been approved in order to “fully address the issue.”

Fandango and Regal Cinemas, whose apps and websites also drew complaints amid ongoing glitches, did not immediately return requests for comment. A representative for IMAX, which is not involved in ticket sales, declined to comment on the record. IMAX currently has more than 1,800 locations worldwide; in a quarterly financial update earlier this year, CEO Rich Gelfond said they saw the potential to double their footprint.

This depends, however, on exhibitors actively investing in more IMAX venues, as well as the availability of new or retrofitted auditoriums big enough for the screens and the theater architecture that goes along with them.

In the meantime, customer exasperation is mounting. Internet film critics bemoaned the “concertification” of movies as they contended with the same overloaded apps and long lines as everyone else.

“I'm done with the shenanigans of trying to be ‘FIRST’ to see these blockbuster films,” Simone Cromer, once known for her “Club Chalamet” fan accounts devoted to Dune star Timothée Chalamet, wrote on X. “I'll watch it on a regular screen sometime that week, without having to travel too far.”

Tech.title: The Best Digital Wall Calendar (2026): Skylight, Everblog, Apolosign
Tech.content:
I won’t lie to you: I hated the first digital wall calendar I tried.

I tested it last year and was left unimpressed. It was expensive and massive, and my calendar details were slow to appear (if they appeared at all). The device felt more like clutter than a useful addition to my home. So, I wrote off the idea of using a digital wall calendar, but to my surprise, they have only picked up in popularity and options since then. After trying a few new models myself this year, I can now see why.

These gadgets work by taking your online calendar—whether your Google Calendar, the calendar app on your iPhone, or your corporate Microsoft calendar account—and putting it on a digital screen that you can mount on the wall or prop up on a countertop or table. They’re often more than just calendars, also functioning as chore charts, meal planners, and sometimes even digital photo frames. I usually have smart displays all over my home, especially in my kitchen and living area, but for the past two weeks, I’ve replaced them all with digital wall calendars. And you know what? I don't miss talking to those annoying AI-powered assistants.

Instead, as someone who already lives and breathes by her Google Calendar, I love being able to see it on a large display in the middle of the kitchen, without needing my phone—especially when it’s on a digital wall device that immediately reflects my most up-to-date calendar. My husband and I have also been using the extra features more often, particularly to guide my 4-year-old through his evening bedtime routine with the help of his own companion device. Here's everything you need to know about the best digital wall calendars and whether they're right for you.

Updated August 2026: I've added the Skylight Buddy as a kid-friendly tool that includes some features of these digital calendar devices. I’ve also ensured accuracy and up-to-date information throughout.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

What’s a Digital Wall Calendar?

Video: Nena Farrell Photograph: Nena Farrell

You might have heard these gadgets called by various names. Maybe “digital wall calendar” or “smart calendar device.” Maybe you've just heard the name Skylight Calendar, which is a notably popular model right now. No matter what you call them, these devices all do the same thing: replace a paper calendar with a digitized one that connects to the calendar tools you're already using, like Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. The devices let you see your entire family’s schedule in one view, with the ability to update or add to it without needing a phone or a separate account. It also erases issues like unreadable handwriting and forgetting to write down an event you've already scheduled digitally, and its color-coding system makes it easy to see who's on the hook for which activities.

Tech.title: I Tried a Window-Cleaning Robot: Do Not Recommend
Tech.content:
I love the idea of robots taking over menial tasks, so I was excited to try the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni. This premium window-cleaning robot is highly rated online. I have a robot vacuum and a robot mower, and I would never go back to doing these chores myself. Sadly, I had such a traumatically awful experience with the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni that I’m left wondering why anyone would want a window-cleaning robot at all.

Before I embark on this tale of woe, I should point out that most of my issues are with the whole category, not the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni specifically. There are circumstances where I can imagine it working well. I briefly tested another window-cleaning robot, the much cheaper Mova N1 ($199), for comparison, and can attest that the Ecovacs has a much smarter design and cleans more efficiently. It might even be the best window-cleaning robot you can get; I just don’t think a robot for cleaning windows is worthwhile for most homes.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

The Good

The Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni has a smart design and comes in a charging case that includes its own battery. The case has slots and compartments for cables, spare pads, cleaning solution, and the bot itself, attached with a retractable, braided, 18-foot cable. It looks like a little cooler with a folding handle and weighs around 15 pounds. A full charge gives you 110 minutes of cleaning.

The Winbot is 10 by 10 by 2.5 inches and weighs around 4 pounds. You attach a cleaning pad to the Velcro sections and fill it with the cleaning solution. It has a leatherlike strap for picking it out of the case and sticking it to the window. Press the button on the front to start it up. It takes a few seconds to ramp up the suction, then tells you when it’s firmly in place, so you can let go. This is a nerve-racking moment the first few times, but the suction is plenty powerful.

Tech.title: ‘Your Excel Skills Suck’: The Power Users Turning Spreadsheets Into a Spectator Sport
Tech.content:
For many people, Microsoft Excel is to be avoided at all costs.

Maybe you lied about being “proficient” with the spreadsheet program to pad out your résumé and have lived in fear of being found out ever since. Or it could be that you do have a grasp on a few basic formulas but find the interface too labyrinthine to truly master.

Still, like it or not, Excel remains an integral part of businesses, with Microsoft claiming “hundreds of millions” of users worldwide. But for a thriving community of content creators, Excel’s uses go far beyond practicality. They live for the thrills of ninja-like Excel efficiency, and they’re happy to impart their esoteric knowledge to those brave enough to seek it out. They amass huge fandoms by demonstrating their flair for unexpected productivity hacks and posting record times on “obstacle runs,” with some even competing in official Excel championships for prize money (and bragging rights).

Vying for spreadsheet glory is just part of the fun, however. At the end of the day, everyone really wants to help each other get better.

Dan Kidney, 32, in London, tells WIRED he “accidentally” leveled up his Excel skills while working as an insurance data analyst and building his own ecommerce company from scratch, though he never expected to teach others the tricks he’d picked up in that time.

“I decided to start using my spare time to post on TikTok as an experiment during a planned employment break,” he explains, first sharing videos covering the Excel functions a beginner should know. A few weeks in, Kidney posted footage of himself racing through the varied challenges of an Excel obstacle course he’d designed himself—and engagement suddenly exploded, pushing the clip to 1 million views within days. Commenters replied that he had completed each page before they’d even had time to read the instructions on it.

Today, Kidney has a combined 300,000 followers on Instagram and TikTok accounts, both called “Functional Excel,” and his speedruns have had a surprising impact beyond his own office. He says a schoolteacher in rural Germany saw his videos and assigned his students to practice Excel on his templates, leading to a class competition.

“Your Excel skills suck,” says Jonathan Tristan, a 29-year-old content creator known as “Your Finance Brother,” in a video recently posted to his TikTok and Instagram pages. Like other influencers in the space, Tristan, who is based in Los Angeles and was previously an investment banker, advocates for dispensing entirely with the mouse and relying only on a flurry of keyboard combination moves to navigate Excel. And he goes one step further: “Pop the F1 key off your keyboard,” he instructs his viewers.

Excel’s power users end up with “stylistic preferences,” Tristan says, and ditching the F1 key is an example of a choice that is both practical and something of a flex. “A really common shortcut you'll use is that you'll basically toggle between the Escape and the F2 key to see what your formula is doing in Excel,” he explains. The problem is that if you accidentally hit F1, which sits between those keys, it brings up a help menu, slowing down your work. (Plus, would a genuine operator ever need help?)

Tristan, who has shared his own impressive Excel speedruns, says he imparts this kind of wisdom to his approximately 700,000 followers because every minute counts when you’re working around the clock on Wall Street—going 10 percent faster if you spend 10 hours a day in Excel, he says, is the difference between “getting five hours of sleep versus six hours of sleep.”

Tech.title: Peacock Is Testing Out a Rewards Program for Subscribers
Tech.content:
There aren’t too many streaming services that lean into membership perks for their subscribers, but Peacock is testing the waters with a rewards program. On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of a beta test for a select group of Peacock Premium and Premium Plus subscribers, aimed at providing “meaningful recognition, exclusive access, flexibility, and experiences that extend beyond traditional discounts.”

The news arrives the same week the streamer announced a round of price hikes across its plans.

The rewards membership is included with the streaming subscription at no extra cost, and is offered in three tiers based on how long you’ve subscribed to the service. Customers who’ve had an account for three months to one year are in the Gold tier; Platinum members are those with one to three years under their belts; any subscriber who’s had one of the eligible Peacock plans for more than three years is in the Diamond tier.

For now, the beta version has rewards that fall under four categories. NBCUniversal rewards are tailored for Peacock and NBCU programming brands, and currently, subscribers can get discounts on items in the NBCU Shop or Bravo Shop. Partner rewards are tied to perks from the brand’s partners, and at rollout, that includes a free Instacart Plus membership. Subscribers can also tap into Engagement rewards (based on app activity) or Experiential rewards, which are designed to give fans real experiences within the NBCUniversal world.

As the testing phase continues, Peacock plans to expand the program and offer more rewards and benefits connected to Universal Parks, early entry to live events from NBCUniversal and previews of TV shows and films.

Loyalty programs from platforms such as Disney Plus and Crunchyroll give members the opportunity to buy products at a discount, receive exclusive or early access to events or take advantage of savings at partner companies. While Peacock’s rewards program doesn’t cost extra for subscribers, some offers may have small fees attached.

Tech.title: Whoop Expands Beyond Its Wearable Membership With Blood Tests
Tech.content:
Health-tracking wearables offer insight into what’s going on inside our bodies, and it’s become increasingly common for those details to come at a cost – not just once, at purchase, but as part of a monthly or yearly membership. On Tuesday, Whoop, maker of the screenless Whoop 5.0 fitness tracker, announced that it’s branching beyond that model by offering blood tests with a la carte prices.

For this Advanced Labs initiative, Whoop is working with the US medical lab testing company Quest Diagnostics to test for over 122 biomarkers across heart, metabolic, performance, hormonal health and more.

How Whoop’s blood tests work

For $69 to $299, after you choose your blood work panel, you can schedule a test at a Quest location in the Whoop app, and a doctor will order it for you. You have up to 12 months to schedule your test after the date of purchase, and you may be able to use your HSA or FSA funds, but you should check with your plan provider first to confirm eligibility.

Those fees are separate from Whoop’s membership, which ranges from $199 to $359.

Once your results are in, a doctor will review them and provide you with an action plan, which will also be available in the Whoop app. You’ll also receive personalized AI insights that give “added context to the results and support with building the action plan,” a Whoop representative told CNET via email. No wearable is required for these insights.

Different states, different rules

Currently, Whoop’s Advanced Labs is unavailable in Hawaii, Wyoming, South Dakota and North Dakota.

If you live in New York, New Jersey or Rhode Island, state law requires that you pay an additional fee for each blood panel. According to Whoop, the fee varies by panel and will be collected at your lab appointment once you check in. No information is provided on the exact fee per panel or per state, but your Quest location should be able to provide that information.

Whoop’s blood panels can measure glucose, sodium, calcium and more. Whoop

A new multicancer early detection test

Announced alongside its Advanced Labs expansion, Whoop has added the Galleri multicancer early detection test to its offerings. Created by the Grail clinical laboratory, Galleri is a $799 test designed to detect cancer signals associated with over 50 cancer types. After your blood is drawn at a Quest location, the test is then performed at Grail’s North Carolina lab.

According to Whoop’s July 30 announcement about its Grail collaboration, Galleri isn’t a diagnosis, hasn’t been FDA-approved, doesn’t detect all cancers and shouldn’t be used as a replacement for the routine cancer screenings recommended by your doctor.

Galleri is specifically recommended for adults who have an elevated cancer risk, such as people age 50 or older. It isn’t recommended for pregnant people, individuals age 21 or younger or those actively being treated for cancer. If you’re unsure if this test is right for you, speak with your doctor.

If a cancer signal is detected, follow-up testing will be required for more information. A doctor will reach out about next steps, and you can also contact a Grail patient advocate.

Will other companies follow suit?

New product offerings in the wearables industry often become trends. When one company starts offering a certain feature to its users, others soon follow.

Ultrahuman, maker of the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, already offers blood testing through its Blood Vision platform, while Oura Ring creator Oura provides lab tests with its Health Panels service. However, both Oura and Ultrahuman currently require membership plans for their lab tests.

Whoop’s move away from its membership model, centered on a wearable, toward a broader health platform with lab testing could signal a shift in the industry. Perhaps it’s no longer enough to provide a health-tracking device that comes with recurring payments. For a company to stand out , it may need to become a one-stop shop with one-time prices for a variety of consumers’ health needs.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Is One of My Favorite Android Phones, but It’s Not a Revolution
Tech.content:
The Pixel 11 Pro isn’t a revolution. It’s a scattering of upgrades, most of which are minor. While Google could have tried harder to overhaul its flagship, I actually don’t think it needed to. The Pixel 10 Pro was already a superb, award-winning Android phone, and the 11 Pro simply builds on that success. The result is a slick device I really enjoy using.

There’s the new Tensor G6 processor, a bevy of fresh camera tricks and faster charging speeds. It’s got a polished design with a new notification light and a peachy color that’s glorious to look at. Sure, there’s some new AI stuff thrown in too. It all adds up to the Pixel 11 Pro being one of the most refined phones Google has ever made.

While I was expecting a significant price bump everywhere due to the ongoing components shortage, Google technically made its base model cheaper in some regions and more expensive in others. It depends on where you live.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET Google Pixel 11 Pro 8.0 Preorder at Amazon Pros & Cons Beautiful design

Easy to use

Solid camera with creative filters Battery life could be better

Base models have less RAM

Google eliminated the $999 128GB storage option from its Pro lineup, making the $1,099 Pixel 11 Pro with 256GB of storage the new entry point for the premium models. If you’re lucky enough to live in the UK, like me, 256GB of storage is now marginally more affordable with the Pixel 11 Pro starting at £1,079, £20 less than the 256GB Pixel 10 Pro. The Pixel 11 Pro XL is more expensive, starting at $1,299 in the US and £1,279 in the UK, amounting to $100 and £80 price increases, respectively, over the Pixel 10 Pro XL.

I was expecting worse. But RAM is another matter: All Pixel 11 Pro models start with 12GB of memory at their lowest storage tiers, compared to the Pixel 10 Pro and 10 Pro XL, which had 16GB. While those UK prices might seem positive, it’s important to keep in mind that the starting RAM has dropped from 16GB to 12GB. If you want more, it’ll cost you. The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL variants with 512GB and 1TB of storage come with 16GB of RAM. My review model, for reference, has 512GB of storage and 16GB of RAM.

Let’s jump into more Gemini features on the Pixel 11 Pro, shall we? Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The phones do have seven years of software and security updates, so they’ll still be good to use until at least 2033, as long as you look after them. Remember that the longer you keep using your phone before upgrading, the more value you squeeze out of it.

The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL are available to preorder and are in stores starting August 20.

Pixel 11 Pro: Refined design with HiLight

As in previous generations, the only difference between the 6.3-inch Pixel 11 Pro and the 6.8-inch 11 Pro XL is the screen size and a slightly bigger battery in the latter. Neither looks significantly different from their predecessors, with a glass-and-metal construction and a pill-shaped camera bar stretching across the back. The glass on the bar now fills the whole “island camera block,” which looks classier as a result, while Corning Gorilla Glass Victus 2 makes them the most durable Pixel phones yet, Google says. That’s great news for clumsy people — a group in which I count myself a proud member.

The HiLight circle glows peacefully when Gemini is activated. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The camera bar gets the Pixel 11 Pro’s most noticeable new hardware feature: a revamped LED flash that Google calls HiLight, and functions as a notification alert. If your phone is face down on your desk, the HiLight circle will light up to tell you of an incoming call or notification — or will glow softly to show that Gemini has been voice-activated and is listening to your commands.

It’s a neat idea, especially as you can customize the colors according to who’s calling (a nice calming blue for your partner and an angry red for your boss, perhaps?), but it’s hardly a cutting-edge feature. We’ve seen notification lights on phones for years — most notably in the dazzling array of LEDs on the backs of Nothing’s phones — and while I’ve found them useful, I prefer keeping my phone screen-up so I can see the notifications for real. If I turn my phone over, it’s because I don’t want to be distracted by incoming notifications.

The phone comes in a variety of new colors, including a nice sage green and a soft pink with gold accents, called Canyon, that I absolutely love. I have a thing for pink gadgets (I turned my orange iPhone 17 Pro pink with chemicals and customized my $8,000 Leica camera with a bright pink wrap) and I these tones are the most beautiful Google has used on its phones. Don’t want the lovely pink? Fine, there’s also a matte black option, but just know I’ll be disappointed in you. Not angry, just disappointed.

Pixel 11 Pro cameras: New color profiles for creative shooters

While it might seem that the camera hardware hasn’t changed since last year (it’s the same trio with the same resolution: wide, ultrawide and telephoto), Google reckons that a lot has been done to improve camera performance. For one, the main camera uses an “all-new” 50-megapixel image sensor to deliver better dynamic range and light tones in a variety of conditions, despite being the same size as the 10 Pro’s 1/1.3-inch sensor. The 48-megapixel telephoto zoom uses a larger sensor, promising a 30% increase in light capture.

Taken with the main camera, I love the warmer tones captured with the Camera Looks. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It looks just as good with the ultrawide camera Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Taken with the 5x telephoto lens, I love how much background bokeh there is here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The 5X telephoto lens now supports the Portrait mode, giving deeper background blur. I think the colors in the ‘Editorial’ look have worked well here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I’ve taken a ton of photos, including around Paris, and I’m impressed by the Pixel 11 Pro’s results. Images are packed with detail, with evenly lit exposures that avoid looking overprocessed. To take my shots further, I also used the Pixel’s new Camera Looks tool, which offers a variety of color profiles that give photos a more creative style than the default camera.

There’s a range to choose from — including a high contrast black-and-white mode — and you can customize them further by tweaking the white balance, adding film grain and adjusting the intensity of the shadows. I enjoyed playing around with these, especially the Vanilla look, which lends a warmer, almost filmic feel to the photos.

You can adjust the looks further with tools for contrast, shadows, sharpening and more. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Some looks simply tweak contrast too much for my tastes but I enjoy that it lets you focus on the creative side of photography rather than leaning into AI gimmicks. It reminds me of similar features on Fujifilm’s cameras — including the iconic X100VI — which offers a variety of built-in filmic styles to shoot with. I don’t think Google takes full advantage of this tool yet, but it’s a step in the right direction and a welcome addition for casual shutterbugs who love to simply snap away without worrying about editing later.

While I initially liked the look I chose when I took this photo, I don’t like how blown out the sky is. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But because I also shot the image in raw, I was able to do my own edit in Lightroom, and I was surprised at how much dynamic range the phone really captured. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Those of you who do love editing images can also shoot in DNG raw and tweak those images to your heart’s content later on in apps like Adobe Lightroom or Snapseed. The latter remains a Google-owned product that bafflingly hasn’t been integrated into the Pixel phone experience for reasons I still don’t understand.

There’s plenty of AI in the cameras, too. Notably, the telephoto zoom can go up to 120x magnification for snaps of distant objects. Anything above 30x digital zoom uses generative AI to artificially recreate your image based on an assessment of the camera’s view. If you shoot your images in JPEG and raw to compare, you can see the wild difference between the pixellated photo of garbled details your camera actually captured, versus the crisp AI-generated version the phone created.

On the left is the raw file from the 120x zoom. It’s basically just a collection of pixels. On the right is the generative AI’s interpretation. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

To be fair, it actually fabricates details well. I took a photo of the French flag flying above a building, and it’s honestly wild that the phone could create a usable image from something impossibly far away. On the other hand, I personally don’t want generative AI anywhere near my photos. As a professional photographer myself, I want to know that what I captured was really there, not approximated by algorithms and machine learning models. I’m impressed at what this tech can do, but morally opposed to using it myself.

I feel better about Google’s other new AI tool, called Magic Capture. This essentially shoots a short video clip and then uses AI to select the best still frames from it for you. It’s aimed at parents taking photos of their kids messing around, and indeed, I used it to snag some cool shots of a young skateboarder hitting a ramp in the heart of Paris. The shots it selected were indeed the best from the set.

Magic Capture really nailed the decisive moment here. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I don’t mind this, as it’s not using generative AI to create something that wasn’t there; it’s simply picking the best frames based on factors like which image is sharper, whether the whole person is in the frame, if the subject has their eyes open, and so on.

There are also new tools aimed at content creators, including an autocue mode that puts your script on-screen just below the front-facing camera, as well as the capability to group your videos into project folders for better organization. How helpful these tools really are for the creator community remains to be seen.

Google arguably could have done a lot more with its cameras. It could have used a larger main image sensor and employed bleeding-edge LOFIC technology, as seen on Xiaomi’s and Leica’s Leitzphone, which helps protect image highlights. The Leitzphone costs far more than the Pixel, so I have to conclude that Google has found a solid balance of performance versus price. Do better camera phones exist? Yes. Will you pay more to get them? Also yes.

Pixel 11 Pro: Android 17 and AI additions

The phone launches with the latest Android 17, and as it’s a Google phone, there’s no additional manufacturer skin on top (like Samsung’s OneUI). You get a neat, fuss-free experience. It’s why Pixels are among my favorite Android phones for everyday use, and the 11 Pro is just as pleasant to use as its predecessors.

There are some new AI tools thrown in, too, including deeper functionality for Gemini Intelligence to surface relevant information automatically as you go about your day (such as bringing up flight info when messaging your friend about your travel plans). Circle to Search also works in the camera to find info on whatever you’re looking at. Yes, it’s mostly designed as a “where can I buy this?” shopping tool, but it also supports live translation and search. For example, if you circled a menu item in Japanese, it could not only translate that to English but also provide more information about the dish itself.

It correctly identified my cat, but AI overview failed to point out how lovely and beautiful and soft he is. I’m appalled. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Speaking of translation, the phone can also translate and provide real-time dubbing for certain videos and apps. My colleague, CNET senior technology reporter Abrar Al-Heeti, got to test the Pixel 11 Pro’s translation/dubbing feature as well as one that translates American Sign Language, and she was floored.

In my own testing, I set the feature to translate from German to English and settled in to watch a cake recipe on YouTube in German. The results were… weird. The speech came back in sporadic chunks, with slightly different tones of voice and some inaccurate words, making the video difficult to follow. I thought I’d give it an easier challenge with a “German for beginners” video, but it had the same problems and was basically unwatchable. It’s a nice idea in theory, yet in my early testing, it’s not exactly breaking down the language barrier for me.

Pixel 11 Pro: Battery life and charging

Google has equipped the 11 Pro with a 4,850-mAh battery, which the company reckons will last for over 30 hours of use. And maybe it can, but it’d have to be through a day of light use, as our own battery test results didn’t exactly impress. After one hour of streaming a 4K YouTube video at max screen brightness, the battery had dropped from full to 95% remaining.

Battery life could definitely be better, but it’s not awful by any means. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It was down to 86% after the second hour and had dropped to 78% after hour three. That’s among the worst we’ve seen this year, on par with last year’s Pixel 10 Pro, the Pixel 10A and the, er, Trump phone. After 45 minutes of mixed use, the battery dropped by 11%, which is again one of the worst results we’ve seen on a 2026 phone.

It’s a disappointing effort, but I will caveat this by saying that these are demanding tests that don’t necessarily reflect how you’d use your phone throughout a typical day. With more moderate use, the phone will perform much better and based on my own testing so far, I don’t think you’d struggle to get through most of a full day of use before needing to recharge.

The Pixel 11 Pro supports 30-watt charging, and my 30-minute test took it from 55% to 88%. The Pixel 11 Pro XL has an even faster 45-watt charging rate.

Pixel 11 Pro: Should you buy it?

Google hasn’t overhauled its Pixel phone formula this time around. The 11 Pro models are best seen as iterative upgrades over the previous generation, but given how good the Pixel 10 Pro was — and the fact that price has effectively remained the same — that isn’t such a bad thing.

It’s a great phone. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There are enough tweaks in the design to keep it feeling fresh, especially with that soft pink color. The new Camera Looks tools for photos, the HiLight notifications alert and the new AI tools feel like they could be genuinely useful additions. Throw in the faster charging speeds and the new Pixel 11 Pro range seems to have a lot to offer.

My camera test in Paris showed me that it’s well-equipped for at least casual photographers, and while the battery life definitely isn’t winning any prizes, it’s got enough juice to keep going for most of your working day.

Those of you with the Pixel 10 Pro or even the Pixel 9 Pro before certainly shouldn’t consider upgrading. There simply aren’t enough new features for you to really appreciate. But anyone with a much older Pixel — or any Android phone more than four or so years old — will get a lot from Google’s most advanced flat phone. Especially if you value an easy-to-use, streamlined experience for everyday use over one that tries to offer a million different options.

Tech.title: OpenAI Pauses Training of New AI Models, Citing Cybersecurity Worries
Tech.content:
ChatGPT maker OpenAI announced on Tuesday that it’s pausing the research and development of its newest AI models. This is a big course reversal for the firm, which has maintained that it can mitigate the significant cybersecurity risks posed by new AI models.

“As models become more capable, the risks associated with developing and testing them internally also grow,” the company wrote in a blog post. It added that its upcoming model, named Astra, may meet its “critical cybersecurity capabilities” threshold, a red flag in its internal benchmarking system. All this follows an incident last month when some AI agents, or bots, escaped a training environment and hacked HuggingFace, a popular AI platform.

Cybersecurity has long been an issue for companies in the age of AI, but three separate incidents of AI agents autonomously hacking websites have raised serious concerns about AI companies’ ability to control the tech they created. Anthropic and Meta, whose agents were responsible for other incidents, have responded with similar promises to improve cybersecurity guardrails. OpenAI says it is strengthening its guardrails in its testing environments, including beefing up its monitoring and alert systems.

The pause makes sense — if you can’t control the tech you already have, don’t keep making more. But the move raises other questions about OpenAI’s operations in what is an ever-changing, financially consequential industry.

Realigning amid financial woes

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told TIME that the pause has allowed the company to reallocate two key resources: researchers and compute. While more OpenAI employees focus on making AI obey humans (a concept called AI alignment), the computer power that was previously being used to train new models can be shifted to other services, like maintaining existing models.

Researching and training new AI models is a compute-intensive process. It’s why so many tech companies want to build new data centers, to give them the computing firepower they need, despite widespread backlash. OpenAI says in its blog post: “Our current estimates put monitoring overhead at roughly 20% of the inference compute being monitored,” meaning that monitoring AI models during the training process accounts for a significant portion of OpenAI’s compute.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment on its plans.

The adjustment also raises questions around OpenAI’s financial viability. AI companies have yet to turn a significant profit; they are burning through billions of investors’ dollars, with compute eating up the lion’s share of their bills. OpenAI’s operating losses are now at a whopping $12.3 billion, growing by $3 billion from last quarter, the Wall Street Journal reports. Anthropic, which makes Claude, is now reportedly bringing in more revenue than OpenAI. Also not helping are the recent departures of the company’s chief revenue officer and former chief operating officer, Denise Dresser and Brad Lightcap, respectively.

In other words, it’s possible that OpenAI has decided to pause the training of new AI models because it can simply no longer afford to keep doing so.

This matters a lot as OpenAI and Anthropic chase what could be record-breaking initial public offerings, which makes them into public companies that anyone can invest in. The AI leaders have to prove to Wall Street, and all of us, that their companies are safe, useful and ultimately economically viable. Serious cybersecurity concerns, in addition to threatening our actual security, cast doubt on the industry’s long-term viability.

Tech.title: Video Found in MacOS Shows Apple’s Rumored Camera-Equipped AirPods in Action
Tech.content:
An uncovered video has supercharged rumors about Apple’s camera-equipped AirPods. MacRumors reported this week that it found a video in the MacOS 26.7 release candidate that shows the AirPods in action.

Here is your first look at AirPods with Cameras in action using Visual Intelligence.



This video file came from macOS 26.7 RC pic.twitter.com/yo7RI4MCeu — Aaron (@aaronp613) August 18, 2026

“With Visual Intelligence, your world becomes savable,” Siri says in the video as a man holds up a book. “See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later.”

MacRumors also reports that these AirPods will warn you if they are covered by your hair, for example.

“To get the most accurate information about things in your environment, make sure AirPods are not covered,” it says.

Bloomberg‘s Mark Gurman reported on Aug. 2 that Apple could release the rumored camera-equipped AirPods later this year. That’s earlier than previous reports of a 2027 launch.

That prediction was based on code found in the iOS 27 beta releases, which are early test versions of the software, that reference a device called B790. This device is reportedly a version of another camera-equipped AirPods device code-named B798, and B790 is supposedly further along in development than its counterpart.

If Apple does release camera-equipped AirPods this year, a September launch would be the most likely scenario. The company has historically used its fall iPhone events to introduce major AirPods updates, including the AirPods 4 in 2024 and AirPods Pro updates in 2025. However, Apple has also announced audio products outside its September events, so a different launch window remains possible.

An Apple representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Bloomberg reported in June that camera-equipped AirPods are meant to be Apple’s first AI-focused wearable product. Rather than capturing photos or videos, the cameras would function as visual sensors, giving Siri more context about what’s happening around the user. The AirPod cameras would analyze images and provide you with context based on what they see.

There are still plenty of unanswered questions about the buds, including how much they will cost. The AirPods 4, Apple’s compact wireless earbuds, start at $129, while the AirPods Max, the company’s over-ear headphones, sell for $549. Depending on how much the camera hardware changes the AirPods design, a new camera-equipped model could end up costing as much as — or even more than — the AirPods Max.

Privacy is another question Apple will likely have to address. Wearable devices with built-in cameras, including Meta’s smart glasses, have drawn criticism over concerns that people could be photographed or recorded without their knowledge or consent. While camera-equipped AirPods would differ from smart glasses, they could face similar scrutiny because they also place cameras on a device that’s worn throughout the day. How Apple plans to address those privacy concerns remains unclear.

For more Apple news, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and everything announced at Apple’s Worldwide Developers Conference in June.

Tech.title: What to Know About Anthropic’s New Claude Watermarking on AI-Generated Text and Files
Tech.content:
If you use Anthropic’s AI chatbot Claude to do your homework, everyone will be able to tell soon. Anthropic said this month that text and files generated by its family of AI models will be watermarked to let consumers know. The change will allow the company to comply with EU regulations governing the transparency of AI use.

The EU’s Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content requires companies that provide and deploy AI systems to inform customers when they are interacting with AI and to include watermarks on AI content. Consumers also must know when they’re exposed to deepfakes and emotion-recognition and biometric-categorization tools. Nearly 200 organizations have agreed to the measures, the European Commission said.

Watermarking — an authentication process that originated in Italy in the 13th century — is entirely different for AI content. The AI system can automatically embed markers in text indicating that the content originated from AI and not a human. Examples could be different spacing between words and numbers, word sequencing and other invisible signals that remain with the text even if the person copies and pastes it across different platforms. Readers can’t see these markers, but computer systems can.

In its announcement, Anthropic said Claude models launched on or after Aug. 2 would include watermarking. That includes content created by Claude through the API, Claude, Claude Code, Claude Cowork and Claude Tag. Watermarking will apply to all Claude-generated content wherever the AI system is offered, not just in the EU.

Anthropic said it would “soon” share details about how customers can check whether text was generated by AI.

AI transparency is a growing trend. Substack partnered with Pangram to let readers know how much, if any, a post was generated by AI. Suno recently announced changes to help listeners know if a song was created by AI. If LinkedIn customers suspect AI slop, they can let LinkedIn know. Spotify’s new feature, AI Persona, allows listeners and creators to know which music was created with AI.

How text will be watermarked

To boil down an otherwise complicated process, Anthropic said that text generated by Claude models will be detectable because of how the words are chosen. If there is enough text, the AI detection tool will be able to spot a pattern that only Claude models would use to generate the text.

Anthropic said that text watermarking would not lessen the quality of the content and that readers will not be able to tell the difference between watermarked text and non-watermarked text, without using the AI detection tool.

“In internal testing, we’ve seen no impact of watermarking on the content, level of creativity or readability of Claude’s text,” the company said.

Anthropic said its tool is based on the SynthID system that Google is using to detect AI in text, images, video and audio. How SynthID detects AI in text content is described in a Nature paper published in 2024.

The watermarks Claude adds to text will remain, even if the text is copied and pasted from text editors such as Windows Notepad or MacOS’s TextEdit. The marks also might not be eliminated through human editing, either.

“Watermarking will be applied at the model level, which means it will be present no matter which Claude product or surface the text comes from,” the company said.



How images will be watermarked

Anthropic said Claude will attach cryptographically signed notes in the metadata of files such as .png, .jpg or .svg to specify that the files were generated or processed with Claude. This is part of a standard practice, known as C2PA, used in photo-editing software and camera manufacturers to record where an image came from, Anthropic said.

If someone tries to tamper with it — for example, trying to hide that it was generated by AI — the cryptographic signature will break and thus will show the reader that it was tampered with.

It’s not foolproof

Anthropic included a caveat in its announcement. The presence of watermarking doesn’t necessarily mean the content or image was created by Claude, nor does the absence of watermarking mean Claude wasn’t involved, either.

For example, let’s say someone wants to repurpose an essay from another writer. They punch the essay into Claude and ask the AI to reword it. The output will have watermarking, but the content’s facts and details came from a writer, not AI. People often use Claude for proofreading, translating and summarizing, the company said.

Someone might also take content from Claude and edit it and combine it with other text. Even if only a small portion of the final draft is from Claude, there could be a watermark, perhaps undermining the legitimacy of the document for the reader.

“Light editing probably won’t remove the watermark completely,” Anthropic said. “A complete rewrite where every word is replaced will.”



Anthropic said content generated or processed by Claude might not have a watermark, for various reasons. It could be that the amount of AI-generated content is too small, or perhaps the content has been “heavily edited, paraphrased, translated or mixed into other writing.”

It’s also possible that a Claude-generated image doesn’t have a watermark, either. For example, if someone takes a screenshot of the image and re-saves it as a different file, it won’t have the metadata.

“A watermark can only determine that Claude was likely involved with the content at some point,” the company said. “It cannot distinguish ‘Claude wrote this’ from ‘Claude heavily edited this,'” the company said.

Although Anthropic is trying to comply with EU rules, AI detection has been significantly less than reliable, according to some reports. For example, content from non-native English speakers is often falsely flagged as AI-generated.

Anthropic said Claude’s watermarking process will not reveal any information about the person using a Claude model, their organization or chats with Claude.

Swift backlash

Many Claude customers weren’t pleased with Anthropic’s announcement. Some people canceled their paid subscriptions, according to Business Insider, and some derided the decision with postings on X.

Some consumers feared that some pieces of content, even with little or insignificant Claude-generated text, would be flagged as coming from AI and become a sort of “scarlet letter” that dooms that content to illegitimacy.

Alon Yamin, CEO of content integrity platform Copyleaks, said in a statement that AI watermarking creates too much risk of false positives and doesn’t let the reader know how much text was truly generated by AI.

“Watermarks are binary,” Yamin wrote. “If someone writes a highly original piece but uses an AI tool just to polish the grammar or structure, the watermark will flag the entire document as 100% AI. This penalizes the modern workflow and completely ignores the value of original human thought.”

Yamin pointed out that several websites — claudewatermark.com, claudewatermarks.com and StealthGPT — were already advertising how to remove Claude watermarks.

Tech.title: The Verdict Is In: CNET Readers Trust These Mobile Carriers More Than the Major Networks
Tech.content:
Between the latest news of inconvenient network outages and rising smartphone costs due to a RAM shortage caused by the AI boom, mobile carriers are vying for your money and business. So which one do your fellow readers recommend?

CNET’s People’s Picks is a community awards program that surveys our readers to get their opinions on the tech gadgets and services they use and love the most, like internet service providers, headphones and TVs. The latest People’s Picks awards zoom in on what readers think about their mobile carriers — that includes everything from price to signal reliability and even data.

The results are surprising. We hear a lot about major network carriers with lots of perks, data and infrastructure. However, our readers’ opinions indicate that mobile virtual network operators have more to offer than cellphone plans from the big three carriers, AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon.

CNET’s People’s Picks: Mobile carriers’ overall satisfaction rating

Overall winner: Mint Mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET

CNET readers chose Mint Mobile as CNET’s People’s Picks overall mobile carrier winner. It has a strong overall satisfaction average rating of 4.68 out of 5.

“Customer satisfaction in general is a fuzzy metric, and Mint Mobile has done an excellent job of reinforcing to its customers that they’ve made the right choice,” said Jeff Carlson, CNET senior editor. “I chalk a lot of that up to its marketing, led by actor and former part-owner Ryan Reynolds, which elevates Mint in a crowded market. But Mint remains affordable and reliable, which solidifies its customers’ choice.”

Value for money

Mint Mobile beats out other MVNOs and major network carriers, giving you the best bang for your buck. It offers flexibility without costing a fortune.

Mint Mobile offers several phone plans depending on your term and data needs. It offers three, six and 12-month plans starting at $15 per month for some plans, but an upfront payment is required. Mint Mobile also offers family plans that let you choose the data amount for each included line at one set price. You’ll also have the option to use your existing phone or buy one through Mint Mobile.

“The position of Mint Mobile and the other MVNOs on this list really shows how much people value simplicity in pricing and features,” said Carlson. “Yes, Mint requires up-front payment to get the best value, but customers can see what that is. They can budget a set amount for the next six months, pay it, and then not worry about fluctuations during that time.”

Carlson also noted that Mint Mobile isn’t trying to load up its plans with features to justify higher costs. It has core features such as 5G coverage and high-speed data, which is what most people are looking for.

Comparatively, major networks struggle in this category. For comparison, Verizon and AT&T are 2.98 and 3.05, respectively. It’s also worth noting that readers are happy with Mint Mobile’s pricing — 90% say their bill has remained consistent over the past year, and 5% say it has decreased.

Cellular data connection

Usually, if your carrier’s cellular data connection isn’t reliable enough, you’ll go looking for a Wi-Fi network. Most CNET readers with Mint Mobile service (70%) give the mobile carrier high ratings for how well they’re able to rely on Mint Mobile’s cellular data without connecting to a Wi-Fi network.

Over half (59%) of CNET readers with Mint Mobile service rarely have that problem, and for some, not at all. Eleven percent of CNET readers with Mint Mobile service say they leave Wi-Fi off entirely because their cellular data is faster.

Carlson said it is surprising that MVNOs, including Mint Mobile, win against major network categories for cellular data connection, but there are many reasons people connect to Wi-Fi instead of relying on their mobile carrier — like downloading files quickly or watching YouTube videos.

Runner-up: Consumer Cellular

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Consumer Cellular wins a few categories in CNET’s People’s Picks, including signal reliability, customer service and the mobile carrier that’s least likely to drop calls. It also comes close to winning in two categories: cellular data connection and unlimited data.

Signal reliability

Consumer Cellular wins in signal reliability, with the highest average rating of 4.60 out of 5. US Mobile and Mint Mobile trail closely behind, with averages of 4.56 and 4.53, respectively.

But that’s not the whole story, because all the MVNOs use the big carriers’ infrastructure – they don’t have their own cell towers. Most are tied to a single carrier, like Mint Mobile, which uses T-Mobile’s network. On its website, Consumer Cellular says, “When you 

If you’re curious about coverage, Consumer Cellular has an interactive map that shows which areas are covered based on your zip code or address. Most areas have 5G or 4G LTE, and Wi-Fi calling is also available.

Least likely to drop calls

If you’re constantly dealing with dropped calls, CNET readers with Consumer Cellular give it high marks compared to other mobile carriers. Most (70%) of Consumer Cellular readers say they rarely or never lose service. Close to 23% experience call drops in rural areas and on road trips — the lowest among mobile carriers. Even fewer experience call drops inside their home. Carlson said that could be because CNET readers with the service are getting the best coverage in their area, which is also why readers have high signal reliability ratings.

Customer service

Consumer Cellular also wins in customer service, with an average rating of 4.72 out of 5, compared to US Mobile’s 4.34. There are two ways to reach Consumer Cellular for assistance: call (888) 345-5509 or use its online chat feature. Consumer Cellular also receives high rankings from CNET readers for its service and fast resolution times. Most say they were able to resolve issues with Consumer Cellular over the phone in fewer than 30 minutes.

T-Mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Most popular

T-Mobile is the most popular mobile carrier among CNET readers (29%), followed by Verizon (18%). T-Mobile has several phone plans to choose from, but CNET editors recommend the T-Mobile Essentials Saver 2.0, which starts at $55 per month if you need only one line; the T-Mobile Experience More 2.0 may be ideal if you’re looking to save money from other perks. We like that T-Mobile’s autopay discount qualifies you for a lower price when you use an eligible payment method.

T-Mobile has a few features that make it worth considering if you’re looking for a new mobile carrier. CNET editors say it has a robust 5G network and some money-saving perks, like plan savings with a new line and T-Mobile Tuesdays — the carrier’s weekly appreciation program. And T-Mobile recently unveiled a three-year phone installment plan to make new phones more affordable.

“One advantage T-Mobile has right now is its visibility – customers respond to T-Mobile Tuesdays, its sponsorship of things like a large section of the Formula One Las Vegas Grand Prix and its broad marketing,” said Carlson. “It feels like a place to be, and its mobile plans are well-received. They aren’t the cheapest, but their position here makes me think people are responding to T-Mobile giving them plenty of features for what they’re paying for.”

US Mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Data speeds

US Mobile earns a nearly perfect average of 4.65 out of 5 from CNET readers who use it, making it the highest among popular mobile carriers. MVNO competitors Mint Mobile and Consumer Cellular come close to winning this category, with average ratings of 4.63 and 4.48, respectively.

Several factors go into determining data speeds. If you own a phone that’s capable of the highest 5G speeds and you’re in an area that can deliver them, you’ll see the best performance. That could be a device such as an iPhone 17 connected within a pocket of T-Mobile’s 5G Ultra Capacity (its name for 5G millimeter-wave spectrum) signal, which can download files much faster or deliver movies at 4K resolution smoothly.

Like Consumer Cellular, US Mobile isn’t tied to a specific carrier for its infrastructure. It’s able to use the best network available in your area – but US Mobile lets you choose which one to use. For example, if you travel to a location with a stronger network (like an extended vacation or for work), you can switch to that network for a fee. It uses its own names for the networks: Dark Star is AT&T, Light Speed is T-Mobile, and Warp is Verizon.

US Mobile’s ability to leverage the best network in your area likely gives it the edge in this category. US Mobile’s Broadband Facts break down each plan’s data speeds. All three Unlimited plans (Flex, Starter and Premium) have unlimited data, but your download and upload speed will depend on which cellular network you’re connected to. US Mobile’s Dark Star has download speeds up to 389 Mbps, while the Light Speed and Warp networks have download speeds up to 357 Mbps and 702 Mbps, respectively. Upload speeds are much different. Dark Star, Light Speed and Warp have upload speeds up to 33, 32 and 702 Mbps.

Fair pricing

Fair pricing eliminates month-to-month surprises — giving you predictability and peace of mind when paying your bill. That’s why US Mobile also wins for CNET’s Fair Pricing category of People’s Picks, with 98% of US Mobile users saying their bill “remained perfectly consistent” or “actually went down” in the last 12 months. While other mobile carriers reported base monthly prices increasing, US Mobile didn’t report any new fees, perks going away or changes.

US Mobile’s plans start at $25 per month for the Unlimited Starter plan, including taxes and fees, whereas the Unlimited Flex is an annual plan that starts at $17.50 per month, including taxes and fees.

Visible by Verizon

J. Hazelwood/CNET

For unlimited data

Visible by Verizon gets the highest marks from readers who use the mobile service for its no-data-throttling policy. CNET found that 73.3% of Visible by Verizon users say their data is truly unlimited and has never been throttled, whereas 72.9% of readers with Consumer Cellular service say the same. Comparatively, 61% of Verizon postpaid users say the same. You may notice slower internet speeds if you reach your monthly high-speed data limit.

Visible by Verizon offers unlimited data across all three plans, with premium (high-speed) data included on Visible Plus and Visible Plus Pro. Customers don’t need to worry about hitting a cap and seeing their speed dropped (though Visible and all carriers reserve the right to slow data if needed). While the Visible plan is listed as the most popular, the Visible Plus and Visible Plus Pro plans also offer unlimited data when roaming in Mexico and Canada, but speeds drop after 2GB per day of use.

Google Fi Wireless

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Roaming features

Most (63%) of readers who have Google Fi Wireless are satisfied with its roaming features, the highest among mobile carriers. There are no reports of dissatisfaction or frustration from CNET readers.

CNET’s director of content, Patrick Holland, says Google Fi is one of Google’s best-kept secrets. “Its competitive pricing, international roaming (at no extra charge) and flexible data plans are some of the main reasons that it’s been my carrier of choice for most of the past decade,” said Holland.

Google Fi Wireless has a few standout roaming features among other competitors. International service is available with Google Fi Wireless’ Unlimited Premium and Unlimited Standard plans. The Unlimited Premium plan includes free texts and calls at 20 cents per minute. Some calls to other countries (over 50) are free. Google Fi Wireless also offers 50GB of high-speed data to over 200 destinations, with 256kbps thereafter. Many other providers offer minimal international features.

Did you agree with these findings? CNET’s People’s Picks is community-driven and helps us spread the word about the tech and services you love. Take our ongoing phones survey to tell us what you love about yours.

Methodology

CNET commissioned Alchemer to conduct the People’s Picks survey to compile data. The survey was carried out online, and all figures are from Alchemer. The total sample comprised 1,198 adults. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus). Fieldwork was undertaken July 1 to July 26, 2026.

Tech.title: New Google Ad Shows a Mysterious Wearable. Is It the Next Fitbit?
Tech.content:
Earlier this month, Google announced multiple new devices at its Made by Google event, including Pixel 11 phones and the Pixel Watch 5. Back in May, the company also released its screenless Fitbit Air health tracker.

But we still haven’t heard anything about the new mystery product that’s appeared in recent Google ads.

A Reddit thread posted on Saturday revealed a Google Pixel ad on YouTube featuring the new Pixel 11 series, the Pixel Watch 5 and an unknown wearable that looks like a cross between the Fitbit Charge 6 and the Watch 5, standing out with its oblong screen with rounded edges in fog white. Sponsored by Google Australia, the ad’s caption reads: “The ultimate power trio for your wrist, ears and hands. Preorder Pixel devices now.”

Some speculate that the product may be the Fitbit Charge 7 or a rebranded Pixel Watch series. Or maybe it’s an entirely new fitness tracker?

A Google representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

That wasn’t the only Google Australia ad featuring the surprise device. The mystery wearable appears in another ad displaying the Pixel 11 phones, Watch 5, Pixel Buds Pro 2, Pixelsnap phone cases and Watch loop bands in the new olive green color.

Comment

byu/Imacharmer3141 from discussion

inpixel_phones

Real or fake?

Some Reddit commenters wondered whether this mystery product was a mistake caused by an AI hallucination — an error caused by generative artificial intelligence.

But this also wouldn’t be the first time Google sneaked an unreleased product into its promotional content. Back in March, two months before its release, the Fitbit Air was spotted in a paid partnership video with NBA star Steph Curry, who is also a Google performance adviser.

It would seem that Google is releasing a new wearable, potentially as part of its Pixel line, in both fog and olive colors. If the time between these ad leaks and the device’s release follows the same pattern as the Fitbit Air’s appearance in Curry’s video, we should know more in the coming weeks.
